question: Which prophet built the ark by Allah's command?
explanation: Allah commanded Nuh to build the ark to save the believers from the flood.
detail: In Surah Hud, Nuh is told that no more of his people will believe (11:36), and then receives the order: "And build the ship under Our eyes and Our inspiration, and do not address Me concerning those who have wronged; indeed, they are to be drowned" (11:37). As he built it, the chiefs of his people passed by and mocked him, and he answered that they would be mocked in turn (11:38). A Muslim learns from Nuh to keep at what Allah has commanded even while others laugh.

question: Which prophet was thrown into a fire that Allah made cool and safe for him?
explanation: Allah commanded the fire to be cool and safe for Ibrahim.
detail: In Surah Al-Anbiya, Ibrahim has broken his people's idols and shown them that idols cannot even speak (21:58-65). Their answer is, "Burn him and support your gods" (21:68). Then Allah speaks: "O fire, be coolness and safety upon Ibrahim" (21:69), and the next verse adds, "They intended for him harm, but We made them the greatest losers" (21:70). A Muslim learns that the fire obeys its Creator, and that whoever stands for Allah's oneness is in His care.

question: Which prophet was swallowed by a huge fish?
explanation: Yunus was swallowed by the fish after leaving his people in anger; Allah forgave him.
detail: Surah As-Saffat tells that Yunus fled to the laden ship, drew lots and lost (37:140-141); "then the fish swallowed him while he was blameworthy" (37:142). It adds: "Had he not been of those who glorify Allah, he would have remained in its belly until the Day they are resurrected" (37:143-144). Allah cast him onto the bare shore, ill, grew a gourd plant over him, and sent him back to his people, who believed (37:145-148). A Muslim learns that glorifying Allah in the darkest place is what brings the way out.

question: Which prophet interpreted the king's dream of seven fat cows and seven lean cows?
explanation: Yusuf interpreted the king's dream, foretelling seven years of abundance followed by seven years of famine.
detail: Surah Yusuf records the king's words: "I have seen seven fat cows being eaten by seven lean ones, and seven green ears of grain and others dry" (12:43). His courtiers called it a jumble of dreams, but the cupbearer remembered Yusuf, still in prison, and went to ask him (12:44-46). Yusuf explained: seven years of sowing, seven hard years that would eat what was stored, then a year of rain (12:47-49). A Muslim learns that knowledge given by Allah is used to help people, even those who wronged us.

question: Which prophet, according to the Quran, was spoken to directly by Allah?
explanation: The Quran states that Allah spoke to Musa directly.
detail: Surah An-Nisa singles out one messenger: "And messengers We have told you about before, and messengers We have not told you about; and Allah spoke to Musa directly" (4:164). Surah Ta-Ha shows the scene in the sacred valley of Tuwa: "Indeed, I am your Lord, so remove your sandals" (20:12), and, "Indeed, I am Allah; there is no god but Me, so worship Me and establish prayer for My remembrance" (20:14). A Muslim learns that Allah honoured Musa with His speech, and that its first message was worship and prayer.

question: Which prophet could understand the speech of birds?
explanation: Allah taught Sulaiman the speech of birds.
detail: The verse opens the story of Sulaiman in Surah An-Naml: "And Sulaiman inherited Dawud. He said, 'O people, we have been taught the speech of birds, and we have been given from all things. Indeed, this is clear bounty'" (27:16). The surah then shows him hearing an ant warn its colony and thanking Allah for His favour (27:18-19), and questioning the hoopoe that brought news of Saba (27:20-22). A Muslim learns that Sulaiman called his gift a bounty from Allah, and met it with thanks rather than pride.

question: Which prophet was given the scripture called the Zabur (Psalms)?
explanation: The Quran mentions that the Zabur was given to Dawud.
detail: The verse belongs to Surah Al-Isra: "And your Lord is most knowing of whoever is in the heavens and the earth. And We have made some of the prophets exceed others, and to Dawud We gave the Zabur" (17:55). Surah An-Nisa repeats it (4:163), and Surah Al-Anbiya quotes from it: "We have written in the Zabur, after the reminder, that the earth will be inherited by My righteous servants" (21:105). A Muslim believes in the Zabur as a Book of Allah given to a prophet who was also a king.

question: Which prophet was born without a father, by Allah's word 'Be, and it is'?
explanation: The Quran describes Isa's miraculous birth without a father, by Allah's word alone.
detail: In Surah Al 'Imran the angels tell Maryam of a son, the Messiah 'Isa (3:45). She asks how she can have a child when no man has touched her, and the answer comes: "Such is Allah; He creates what He wills. When He decrees a matter, He only says to it, 'Be,' and it is" (3:47). Later the surah compares him to Adam, created from dust by the same word, "Be" (3:59). A Muslim learns that 'Isa's birth was a sign of Allah's power, not a sign of divinity.

question: Which chapter (surah) of the Quran is named after a prophet's mother?
explanation: Surah 19, Maryam, is named after the mother of the prophet Isa.
detail: The surah takes its name from the verse that opens her story: "And mention in the Book Maryam, when she withdrew from her family to a place toward the east" (19:16). The angel came to her as a man and said, "I am only the messenger of your Lord to give you a pure boy" (19:19); when she asked how, he answered that her Lord had said it was easy for Him (19:21). A Muslim honours Maryam as a woman the Qur'an names and praises.

question: Which prophet was tested with severe illness and is praised for his patience?
explanation: Ayyub remained patient through a very difficult trial, and Allah rewarded him.
detail: Surah Al-Anbiya records his prayer: "And Ayyub, when he called to his Lord, 'Indeed, adversity has touched me, and You are the most merciful of the merciful.' So We responded to him and removed what afflicted him" (21:83-84). The verse adds that his family was restored to him, as mercy from Allah (21:84). Surah Sad gives the verdict: "We found him patient, an excellent servant; he was ever turning back" (38:44). A Muslim learns that patience is not silence before Allah; Ayyub complained to Him alone, and was healed.

question: Whom did Allah command the angels to prostrate to, as a sign of honor?
explanation: Allah commanded the angels to prostrate to Adam as a mark of honor, not worship.
detail: The verse follows Allah's announcement to the angels of a successor on the earth, and the names that Adam knew and they did not (2:30-33). Then: "And when We said to the angels, 'Prostrate before Adam,' so they prostrated, except Iblis. He refused and was arrogant and became of the disbelievers" (2:34). Surah Al-A'raf records his excuse: "I am better than him; You created me from fire and created him from clay" (7:12). A Muslim learns that Adam was honoured by Allah's command, and that arrogance was the first sin.

question: Which prophet is called 'Khalilullah', the close friend of Allah?
explanation: The Quran describes Ibrahim as the close friend (khalil) of Allah.
detail: The title closes a verse of Surah An-Nisa: "And who is better in religion than one who submits himself to Allah, does good, and follows the way of Ibrahim, inclining toward truth? And Allah took Ibrahim as a close friend" (4:125). Surah An-Nahl describes the friend: "Ibrahim was a nation in himself, devoutly obedient to Allah, inclining toward truth, and he was not of the polytheists" (16:120). A Muslim learns that closeness to Allah is reached by submission and doing good, the two things the verse names before the friendship.

question: Which prophet was thrown into a well by his brothers?
explanation: Yusuf's brothers threw him into a well out of jealousy.
detail: Surah Yusuf tells that his brothers, jealous of their father's love for him, spoke of killing him, until one proposed the well so that a caravan would pick him up (12:8-10). "So when they took him and agreed to put him into the bottom of the well, We inspired to him: you will surely tell them of this deed of theirs while they do not perceive" (12:15). A Muslim learns that Allah was with Yusuf in the well, and kept the promise made there.

question: Whose people were destroyed by a flood after rejecting him?
explanation: Nuh's people were engulfed by the flood after persistently rejecting his message.
detail: Surah Hud tells the flood from the ark's building (11:37) to its end. When the oven gushed, Nuh loaded two of every kind and those who believed, "and none had believed with him except a few" (11:40). The ark sailed through waves like mountains; Nuh's son refused to board, chose a mountain and drowned (11:42-43). Then: "O earth, swallow your water, and O sky, withhold", and the ark settled on al-Judiyy (11:44). A Muslim learns that safety came from obeying Allah, not from family ties or high ground.

question: Which prophet saw the sea part to save his people from Pharaoh?
explanation: Allah commanded Musa to strike the sea, and it parted so the believers could pass.
detail: Surah Ash-Shu'ara tells that Pharaoh's army pursued until the two groups saw each other, and Musa's companions cried, "We are surely overtaken" (26:61). He answered, "No! Indeed, with me is my Lord; He will guide me" (26:62). "Then We inspired to Musa: strike the sea with your staff, and it parted, and each part was like a great towering mountain" (26:63). Allah saved Musa and those with him (26:65). A Muslim learns from Musa's answer that certainty in Allah stands even with the sea ahead and the enemy behind.

question: Which prophet, alongside his father Dawud, judged the case of a field grazed by sheep?
explanation: The Quran relates that Sulaiman and Dawud judged this case, and Allah granted Sulaiman the understanding of it.
detail: Surah Al-Anbiya tells the case: "And Dawud and Sulaiman, when they judged concerning the field, when the sheep of a people had strayed into it at night, and We were witness to their judgement. And We gave understanding of it to Sulaiman, and to each We gave judgement and knowledge" (21:78-79). The same verse adds that the mountains and the birds glorified Allah with Dawud (21:79). A Muslim learns that both prophets were honoured, and that sound judgement is a gift from Allah, not a matter of age.

question: Whose mother was instructed to place her baby into a river?
explanation: Allah inspired Musa's mother to place him in a chest on the river to protect him.
detail: Surah Ta-Ha recalls: "When We inspired to your mother what We inspired: cast him into the chest and cast it into the river, and the river will throw it onto the bank; there an enemy of Mine and an enemy of his will take him" (20:38-39). Allah adds, "I bestowed upon you love from Me" (20:39); he was returned to his mother so that her eye would be comforted (20:40). A Muslim learns that Allah's plan ran through Pharaoh's house, and that a mother's obedience was rewarded.

question: Whose she-camel was a sign given to his people, the Thamud?
explanation: Allah sent a she-camel as a sign to the people of Thamud through the prophet Salih.
detail: In Surah Al-A'raf, Salih calls Thamud to worship Allah alone and shows them the sign: "This is the she-camel of Allah, a sign for you. So leave her to eat in Allah's land and do not touch her with harm, lest a painful punishment seize you" (7:73). They hamstrung her and defied him to bring what he threatened (7:77), and the earthquake seized them in their homes (7:78). A Muslim learns that a sign from Allah is to be respected, and that mocking it brings its own end.

question: In which city was the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ born?
explanation: The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ was born in Makkah, in the Hijaz.
detail: The Qur'an names the city where the Prophet ﷺ was born: it speaks of "the valley of Makkah" (48:24) and calls it "the Mother of Cities" (6:92). Surah Al-Balad swears by it: "I swear by this city" (90:1). Makkah is the town of the Ka'ba, the House that Ibrahim and Isma'il raised (2:127), and the Prophet ﷺ was born there among Quraysh, the tribe that kept it. A Muslim learns that the last prophet was born beside the first House built for the worship of Allah.

question: What is the year of the Prophet's ﷺ birth called, marked by the Event of the Elephant?
explanation: The Event of the Elephant, in which Allah protected the Kaaba, is recounted in Surah Al-Fil.
detail: Surah Al-Fil asks the Prophet ﷺ: "Have you not seen how your Lord dealt with the companions of the elephant? He sent against them birds in flocks, striking them with stones of baked clay, and made them like straw eaten up" (105:1-5). The surah that follows draws the lesson for Makkah: "Let them worship the Lord of this House, who has fed them against hunger and made them safe from fear" (106:3-4). A Muslim learns that his birth year was marked by Allah's protection of His House.

question: What was the name of the Prophet's ﷺ first wife?
explanation: Khadijah bint Khuwaylid was the Prophet's ﷺ first wife and the first person to believe in his message.
detail: Khadijah was a merchant of Makkah whose goods the Prophet ﷺ had carried in trade before she proposed marriage to him. When he came down from the cave of Hira trembling after the first revelation, he said to her, "Cover me", and she answered that Allah would never disgrace him, because he kept the ties of kinship, bore people's burdens, gave to the poor and honoured the guest. A Muslim learns that the first believer was a wife who knew the character of the man she believed in.

question: In which cave did the Prophet ﷺ receive the first revelation?
explanation: The first revelation took place in the Cave of Hira, on Jabal an-Nur near Makkah.
detail: Before his mission, the Prophet ﷺ used to withdraw to the cave of Hira for nights of worship. There the angel came and said, "Read", and he answered that he could not read; the angel pressed him three times, then recited: "Read in the name of your Lord who created. Read, and your Lord is the most Generous, who taught by the pen, taught man what he did not know" (96:1-5). A Muslim learns that the first word of the revelation was a command to read.

question: Which angel brought revelation to the Prophet ﷺ?
explanation: The Quran explicitly mentions that Jibril brought revelation by Allah's permission.
detail: Surah Al-Baqarah answers those who took Jibril as an enemy: "Say: whoever is an enemy to Jibril, it is he who brought it down upon your heart by permission of Allah, confirming what came before it, and as guidance and good tidings for the believers" (2:97). Surah Ash-Shu'ara calls him "the Trustworthy Spirit", who brought the Qur'an down upon the Prophet's ﷺ heart in clear Arabic (26:193-195). A Muslim learns that the Qur'an came by a trusted messenger from Allah to the heart of the Prophet ﷺ.

question: What is the migration of the Prophet ﷺ and his companions from Makkah to Madinah called?
explanation: Al-Hijrah refers to the historic migration to Madinah, the starting point of the Islamic calendar.
detail: The word hijrah means leaving one's home for another, and the Qur'an names the emigrants from it: "the first forerunners among the Muhajirun and the Ansar" (9:100), those who left and those who took them in. Surah Al-Hashr calls them "the poor emigrants who were expelled from their homes and their properties, seeking bounty from Allah and His approval" (59:8), and praises the people of Madinah who loved whoever emigrated to them (59:9). A Muslim dates the years from the Hijrah because that departure founded the community.

question: To which city did the Prophet ﷺ and Abu Bakr migrate?
explanation: The Prophet ﷺ and Abu Bakr migrated from Makkah to Madinah (then called Yathrib).
detail: The Qur'an uses both names of the city. It quotes the hypocrites at the Trench: "O people of Yathrib, there is no place for you here, so return" (33:13), and elsewhere it speaks of "the people of al-Madinah and the bedouins around them" (9:120). Al-Madinah means "the city": it became the Prophet's ﷺ city, where its people, the Ansar, sheltered and aided those who emigrated (8:72). A Muslim learns that Madinah welcomed the Prophet ﷺ when Makkah drove him out, and holds his grave.

question: The Quran describes a companion as 'the second of two, when they were in the cave' during the Hijrah. Who was it?
explanation: The Quran refers to Abu Bakr, who accompanied the Prophet ﷺ in the Cave of Thawr during the Hijrah.
detail: The verse is in Surah At-Tawbah: "If you do not aid him, Allah has already aided him when those who disbelieved drove him out, the second of two, when they were in the cave, and he said to his companion, 'Do not grieve; indeed Allah is with us'" (9:40). The Qur'an leaves the companion unnamed, but every account of the Hijrah names Abu Bakr, who hid with the Prophet ﷺ while the pursuers searched. A Muslim learns that the calm of the cave came from trust in Allah.

question: Which battle, mentioned in the Quran, saw a small Muslim army defeat a much larger force?
explanation: At Badr, Allah granted victory to a small group of believers over a much larger army.
detail: Surah Al 'Imran reminds the believers: "Allah had already given you victory at Badr while you were few; so fear Allah, that you may be grateful" (3:123). The next verses recall the Prophet ﷺ promising them three thousand angels, and five thousand if they held firm (3:124-125), then: "Allah made it only as good tidings for you; and victory is not except from Allah" (3:126). A Muslim learns that Badr is remembered not for numbers, but for the help that came from Allah to a few who stood firm.

question: What is the largely peaceful return of the Prophet ﷺ and his companions to Makkah called?
explanation: The Conquest of Makkah took place largely peacefully, without widespread bloodshed.
detail: Surah Al-Fath had promised it: "You will surely enter the Sacred Mosque, if Allah wills, in safety, with heads shaved and hair shortened, not fearing" (48:27). Entering Makkah, the Prophet ﷺ rode with his head bowed low in humility, went to the Ka'ba and cast down the idols around it reciting, "Truth has come and falsehood has departed" (17:81), and pardoned the people who had driven him out. A Muslim learns that the greatest victory was met with humility and forgiveness.

question: What is the final sermon delivered by the Prophet ﷺ near the end of his life called?
explanation: The Farewell Sermon (Khutbat al-Wada') was delivered during the Prophet's ﷺ final pilgrimage.
detail: The Farewell Sermon was delivered at 'Arafat during the Prophet's ﷺ only hajj. He told the people that their blood and property were as sacred to one another as that day; he charged them to treat women well and to hold to the Book of Allah. On that day was revealed: "This day I have perfected for you your religion and completed My favour upon you" (5:3). A Muslim learns that the Prophet's ﷺ last teaching was about the rights people owe each other.

question: During which month does the Quran state its revelation began?
explanation: The Quran states that Ramadan is the month in which the Quran was revealed.
detail: The verse belongs to the passage of Surah Al-Baqarah on fasting: "The month of Ramadan, in which the Qur'an was sent down. So whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it" (2:185). Surah Al-Qadr names the night within it: "Indeed, We sent it down in the Night of Decree" (97:1), and Surah Ad-Dukhan calls it "a blessed night" (44:3). A Muslim learns that the fast of Ramadan is tied to the Qur'an: the month of the Book is honoured by the fast.

question: What was the Prophet's ﷺ profession before he received revelation?
explanation: The Prophet ﷺ worked in trade, a well-established fact of his biography.
detail: Before revelation the Prophet ﷺ travelled with trade caravans, carrying the goods of Khadijah to Syria, and his honesty earned him the name al-Amin, the trustworthy. The Qur'an records his opponents' objection, "What is this messenger who eats food and walks in the markets?" (25:7), and answers that every messenger before him ate food and walked in the markets (25:20). A Muslim learns that honest trade was the daily work of the Prophet ﷺ, and that a believer's truthfulness is tested in the marketplace.

question: Which grandfather of the Prophet ﷺ cared for him after his mother's death?
explanation: Abdul Muttalib cared for the young Muhammad ﷺ after the death of his mother Aminah.
detail: The Prophet's ﷺ father, 'Abdullah, died before he was born, and his mother, Aminah, while he was still a small child, so his grandfather 'Abd al-Muttalib took him into his care and kept the boy beside him at his seat by the Ka'ba. When the grandfather died, the care passed to his son Abu Talib. Surah Ad-Duha recalls this time: "Did He not find you an orphan and give you shelter?" (93:6). A Muslim learns that Allah watched over the orphan of Makkah through the hands of his family.

question: Which uncle raised the Prophet ﷺ after his grandfather's death?
explanation: Abu Talib took charge of raising his nephew after Abdul Muttalib's death.
detail: Abu Talib was the brother of the Prophet's ﷺ father, 'Abdullah, and the father of 'Ali. He took his nephew into his household after 'Abd al-Muttalib died, brought him on a trade journey to Syria, and after the revelation began he stood between him and Quraysh. He died in Makkah in the same year as Khadijah. The Qur'an says of those years, "Did He not find you an orphan and give you shelter?" (93:6). A Muslim learns that Allah made a loving uncle the shield of His Messenger.

question: What is the Prophet's ﷺ night journey from Makkah to Jerusalem, mentioned in the Quran, called?
explanation: Surah Al-Isra opens by describing this miraculous night journey.
detail: Surah Al-Isra opens with the journey: "Exalted is He who took His servant by night from the Sacred Mosque to the Farthest Mosque, to show him of Our signs" (17:1). Isra means a journey by night. Surah An-Najm tells of what followed, when the Prophet ﷺ saw the angel again "at the Lote Tree of the utmost boundary" (53:13-14) and "saw of the greatest signs of his Lord" (53:18). A Muslim learns that Makkah and Jerusalem are joined in one night's journey.

question: Which of the Prophet's ﷺ daughters married Ali ibn Abi Talib?
explanation: Fatimah, daughter of the Prophet ﷺ and Khadijah, married Ali ibn Abi Talib — a widely established fact.
detail: Fatimah was a daughter of the Prophet ﷺ and Khadijah, and 'Ali, son of Abu Talib, was his cousin, raised in his own household. Their marriage took place in Madinah, and from it came al-Hasan and al-Husayn, his grandsons. He said of her, in Sahih al-Bukhari, "Fatimah is a part of me; whoever angers her angers me." She outlived him by a few months. A Muslim honours Fatimah as the daughter closest to the Prophet ﷺ, and her home as the one in which his grandsons grew up.

question: Which month marks the start of the Islamic calendar year, referencing the Hijrah?
explanation: The Islamic calendar begins with the month of Muharram, referencing the year of the Hijrah.
detail: Surah At-Tawbah sets the year: "Indeed, the number of months with Allah is twelve months in the register of Allah; of them, four are sacred" (9:36). Muharram, whose name means "the sacred one", is one of those four and the first month; its tenth day, 'Ashura, is a day of fasting. The Muslims counted their years from the Hijrah, so the year begins with Muharram and the era with the migration to Madinah. A Muslim learns to see the calendar as a reminder of the Hijrah.

question: What is the name of the first chapter (surah) of the Quran?
explanation: Al-Fatiha, 'The Opening', is the first chapter of the Quran.
detail: The surah is seven verses. It begins, "In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful. All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds" (1:1-2), and ends with the request, "Guide us to the straight path" (1:6-7). The Qur'an refers to it in Surah Al-Hijr as "seven of the oft-repeated" (15:87), and the Prophet ﷺ called it the Mother of the Qur'an. A Muslim learns Al-Fatiha first of all, because every prayer is built on it: praise, then a plea for guidance.

question: How many chapters (surahs) does the Quran contain?
explanation: The Quran is composed of 114 surahs.
detail: The Qur'an opens with Al-Fatiha and closes with An-Nas, "Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of mankind" (114:1); between them stand 112 more, 114 in all. They are not arranged by order of revelation: the first verses revealed stand in the 96th surah, Al-'Alaq. Every surah begins with "In the name of Allah" except At-Tawbah, the ninth, and the whole is divided into thirty parts for reading in a month. A Muslim learns the count as the frame of the Book he will spend a lifetime reading.

question: What is the longest surah in the Quran?
explanation: Al-Baqarah is the longest surah in the Quran, with 286 verses.
detail: Al-Baqarah, "The Cow", takes its name from the cow that the Children of Israel were told to sacrifice (2:67-71). It holds the longest verse of the Qur'an, on writing down a debt (2:282), and the Throne Verse, "Allah, there is no god but Him" (2:255). It ends with a prayer the believers still recite: "Our Lord, do not burden us with what we have no strength to bear" (2:286). A Muslim learns that the longest surah is a full course in the religion: belief, law and prayer together.

question: What is the shortest surah in the Quran?
explanation: Al-Kawthar, with 3 verses, is the shortest surah in the Quran.
detail: Three verses make up the surah: "Indeed, We have granted you al-Kawthar. So pray to your Lord and sacrifice. Indeed, your enemy is the one cut off" (108:1-3). Al-Kawthar means great abundance: the gift comes first, then the response it asks for, prayer and sacrifice to Allah alone, then the reply to his enemy. A Muslim learns that the shortest surah holds the whole pattern of gratitude: Allah gives, and the servant answers with worship.

question: In which language was the Quran revealed?
explanation: The Quran explicitly states it was revealed in the Arabic language.
detail: Surah Yusuf opens with the verses of the clear Book (12:1) and then states it: "Indeed, We have sent it down as an Arabic Qur'an so that you may understand" (12:2). The Qur'an repeats the point: it came "in a clear Arabic tongue" (26:195), and had it been foreign its hearers would have asked why its verses were not made plain (41:44). A Muslim learns that the words of the Qur'an are Arabic, and reads a translation as its meaning, not as the Qur'an itself.

question: What is the name of the 19th surah, named after the mother of Isa?
explanation: The Quran's 19th surah is named Maryam, after the mother of the prophet Isa.
detail: Surah Maryam opens with five letters, "Kaf, Ha, Ya, 'Ayn, Sad" (19:1), tells of Zakariyya, given the son Yahya (19:2-11), then turns to Maryam: "And mention in the Book Maryam, when she withdrew from her family to a place toward the east" (19:16). Her infant son speaks his first words in the surah: "Indeed, I am the servant of Allah" (19:30). A Muslim learns that the surah named after a mother is a surah about Allah's mercy to those who call on Him.

question: What is a chapter of the Quran called?
explanation: The Quran is divided into chapters called surahs.
detail: The Qur'an uses the word of its own chapters. It challenges its doubters, "then produce a surah like it" (2:23), and introduces Surah An-Nur with, "A surah which We have sent down and made obligatory" (24:1). Each surah bears a name taken from a word or story inside it; the longest has 286 verses and the shortest three. All but one begin with "In the name of Allah." A Muslim learns to find his way in the Book by the names of its surahs.

question: What is a verse of the Quran called?
explanation: Each verse of the Quran is called an ayah, meaning 'sign'.
detail: The word ayah means a sign, and the Qur'an uses it for its verses and for the signs in creation. Surah Yusuf begins, "These are the verses of the clear Book" (12:1), while Surah Al-Baqarah says that in the heavens and the earth, night and day "are signs for a people who use reason" (2:164). Surah Fussilat: "We will show them Our signs in the horizons and within themselves" (41:53). A Muslim learns that reading a verse and looking at the sky are one act: reading the signs of Allah.

question: Which surah is obligatorily recited in every unit (rak'ah) of the prayer?
explanation: Reciting Al-Fatiha is a pillar of the prayer reported in an authentic hadith.
detail: The hadith is narrated by 'Ubadah ibn as-Samit in Sahih al-Bukhari 756: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, "There is no prayer for the one who does not recite the Opening of the Book." The Opening of the Book is Al-Fatiha, the seven verses the Qur'an calls "seven of the oft-repeated" (15:87). It is recited in every rak'ah, before any other surah, and it closes with the prayer for guidance to the straight path (1:6-7). A Muslim learns Al-Fatiha by heart, because no rak'ah stands without it.

question: To whom was the Quran revealed?
explanation: The Quran was revealed to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, through the angel Jibril.
detail: The Qur'an names the one it was sent to: "Muhammad is not the father of any of your men, but the Messenger of Allah and the seal of the prophets" (33:40). It came down upon his heart by the Trustworthy Spirit, in clear Arabic (26:192-195), and in parts, "that you may recite it to the people over a prolonged period" (17:106). A Muslim learns that the Book and the Messenger are received together: the Qur'an is read as it was given to him.

question: How many pillars does Islam have?
explanation: The hadith of Jibril and the hadith reported by Ibn Umar list the five pillars of Islam.
detail: The hadith is narrated by Ibn 'Umar in Sahih al-Bukhari 8: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, "Islam is built on five: the testimony that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, establishing the prayer, giving the zakat, the hajj, and fasting Ramadan." The picture is a building on five supports, the testimony named first because the other four stand on it. A Muslim learns the five by name as the frame of the whole religion.

question: What is the declaration of faith in Islam called?
explanation: The Shahadah, the testimony of faith, is the first pillar of Islam.
detail: Sahih al-Bukhari 8, narrated by Ibn 'Umar, names it first of the five: "the testimony that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah." Both halves are in the Qur'an: "So know that there is no god but Allah" (47:19) and "Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah" (48:29). The same words ring out in every adhan. A Muslim learns that the religion opens with a witness spoken by the tongue and held in the heart.

question: How many times a day is the obligatory prayer performed in Islam?
explanation: The five daily obligatory prayers are a foundational pillar of Islam.
detail: Sahih al-Bukhari 8 lists "establishing the prayer" as the second of the five on which Islam is built. The Qur'an says that "prayer has been decreed upon the believers at fixed times" (4:103), and marks them: "Establish prayer from the decline of the sun until the darkness of the night, and the recitation of dawn" (17:78). The five are Fajr, Dhuhr, 'Asr, Maghrib and 'Isha. A Muslim learns that the day is shaped by five appointments with Allah, from before sunrise to after dark.

question: What is the obligatory charity in Islam called?
explanation: Zakah is the obligatory charity, one of the five pillars of Islam.
detail: Sahih al-Bukhari 8 places "giving the zakat" third among the five. The Qur'an joins the two: "Establish prayer and give zakat" (2:43). It tells the Prophet ﷺ, "Take from their wealth a charity by which you purify them and cause them increase" (9:103), and the word zakat itself carries both meanings, purity and growth. Surah At-Tawbah names those who receive it (9:60). A Muslim learns that a share of his wealth belongs to others by right, and that giving it cleans what he keeps.

question: What is the obligatory fasting month in Islam called?
explanation: The Quran commands fasting during the month of Ramadan.
detail: The command is in Surah Al-Baqarah: "O you who believe, fasting has been decreed upon you as it was decreed upon those before you, so that you may become mindful of Allah" (2:183). The next verse says the days are numbered, and lets the ill and the traveller make them up later (2:184); then the month is named: "The month of Ramadan, in which the Qur'an was sent down" (2:185). A Muslim learns that the fast is old, and that its purpose is a heart mindful of Allah.

question: What is the pilgrimage to Makkah, obligatory once in a lifetime for those able, called?
explanation: The Quran makes Hajj obligatory, at least once in a lifetime, for anyone able to undertake it.
detail: The duty is stated in Surah Al 'Imran, after the Ka'ba is called the first House established for mankind (3:96): "And due to Allah from the people is a pilgrimage to the House, for whoever is able to find a way" (3:97). Surah Al-Hajj tells how the call began, when Allah ordered Ibrahim to proclaim the hajj so that people would come from far (22:27). A Muslim learns that the hajj is owed to Allah by whoever can reach His House, answering a call first given to Ibrahim.

question: Which direction do Muslims face for prayer?
explanation: The Quran established the Kaaba as the direction of prayer (Qiblah).
detail: Surah Al-Baqarah records the change of direction: "We have certainly seen the turning of your face toward the heaven. So turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque; and wherever you are, turn your faces toward it" (2:144). The verses before it foresee the foolish asking what turned the believers from their former qiblah, and answer that to Allah belong the east and the west (2:142). A Muslim learns that facing the Ka'ba is obedience to a verse, and that every mosque turns its rows toward one House.

question: According to a well-known hadith, how many articles of faith (pillars of Iman) are commonly taught?
explanation: The hadith of Jibril lists six articles of faith: Allah, the angels, the books, the messengers, the Last Day, and divine decree.
detail: Sahih Muslim 8 is the hadith of Jibril, narrated by 'Umar ibn al-Khattab. A man in white clothes and black hair sat before the Prophet ﷺ and asked him about Islam, then iman. The answer was: "To believe in Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers, the Last Day, and to believe in the decree, its good and its bad." Afterwards the Prophet ﷺ said, "That was Jibril; he came to teach you your religion." A Muslim learns the six as faith, taught by a question.

question: According to a hadith reported by Imam al-Bukhari, what should someone who believes in Allah and the Last Day do with their speech?
explanation: The Prophet ﷺ said: 'Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day should speak good or remain silent.'
detail: The hadith is narrated by Abu Hurayrah in Sahih al-Bukhari 6018. It ties three duties to belief in Allah and the Last Day: the believer does not harm his neighbour, honours his guest, and "speaks good or keeps silent." Every word will be answered for: "Not a word does he utter except that with him is an observer prepared" (50:18). A Muslim learns to weigh a sentence before speaking it, and to count silence as a good deed when nothing good is there to say.

question: According to that same hadith, whom else should a believer honor, besides their guest?
explanation: The hadith continues: '...and whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day should honor their neighbor.'
detail: Sahih al-Bukhari 6018, narrated by Abu Hurayrah, binds the neighbour's rights to faith itself: whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day does no harm to his neighbour. The Qur'an sets the neighbour in the same list as parents and kin: "Worship Allah and associate nothing with Him, and to parents, relatives, orphans, the needy, the near neighbour, the neighbour farther away, and the companion at your side" (4:36). Two kinds of neighbour are named. A Muslim learns that treating the neighbour well is part of believing.

question: This same hadith also mentions honoring whom, when they arrive at one's home?
explanation: The full hadith says: '...whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day should honor their guest.'
detail: In Sahih al-Bukhari 6018 the Prophet ﷺ said that whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day should honour his guest. The Qur'an shows the model in Ibrahim: when "the honoured guests" came to him, he slipped away to his family, brought a fat calf, set it before them and said, "Will you not eat?" (51:24-27). He served them himself, quickly and unasked. A Muslim learns that a guest is an occasion for faith to show itself, and that welcoming him is a habit of the prophets.

question: According to an authentic hadith, a believer's faith is not complete until he loves for his brother what he loves for...
explanation: The Prophet ﷺ said: 'None of you truly believes until he loves for his brother what he loves for himself.'
detail: The hadith is narrated by Anas ibn Malik in Sahih al-Bukhari 13: the Prophet ﷺ said, "None of you believes until he loves for his brother what he loves for himself." The Qur'an calls the believers brothers (49:10) and shows the love it means in the Ansar of Madinah, who "prefer them over themselves, even though they are in need" (59:9). A Muslim learns that faith is tested by what he wishes for other people, and lets that wish guide his hands.

question: According to an authentic hadith, the true Muslim is the one from whose tongue and ___ other people are safe.
explanation: The Prophet ﷺ said: 'The Muslim is the one from whose tongue and hand other Muslims are safe.'
detail: The hadith is narrated by 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr in Sahih al-Bukhari 10: the Prophet ﷺ said, "The Muslim is the one from whose tongue and hand the Muslims are safe, and the emigrant is the one who leaves what Allah has forbidden." Surah Al-Hujurat spells out what the tongue must not do: mock, insult, call people by hurtful names, suspect, spy or backbite (49:11-12). A Muslim learns that the name Muslim, from the root of peace and safety, is earned when others are safe from him.

question: The Quran commands kindness to parents and forbids even saying which word of annoyance to them?
explanation: The Quran calls for the utmost kindness to parents, forbidding even the slightest word of contempt.
detail: Surah Al-Isra sets kindness to parents after the worship of Allah: "Your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him, and to parents, good treatment. Say not to them 'uff', nor rebuke them, but speak to them a noble word" (17:23). The next verse adds a prayer: "Lower to them the wing of humility, and say: My Lord, have mercy upon them as they brought me up when I was small" (17:24). A Muslim learns that even a sigh of impatience toward an ageing parent is too much.

question: Which prophet did Allah teach the names of all things?
explanation: Allah taught Adam the names of all things, and the angels acknowledged Allah's wisdom.
detail: Surah Al-Baqarah tells how, after the announcement of a successor on the earth (2:30), "He taught Adam the names; then He showed them to the angels and said, 'Inform Me of the names of these, if you are truthful'" (2:31). The angels answered, "Exalted are You; we have no knowledge except what You have taught us" (2:32), and Adam told them the names (2:33). A Muslim learns that knowledge is a gift from Allah, that it raised Adam before the angels, and that the angels' answer is the honest one.

question: Which prophet spoke to people while still a baby in the cradle?
explanation: Baby Isa spoke from the cradle: 'I am the servant of Allah; He has given me the Scripture.'
detail: Surah Maryam tells how Maryam carried her newborn to her people, who accused her; she only pointed to the child, and they asked, "How can we speak to one who is in the cradle, a child?" (19:29). Then he spoke: "Indeed, I am the servant of Allah. He has given me the Scripture and made me a prophet" (19:30). He added that Allah enjoined on him prayer and zakat and made him dutiful to his mother (19:31-32). A Muslim learns that the first words of 'Isa declared him a servant of Allah.

question: With which son did Ibrahim raise the foundations of the Ka'bah?
explanation: 'And when Ibrahim and Ismail were raising the foundations of the House…' — they built together.
detail: Surah Al-Baqarah records the building and the prayer that went with it: "And when Ibrahim was raising the foundations of the House, and Isma'il with him: Our Lord, accept this from us. Indeed, You are the Hearing, the Knowing" (2:127). Father and son went on to ask that a submissive nation come from their descendants and that a messenger be raised among them (2:128-129). Just before, Allah had charged them to purify His House for those who circle it (2:125). A Muslim learns that even the Ka'ba was raised with a prayer for acceptance, not with pride.

question: Which son was announced to the prophet Zakariyya in his old age?
explanation: 'O Zakariyya, We give you good news of a boy whose name will be Yahya.'
detail: Surah Maryam opens with Zakariyya calling on his Lord in a low voice: his bones had weakened, his head was white, and his wife was barren, yet he asked for an heir (19:3-6). The answer came: "O Zakariyya, indeed We give you good tidings of a boy whose name will be Yahya. We have not given this name to anyone before" (19:7). When he asked how, he was told, "It is easy for Me" (19:9). A Muslim learns that a quiet, persistent prayer is heard even when the answer looks impossible.

question: What did Musa's staff become when Allah told him to cast it down?
explanation: 'Throw it down, O Musa!' He threw it, and it became a serpent, moving swiftly.
detail: The scene is the sacred valley of Tuwa, where Allah first spoke to Musa (20:11-13). Allah asked what was in his right hand, and Musa said it was his staff, which he leaned on and used to beat down leaves for his sheep (20:17-18). "He said: Throw it down, O Musa. So he threw it down, and behold, it was a serpent, moving swiftly" (20:19-20). Then: "Take hold of it and do not fear" (20:21). A Muslim learns that a plain staff became a sign the moment Allah commanded it, and that the order not to fear came with it.

question: In his dream, what did young Yusuf see bowing before him?
answers: Eleven stars, the sun and the moon
explanation: Yusuf saw eleven stars and the sun and the moon prostrating to him — a sign of his destiny.
detail: Surah Yusuf begins with the dream: "When Yusuf said to his father: O my father, indeed I have seen eleven stars and the sun and the moon; I saw them prostrating to me" (12:4). Ya'qub told him not to relate it to his brothers, lest they plot against him (12:5). At the end of the surah, when his parents and brothers fell down before him, Yusuf said, "This is the interpretation of my dream of before; my Lord has made it reality" (12:100). A Muslim learns that what Allah shows comes true in His time.

question: To which people was the prophet Hud sent?
explanation: 'And to 'Ad, their brother Hud…' — he called them to worship Allah alone.
detail: Surah Al-A'raf sets the prophets one after another, and after Nuh comes Hud: "And to 'Ad We sent their brother Hud. He said: O my people, worship Allah; you have no deity other than Him. Then will you not fear Him?" (7:65). The chiefs called him a fool; he answered that he was a messenger from the Lord of the worlds (7:66-68), and reminded them that Allah had made them successors after the people of Nuh (7:69). A Muslim learns that every messenger began with the same call: worship Allah alone.

question: To which people was the prophet Shu'ayb sent?
explanation: 'And to Madyan, their brother Shu'ayb…' — he commanded them to give fair measure and weight.
detail: Surah Al-A'raf tells of Shu'ayb after Hud, Salih and Lut: "And to Madyan We sent their brother Shu'ayb. He said: O my people, worship Allah; you have no deity other than Him. There has come to you clear evidence from your Lord. So give full measure and weight and do not deprive people of their due, and do not cause corruption in the land" (7:85). He also told them not to sit on every road threatening people (7:86). A Muslim learns that worship of Allah and honesty in trade were preached in one breath.

question: Which prophet is called 'Dhun-Nun' (the man of the fish) in the Quran?
explanation: 'And Dhun-Nun, when he went off in anger…' — this is Yunus, later swallowed by the fish.
detail: Surah Al-Anbiya gives the prayer from inside the fish: "And Dhun-Nun, when he went off in anger and thought that We would not decree anything upon him. Then he called out within the darknesses: There is no deity except You; exalted are You. Indeed, I have been of the wrongdoers" (21:87). The next verse answers: "So We responded to him and saved him from the distress. And thus do We save the believers" (21:88). Surah As-Saffat names him Yunus (37:139). A Muslim learns this prayer for every distress of his own.

question: In which surah does Musa travel to learn from a servant to whom Allah gave special knowledge?
explanation: In Surah Al-Kahf, Musa accompanies a knowledgeable servant and learns patience with what he does not yet understand.
detail: Musa set out saying, "I will not give up until I reach the junction of the two seas" (18:60), and there found "one of Our servants, to whom We had given mercy from Us and taught knowledge from Us" (18:65). Musa asked to follow him and was told, "You will never be able to have patience with me" (18:67). Three times the servant did what Musa could not bear: a boat damaged, a boy killed, a wall rebuilt without payment (18:71-77). Each act was then explained (18:78-82). A Muslim learns that Allah's wisdom is often hidden until later.

question: Which prophet is mentioned by name most often in the Quran?
explanation: Musa is the most frequently named prophet in the Quran; his story with Pharaoh returns many times.
detail: The Qur'an returns to Musa in surah after surah: the basket on the river under Pharaoh (28:7), the fire at the valley of Tuwa where Allah spoke to him (20:11-13), the parting of the sea (26:63), and the Tawrat given to him (2:87). Allah says, "And Allah spoke to Musa with direct speech" (4:164), and asks the Prophet ﷺ, "Has the story of Musa reached you?" (20:9). A Muslim learns that Allah repeated this story so that its lessons of patience and trust would not be missed.

question: How many prophets are mentioned by name in the Quran?
explanation: Twenty-five prophets are named in the Quran, from Adam to Muhammad ﷺ.
detail: The twenty-five are Adam, Idris, Nuh, Hud, Salih, Ibrahim, Lut, Isma'il, Ishaq, Ya'qub, Yusuf, Ayyub, Shu'ayb, Musa, Harun, Dhul-Kifl, Dawud, Sulayman, Ilyas, Al-Yasa', Yunus, Zakariyya, Yahya, 'Isa and Muhammad ﷺ. Surah Al-An'am names eighteen of them in one passage and says, "Those are the ones whom Allah has guided, so follow their guidance" (6:83-90). The Qur'an also speaks of messengers whose stories were not related (4:164). A Muslim believes in all of them alike: "We make no distinction between any of His messengers" (2:285).

question: By Allah's permission, which prophet healed the blind and the leper?
explanation: Isa healed the blind and the leper by Allah's permission — a sign for his people.
detail: The verse gives the message 'Isa carried to the Children of Israel: "I have come to you with a sign from your Lord: I make for you from clay the form of a bird, then I breathe into it and it becomes a bird by permission of Allah. And I heal the blind and the leper, and I give life to the dead, by permission of Allah" (3:49). In Surah Al-Ma'idah Allah reminds 'Isa of the same favours, each "by My permission" (5:110). A Muslim learns that every miracle of a prophet was Allah's doing.

question: According to the Quran, how long did Nuh remain among his people calling them to Allah?
explanation: 'He remained among them a thousand years minus fifty' — 950 years of patient calling.
detail: Surah Al-'Ankabut gives the figure in one line: "And We certainly sent Nuh to his people, and he remained among them a thousand years minus fifty years, and the flood seized them while they were wrongdoers" (29:14). The next verse adds: "But We saved him and the companions of the ship, and We made it a sign for the worlds" (29:15). In Surah Nuh he tells his Lord that he called them night and day (71:5). A Muslim learns that a caller's duty is to keep calling; the result belongs to Allah.

question: What is the famous verse 255 of Surah Al-Baqarah called?
explanation: Verse 2:255, Ayat al-Kursi, describes Allah's greatness: 'Allah — there is no deity except Him, the Ever-Living…'
detail: The verse takes its name from the word Kursi in it: "Allah, there is no deity except Him, the Ever-Living, the Self-Sustaining. Neither drowsiness overtakes Him nor sleep. To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and on the earth. Who can intercede with Him except by His permission? His Kursi extends over the heavens and the earth, and guarding them does not tire Him. And He is the Most High, the Most Great" (2:255). The verse after it says there is no compulsion in religion (2:256). A Muslim memorises Ayat al-Kursi early, as a declaration of who Allah is.

question: Which surah does not begin with 'Bismillah ir-Rahman ir-Rahim'?
explanation: At-Tawba (surah 9) is the only surah that does not open with the basmala.
detail: Surah At-Tawba, the ninth, opens directly on its subject: "A declaration of disassociation from Allah and His Messenger to those with whom you had made a treaty among the polytheists" (9:1). In every mushaf the basmala heads the other one hundred and thirteen surahs. It also appears inside a surah, in Sulayman's letter to the queen of Saba: "Indeed, it is from Sulayman, and indeed it is: In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate" (27:30). A Muslim begins At-Tawba as the mushaf does, without the basmala.

question: What is the subject of the longest verse of the Quran (2:282)?
explanation: The Quran's longest verse teaches writing debts down and taking witnesses — honesty is protected.
detail: The verse is a whole page of guidance: "O you who believe, when you contract a debt for a specified term, write it down. And let a scribe write it between you in justice" (2:282). It tells the debtor to dictate and fear Allah, the scribe not to refuse, and the parties to call two witnesses; it adds, "Do not be weary of writing it, whether small or large" (2:282). The next verse allows a pledge when travelling without a scribe (2:283). A Muslim learns that clear records protect friendship as well as money.

question: With which word do the very first revealed verses of the Quran begin?
explanation: The first revealed verses begin with 'Iqra'': 'Read, in the name of your Lord who created.'
detail: The opening of Surah Al-'Alaq is the first passage of the Qur'an sent to Muhammad ﷺ: "Read, in the name of your Lord who created. Created man from a clinging clot. Read, and your Lord is the Most Generous, who taught by the pen, taught man what he did not know" (96:1-5). The command to read comes twice, and the pen is named as a gift of the Creator. The surah ends, "Prostrate and draw near" (96:19). A Muslim learns that reading and learning are the first order of his religion.

question: According to the Quran, the Night of Al-Qadr is better than how many months?
explanation: 'The Night of Al-Qadr is better than a thousand months' — one night of Ramadan worth more than a lifetime of worship.
detail: The whole surah is five verses: "Indeed, We sent it down in the Night of Al-Qadr. And what can make you know what the Night of Al-Qadr is? The Night of Al-Qadr is better than a thousand months" (97:1-3). Then: "The angels and the Spirit descend in it by permission of their Lord for every matter. Peace it is until dawn" (97:4-5). Surah Al-Baqarah places that sending in Ramadan, "the month in which the Qur'an was revealed" (2:185). A Muslim learns to seek this night in Ramadan with prayer, since 97:3 sets one night above a lifetime.

question: What are the last two surahs, Al-Falaq and An-Nas, recited for protection, called?
explanation: Al-Falaq and An-Nas are called 'al-mu'awwidhatan': they are recited to seek Allah's protection.
detail: Both surahs begin with the same command, and the name comes from it: "Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of daybreak, from the evil of what He created" (113:1-2), and "Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of mankind, the King of mankind, the God of mankind" (114:1-3). Al-Falaq names the dangers of darkness, of those who blow on knots, and of the envier (113:3-5); An-Nas names the whisperer who withdraws, from among jinn and men (114:4-6). A Muslim learns these two short surahs as his daily protection, asked from Allah alone.

question: Into how many parts (juz') is the Quran traditionally divided?
explanation: The Quran is divided into 30 juz', which helps complete it in a month — for example during Ramadan.
detail: The thirty juz' are of nearly equal length and do not follow the surah boundaries: the first opens with Al-Fatiha, and the thirtieth begins with Surah An-Naba, whose first word gives it its common name, Juz' 'Amma. The Qur'an describes its own gradual sending: "And a Qur'an which We have divided, that you may recite it to the people over a prolonged period" (17:106), and commands, "Recite the Qur'an with measured recitation" (73:4). A Muslim uses the thirty parts to pace his reading, one each night of Ramadan.

question: How many verses does Surah Al-Fatiha contain?
explanation: Al-Fatiha has seven verses, recited in every unit of the prayer.
detail: Al-Fatiha, the Opening, is the first surah of the mushaf. Its verses run from "All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds" (1:2) through the names of mercy and the Day of Judgement (1:3-4) to "You alone we worship and You alone we ask for help" (1:5), and close with "Guide us to the straight path" (1:6-7). The prayer cannot be prayed without it, so every Muslim recites its seven verses at least seventeen times a day. A Muslim learns them first of all the Qur'an, as the words with which he speaks to Allah.

question: Which surah is named after a metal?
explanation: Surah 57 is called Al-Hadid: 'We sent down iron, in which is great might and benefits for people.'
detail: The surah takes its name from this verse: "We have certainly sent Our messengers with clear proofs and sent down with them the Scripture and the balance, so that people may maintain justice. And We sent down iron, in which is great might and benefits for the people, and so that Allah may make evident those who support Him and His messengers unseen" (57:25). Scripture, balance and iron stand together: guidance, justice and the strength to uphold them. A Muslim learns that even a metal is counted among what Allah sent down for people's good.

question: Which story does the Quran call 'the best of stories'?
answers: The story of the people of the cave
explanation: 'We relate to you the best of stories' — so opens the story of Yusuf.
detail: The surah announces itself: "We relate to you the best of stories in what We have revealed to you of this Qur'an, though before it you were among the unaware" (12:3). The story then runs from Yusuf's dream (12:4) through the well, slavery and the prison to the reunion in which his brothers bow before him and he forgives (12:92-100). It closes with the reason: "In their stories is a lesson for those of understanding" (12:111). A Muslim learns from Yusuf that patience, purity and forgiveness make the story Allah calls the best.

question: How many verses does Al-Baqarah, the longest surah, contain?
explanation: Al-Baqarah has 286 verses — the longest surah of the Quran.
detail: Al-Baqarah opens with "Alif Lam Mim. This is the Book about which there is no doubt" (2:1-2). Its name comes from the cow the Children of Israel were told to sacrifice (2:67-73). Within its 286 verses are the change of qibla (2:144), the fast of Ramadan (2:183-187), Ayat al-Kursi (2:255) and the longest verse of all (2:282). Its last verse ends with a prayer: "Our Lord, do not burden us with what we have no strength to bear; pardon us, forgive us and have mercy on us" (2:286). A Muslim learns that the longest surah closes with the gentlest request.

question: Which short surah proclaims: 'Say: He is Allah, the One'?
explanation: Al-Ikhlas proclaims Allah's perfect oneness in four verses.
detail: The surah is four verses long: "Say: He is Allah, the One. Allah, the Eternal Refuge. He neither begets nor is born, nor is there to Him any equivalent" (112:1-4). Each line removes something from the idea of Allah: partners, need, origin, offspring and likeness. The name Al-Ikhlas, sincerity, is not a word in the surah; it names what the surah does, purifying belief in Allah of everything else. Surah Al-Baqarah says the same: "Your God is one God" (2:163). A Muslim learns Al-Ikhlas as a child and carries in it his whole belief about Allah.

question: Over roughly how many years was the Quran revealed?
explanation: The Quran was revealed gradually over about 23 years, in Makkah and then Madinah.
detail: The Qur'an explains why it did not come all at once: "And a Qur'an which We have divided, that you may recite it to the people over a prolonged period, and We have sent it down progressively" (17:106). The answer to those who asked why it came in pieces: "that We may strengthen your heart by it" (25:32). It began with "Read, in the name of your Lord" (96:1) in Makkah, and in the Prophet's ﷺ last year came, "This day I have perfected for you your religion" (5:3). A Muslim learns that the Qur'an was taught slowly, to be lived as it came.

question: According to the Quran, what was the first House established for people to worship Allah?
explanation: 'The first House established for mankind is the one at Bakkah, blessed…' — the Ka'bah in Makkah.
detail: The verse is in Surah Al 'Imran: "Indeed, the first House established for mankind was that at Bakkah, blessed and a guidance for the worlds" (3:96). The next verse names "the standing place of Ibrahim" within it, says that whoever enters it is safe, and lays the duty of pilgrimage on those able to reach it (3:97). Surah Al-Baqarah shows Ibrahim and Isma'il raising its foundations (2:127). A Muslim learns that the Ka'ba is the oldest house of worship on earth, and faces it in every prayer.

question: Who was the first muezzin of Islam, chosen by the Prophet ﷺ to call to prayer?
explanation: Bilal, with his beautiful voice, was chosen as Islam's first muezzin.
detail: Bilal ibn Rabah came from Abyssinia and was enslaved in Makkah, where he was tortured for his faith until Abu Bakr freed him; every biography records this. After the Hijra, when the call to prayer was instituted in Madinah, the Prophet ﷺ chose Bilal to raise it. The Qur'an speaks of that call: "When the call to prayer is made on the day of Jumu'ah, hasten to the remembrance of Allah" (62:9). A Muslim learns that the first voice of the adhan belonged to a freed slave, and that rank before Allah is by faith.

question: What was the first mosque founded by the Prophet ﷺ upon arriving near Madinah?
answers: The mosque of the two qiblas
explanation: Arriving at Quba, at the gates of Madinah, the Prophet ﷺ founded the first mosque there.
detail: On the journey of the Hijra from Makkah, the Prophet ﷺ and Abu Bakr reached Quba, a settlement on the edge of Madinah, before entering the city; there he stayed some days and laid the foundation of a mosque. The Qur'an recalls the journey: "when the two were in the cave and he said to his companion, Do not grieve; indeed Allah is with us" (9:40). Quba still stands, and Muslims visiting Madinah pray in it. A Muslim learns that the first thing the Prophet ﷺ built on arriving was a place of prayer.

question: What was the name of the Prophet's ﷺ mother?
explanation: Amina bint Wahb was the Prophet's ﷺ mother; Halima was his wet-nurse.
detail: Amina bint Wahb was of the Quraysh clan of Banu Zuhra, and her husband 'Abdullah died before their son was born. She died while Muhammad ﷺ was still a small child, and he passed into the care of his grandfather 'Abd al-Muttalib and then of his uncle Abu Talib. The Qur'an speaks of these years: "Did He not find you an orphan and give you refuge?" (93:6), and then commands him not to oppress the orphan (93:9). A Muslim learns that the Prophet ﷺ knew the loss of both parents, and that his tenderness toward orphans grew from it.

question: What was the name of the Prophet's ﷺ father, who passed away before his birth?
explanation: 'Abdullah, son of 'Abd al-Muttalib, passed away before his son Muhammad ﷺ was born.
detail: 'Abdullah was the son of 'Abd al-Muttalib, chief of Banu Hashim in Quraysh, and his wife was Amina bint Wahb. He died on a journey before his son was born, so Muhammad ﷺ came into the world fatherless; his grandfather and, after him, his uncle Abu Talib raised him. The Qur'an recalls it: "Did He not find you an orphan and give you refuge?" (93:6), and goes on, "So as for the orphan, do not oppress him" (93:9). A Muslim learns that Allah cared for the Prophet ﷺ from birth, and takes the orphan's cause as his own.

question: What nickname did the Makkans give the Prophet ﷺ before revelation, for his honesty?
explanation: Even before revelation he was called al-Amin: people entrusted him with their belongings.
detail: Years before revelation, Muhammad ﷺ was known in Makkah as al-Amin: the Makkans left their valuables in his keeping. When Quraysh rebuilt the Ka'ba and quarrelled over who should set the Black Stone in place, they accepted him as judge; he spread a cloak, placed the stone on it, and had each clan lift a corner. The Qur'an points to this life lived among them: "I had remained among you a lifetime before it; then will you not reason?" (10:16). A Muslim learns that honesty was the Prophet's ﷺ character before it was his message.

question: In which year of the Hijra did the conquest of Makkah take place?
explanation: In year 8 AH the Prophet ﷺ entered Makkah almost without fighting and pardoned its people.
detail: In year 8 AH the Prophet ﷺ marched on Makkah after Quraysh broke the treaty, and the city gave way with hardly a fight. He entered with his head lowered in humility, cleared the Ka'ba of the idols around it, and forgave those who had driven him out. Surah An-Nasr speaks of this: "When the victory of Allah has come and the conquest, and you see the people entering into the religion of Allah in multitudes, then glorify your Lord with praise and ask His forgiveness" (110:1-3). A Muslim learns that victory is met with praise and forgiveness, not revenge.

question: In which year of the Hijra did the Prophet ﷺ perform his Farewell Pilgrimage?
explanation: The Farewell Pilgrimage took place in year 10 AH; the Prophet ﷺ delivered his final sermon there.
detail: In year 10 AH the Prophet ﷺ led the only hajj of his life, with a great crowd of Companions. Standing at 'Arafat he addressed them, and there the verse came down: "This day I have perfected for you your religion and completed My favour upon you and approved for you Islam as religion" (5:3). The rites he performed on that journey became the pattern of every hajj since. He passed away a few months later, in year 11. A Muslim learns that the Farewell Pilgrimage closed the Prophet's ﷺ mission with the religion complete.

question: How many daughters did the Prophet ﷺ have?
explanation: Zaynab, Ruqayya, Umm Kulthum and Fatima — the Prophet's ﷺ four daughters.
detail: All four daughters were born to Khadija in Makkah. Zaynab was the eldest; Ruqayya and, after her death, Umm Kulthum were married to 'Uthman ibn 'Affan; Fatima, the youngest, married 'Ali ibn Abi Talib and was the mother of al-Hasan and al-Husayn. Three of the four died in their father's lifetime, and Fatima survived him by only months. The Qur'an addresses them: "O Prophet, tell your wives and your daughters and the women of the believers" (33:59). A Muslim learns that the Prophet ﷺ raised daughters with honour, and remembers their names.

question: What are the people of Madinah who welcomed and helped the emigrant Muslims called?
explanation: The Ansar, 'the Helpers', shared their homes and wealth with their emigrant brothers.
detail: The Ansar were the Muslims of Madinah, from the tribes of Aws and Khazraj, who received the Prophet ﷺ and the emigrants. Surah Al-Hashr describes them: "Those who were settled in the home and in faith before them love those who emigrated to them, and find in their breasts no need for what the emigrants were given, but give them preference over themselves, even though they are in want" (59:9). Allah names them among "the first forerunners" with whom He is pleased (9:100). A Muslim learns that welcoming a stranger as a brother earns Allah's pleasure.

question: What are the Muslims who left Makkah to emigrate to Madinah called?
explanation: The Muhajirun left homes and belongings in Makkah to preserve their faith.
detail: The Muhajirun are the Companions who made the Hijra from Makkah to Madinah, leaving houses, trade and family for their faith. Surah Al-Hashr describes them: "For the poor emigrants who were expelled from their homes and their properties, seeking bounty from Allah and His approval, and supporting Allah and His Messenger; those are the truthful" (59:8). Surah An-Nahl promises: "Those who emigrated for Allah after they had been wronged, We will surely settle them in this world in a good place" (16:41). A Muslim learns that what is left for Allah is never lost.

question: During which month did the Battle of Badr take place?
explanation: The Battle of Badr took place during Ramadan, in year 2 AH.
detail: Badr was fought in Ramadan of year 2 AH, at the wells of Badr between Madinah and Makkah, when a small Muslim force met the army of Quraysh. The Qur'an calls it "the day of the criterion, the day the two armies met" (8:41), and reminds the believers: "Allah had already given you victory at Badr while you were few in number" (3:123). It tells how they cried for help and Allah answered with a thousand angels (8:9). A Muslim learns that the first great victory came in the month of fasting, to a few who trusted Allah.

question: Before the qibla was fixed toward the Ka'bah, toward which city did Muslims pray?
explanation: Muslims first prayed toward Bayt al-Maqdis; then Allah commanded turning toward the Sacred Mosque (Quran 2:142-144).
detail: After the Hijra, the Muslims in Madinah prayed toward Bayt al-Maqdis, the Farthest Mosque named in the Night Journey (17:1). Then the command came: "We have seen the turning of your face toward the heaven, and We will surely turn you to a qibla with which you will be pleased. So turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque" (2:144). Allah foretold the objection, "What has turned them from their qibla?" and answered, "To Allah belong the east and the west" (2:142). A Muslim learns that the direction of prayer is chosen by Allah, not by habit.

question: What is the routine water purification a Muslim performs before each prayer called?
explanation: 'When you rise for prayer, wash your faces and your hands…' — this is wudu.
detail: The verse lays out the whole ablution in one sentence: "O you who believe, when you rise to prayer, wash your faces and your hands up to the elbows, wipe over your heads, and wash your feet up to the ankles" (5:6). It goes on to require a full washing after major impurity, and to allow clean earth when there is no water (5:6). The reason closes the verse: "Allah does not intend to make difficulty for you, but He intends to purify you" (5:6). A Muslim learns wudu as the doorway to each prayer, and gives thanks for it.

question: According to the Quran, what do the 'noble scribes' (kiraman katibin) do?
explanation: 'Over you are guardians, noble scribes' — angels record every deed.
detail: Surah Al-Infitar describes the Day when the sky splits and every soul knows what it sent ahead and held back (82:1-5). It asks man what deceived him about his generous Lord (82:6), then tells him he is never unwatched: "And indeed, over you are keepers, noble and recording; they know whatever you do" (82:10-12). Surah Qaf says the same of the two receivers on the right and the left: "Not a word does he utter but there is a watcher ready" (50:17-18). A Muslim learns to speak and act as one whose every deed is written down.

question: How many beautiful names of Allah does the authentic tradition report?
explanation: An authentic hadith reported by al-Bukhari and Muslim mentions ninety-nine names — one hundred minus one.
detail: The hadith is narrated by Abu Hurayra and recorded in Sahih al-Bukhari 2736 and Sahih Muslim 2677: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that Allah has ninety-nine names, one hundred minus one, and whoever preserves them enters Paradise. The Qur'an gathers many of them at the end of Surah Al-Hashr, the King, the Holy, the Peace, the Creator, "to Him belong the best names" (59:23-24), and says, "To Allah belong the best names, so call upon Him by them" (7:180). A Muslim learns the names one by one, and calls on Allah with the one that fits his need.

question: What does Allah's name 'Ar-Rahman' mean?
explanation: Ar-Rahman, the Most Merciful — His mercy embraces all things.
detail: Ar-Rahman stands in the first line of the Qur'an, "In the name of Allah, Ar-Rahman, Ar-Rahim", and again in Al-Fatiha after the praise of the Lord of the worlds (1:3). It is also the name of a surah, which opens, "Ar-Rahman taught the Qur'an, created man, taught him speech" (55:1-4). The Qur'an sets the name beside the name Allah: "Call upon Allah or call upon Ar-Rahman; whichever you call, to Him belong the best names" (17:110). A Muslim learns to begin every task with this name, placing mercy at the start.

question: In Al-Fatiha, Allah is called 'Master' of which day?
explanation: 'Master of the Day of Judgment' — the day everyone meets their deeds.
detail: Al-Fatiha moves from praise, "Lord of the worlds" (1:2), through the two names of mercy (1:3), to "Master of the Day of Judgement" (1:4), and only then to "You alone we worship" (1:5). Mercy and judgement stand side by side before the worshipper speaks. Surah Al-Infitar asks what the Day of Judgement is and answers, "The Day when no soul will have power to do anything for another, and the command that Day is Allah's" (82:17-19). A Muslim learns to remember, in every rak'ah, that the One he praises will also judge him.

question: On which day of the week does the Quran call believers to congregational prayer?
explanation: 'When the call to prayer is made on Friday, hasten to the remembrance of Allah.'
detail: The verse gives the surah its name: "O you who believe, when the call to prayer is made on the day of Jumu'ah, hasten to the remembrance of Allah and leave trade. That is better for you, if you only knew" (62:9). The next verse balances it: "And when the prayer has ended, disperse in the land and seek of the bounty of Allah" (62:10). Then the surah rebukes those who rushed to a caravan and left the Prophet ﷺ standing (62:11). A Muslim learns that Friday prayer interrupts work by Allah's command, and work resumes with His blessing.

question: According to the Quran, who guarantees the Quran's preservation from any alteration?
explanation: 'Indeed, We sent down the Reminder, and indeed We are its Guardian.'
detail: The verse comes in Surah Al-Hijr, just after the mockers said, "O you upon whom the Reminder has been sent down, indeed you are mad" (15:6). Allah's reply: "Indeed, it is We who sent down the Reminder, and indeed, We will be its guardian" (15:9). The promise is repeated elsewhere: "Falsehood cannot approach it from before it or from behind it" (41:42), and "Upon Us is its collection and its recitation" (75:17). A Muslim learns to trust the Book in his hands, memorised by millions letter for letter, as the Qur'an the Prophet ﷺ recited.

question: What does the Quran declare about entering the religion?
answers: There is no compulsion in religion
explanation: 'There is no compulsion in religion: right guidance is distinct from error.'
detail: The verse follows Ayat al-Kursi at once: "There is no compulsion in religion. The right course has become clear from the wrong. So whoever rejects false gods and believes in Allah has grasped the most trustworthy handhold, which never breaks" (2:256). Surah Yunus asks the Prophet ﷺ, "Would you then compel the people until they become believers?" (10:99), and Surah Al-Kahf says, "Whoever wills, let him believe; and whoever wills, let him disbelieve" (18:29). A Muslim learns that faith is a choice made when truth is clear, and his task is to make it clear.

question: What is the Muslims' greeting, a wish of peace?
explanation: 'As-salamu 'alaykum': peace be upon you — answered with 'wa 'alaykum as-salam'.
detail: The greeting of peace runs through the Qur'an. Believers are told not to enter houses without greeting their people (24:27) and to "greet one another with a greeting from Allah, blessed and good" (24:61). When the angels came to Ibrahim they said, "Peace," and he answered, "Peace" (51:25). The angels welcome the people of Paradise with "Peace be upon you for what you patiently endured" (13:24), and Allah Himself is named As-Salam, the Peace (59:23). A Muslim gives this greeting to every Muslim he meets, and answers it at least as warmly (4:86).

question: What is the belief in the oneness of Allah, the heart of Islam, called?
explanation: Tawhid — affirming that Allah is One, without partner — is the foundation of all faith.
detail: Tawhid comes from the word for one, and the Qur'an states it in every form: "Your God is one God; there is no deity except Him, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate" (2:163). Every messenger was sent with it: "We sent no messenger before you without revealing to him that there is no deity except Me, so worship Me" (21:25). Surah Al-Ikhlas puts it in four verses (112:1-4), and the testimony "there is no god but Allah" is its shortest form. A Muslim learns that tawhid is the reason for every prayer, fast and good deed.

question: To what does the Quran compare backbiting (speaking ill of someone absent)?
answers: Eating the flesh of one's dead brother
explanation: 'Would one of you like to eat the flesh of his dead brother? You would detest it!' — backbiting is that ugly.
detail: The verse sets three things side by side: "O you who believe, avoid much suspicion, for some suspicion is sin. And do not spy, and do not backbite one another. Would one of you like to eat the flesh of his dead brother? You would hate it. And fear Allah; indeed, Allah is Accepting of repentance and Merciful" (49:12). The one spoken of is absent and cannot defend himself, like a dead man. The verse ends with repentance, leaving a door open. A Muslim learns to stop talk about an absent person as he would refuse a revolting plate.

question: How does the Quran describe the relationship between believers?
explanation: 'The believers are but brothers, so make peace between your two brothers.'
detail: The verse belongs to Surah Al-Hujurat: "The believers are but brothers, so make peace between your brothers. And fear Allah that you may receive mercy" (49:10). It follows the command to reconcile two groups of believers who fight (49:9), and precedes the bans on mocking, insulting and backbiting (49:11-12). Surah Al 'Imran recalls how this brotherhood came: "You were enemies, and He brought your hearts together, and you became by His favour brothers" (3:103). A Muslim learns that peace-making between believers is not optional kindness but the duty of a brother.

question: What does the Quran say about mocking other people?
answers: It is forbidden: the mocked may be better than the mockers
explanation: 'Let no people ridicule another people: perhaps they are better than them.'
detail: The verse addresses men and women alike: "O you who believe, let not a people ridicule another people; it may be that they are better than them. Nor let women ridicule other women; it may be that they are better than them. And do not insult one another, and do not call each other by offensive nicknames" (49:11). It comes right after the declaration that believers are brothers (49:10), and ends by calling those who do not repent wrongdoers. A Muslim learns to measure no one by appearance, since the one he laughs at may stand higher before Allah.

question: According to the Quran, what does Allah promise the one who is grateful?
answers: He will surely give them more
explanation: 'If you are grateful, I will surely increase you.'
detail: The promise is given through Musa. Reminding his people how Allah saved them from the people of Pharaoh (14:6), he continued: "And when your Lord proclaimed: If you are grateful, I will surely increase you; but if you deny, indeed My punishment is severe" (14:7). The same surah says the favours of Allah cannot be counted (14:34), and Luqman is told that "whoever is grateful is grateful for his own soul" (31:12). A Muslim learns to say al-hamdu lillah for what he has, knowing that thanks is itself the way to more.

question: According to the Quran, how will the patient (sabirun) be given their reward?
explanation: 'The patient will be given their reward in full, without account.'
detail: The verse opens an address to the believers: "Say: O My servants who have believed, fear your Lord. For those who do good in this world there is good, and the earth of Allah is spacious. Indeed, the patient will be given their reward in full, without account" (39:10). Elsewhere the Qur'an says, "Allah is with the patient" (2:153), and promises mercy to those who say, "Indeed we belong to Allah" (2:156-157). A Muslim learns that patience is the one deed whose reward is not measured.

question: 'Eat and drink, but…' — how does this verse continue?
explanation: 'Eat and drink, but do not be excessive: Allah does not love the wasteful.'
detail: The verse addresses all people: "O children of Adam, take your adornment at every mosque, and eat and drink, but do not be excessive. Indeed, He does not love those who commit excess" (7:31). The next verse defends enjoying what Allah made: "Who has forbidden the adornment of Allah which He brought forth for His servants?" (7:32). Surah Al-Isra calls the wasteful "brothers of the devils" (17:27), and Surah Al-Furqan praises those who are neither extravagant nor stingy (25:67). A Muslim learns that good food and clothing are Allah's gifts, and the limit is waste.

question: Which verse, often recited in the Friday sermon, sums up what Allah commands?
explanation: 'Allah commands justice, good conduct and generosity to relatives…' — recited every Friday.
detail: The verse gives three commands and three prohibitions: "Indeed, Allah commands justice, good conduct and giving to relatives, and forbids indecency, wrongdoing and oppression. He admonishes you so that you may take heed" (16:90). The next verse adds keeping one's word: "Fulfil the covenant of Allah when you have made a covenant" (16:91).
