In many mosques the imam closes the Friday khutba with 16:90, so the congregation hears it every week. A Muslim learns it as a short measure of his conduct: is it just, is it good, does it hold his family close.

question: Against whom does Surah Al-Mutaffifin open with 'Woe…'?
answers: Those who cheat in measure and weight
explanation: 'Woe to those who give less: who demand full measure when receiving, but give less when measuring for others.'
detail: The surah begins: "Woe to those who give less, who, when they take a measure from people, take in full, but when they measure or weigh for them, give less" (83:1-3). Then comes the question that gives the sin its weight: "Do they not think that they will be resurrected for a tremendous Day, the Day when mankind will stand before the Lord of the worlds?" (83:4-6). Surah Ar-Rahman says, "Establish weight in justice and do not make the balance deficient" (55:9). A Muslim learns that honesty in the smallest measure is watched by Allah.

question: According to Surah Ad-Duha, how should the orphan and the one who asks be treated?
explanation: 'As for the orphan, do not oppress him; and as for the one who asks, do not repel him.'
detail: The two commands answer three favours the surah has just listed to the Prophet ﷺ: "Did He not find you an orphan and give you refuge? And find you lost and guide you? And find you poor and make you self-sufficient?" (93:6-8). Then: "So as for the orphan, do not oppress him. And as for the one who asks, do not repel him. But as for the favour of your Lord, speak of it" (93:9-11). The surah opened by assuring him, "Your Lord has not taken leave of you" (93:3). A Muslim learns to pass on the kindness he received.

question: How does the Quran command people to be spoken to?
explanation: '…and speak good words to people' — kind speech is itself worship.
detail: The words belong to the covenant Allah took from the Children of Israel: "Do not worship except Allah; and to parents do good, and to relatives, orphans and the needy. And speak to people good words, and establish prayer and give zakat" (2:83). Good speech stands between charity and prayer in the list. The verse ends, "Then you turned away, except a few of you" (2:83). Surah Al-Isra gives the same rule: "Tell My servants to say that which is best" (17:53). A Muslim learns that a kind word owed to every person belongs to the same covenant as prayer.

question: In his advice to his son, what does Luqman say about walking and pride?
answers: Do not walk on the earth arrogantly
explanation: 'Do not turn your cheek from people in pride, and do not walk the earth arrogantly.'
detail: Luqman's counsel to his son begins with "do not associate anything with Allah" (31:13) and continues through prayer and patience (31:17) to this: "And do not turn your cheek from people in contempt, and do not walk through the earth exultantly. Indeed, Allah does not love any self-deluded boaster. And be moderate in your pace and lower your voice" (31:18-19). Surah Al-Isra adds the reason: "You will never tear the earth apart, and you will never reach the mountains in height" (17:37). A Muslim learns that humility shows first in how he walks and speaks.

question: According to the very first hadith of al-Bukhari's collection, what are deeds judged by?
explanation: 'Actions are but by intentions, and every person shall have only what they intended.'
detail: The hadith is Sahih al-Bukhari 1, the first in the collection, narrated by 'Umar ibn al-Khattab from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. After stating that deeds count by what was intended, the Prophet ﷺ gave an example: whoever emigrated for Allah and His Messenger, his emigration is for Allah and His Messenger; and whoever emigrated for worldly gain or for a woman to marry, his emigration is for what he emigrated to. The same journey is worth everything or nothing according to the heart behind it. A Muslim learns to set his intention before each deed.

question: According to the Quran, from what did Allah create Adam?
explanation: Allah told the angels: "I am going to create a human being from clay."
detail: The verse belongs to the account of Adam's creation near the end of Surah Sad: "When your Lord said to the angels, 'I am going to create a human being from clay'" (38:71). The next verse completes it: "When I have fashioned him and breathed into him of My spirit, then fall down to him in prostration" (38:72). All the angels prostrated, except Iblis, who was proud (38:73-74). A Muslim remembers that the first human was formed from plain earth and honoured with a spirit Allah breathed into him.

question: Who tempted Adam and his wife to eat from the forbidden tree?
explanation: Shaytan whispered to them so that they would eat from the tree Allah had forbidden.
detail: The Qur'an records the whisper itself: "Your Lord did not forbid you this tree except that you become angels or become of the immortals" (7:20). Shaytan then swore to them, "I am to you a sincere adviser" (7:21), and when they tasted the tree their nakedness appeared and they began covering themselves with leaves of Paradise (7:22). Their Lord reminded them that He had forbidden that tree and had told them Shaytan was a clear enemy (7:22). A Muslim learns that temptation arrives dressed as friendly advice with a false promise attached.

question: What reason did Iblis give for refusing to bow to Adam?
answers: "I am better than him: You created me from fire and him from clay"
He did not know who Adam was
He was afraid of the angels
explanation: Iblis refused out of pride: "You created me from fire, and him You created from clay."
detail: The verse gives the whole exchange: "He said, 'What prevented you from prostrating when I commanded you?' He said, 'I am better than him. You created me from fire and created him from clay'" (7:12). Just before, Allah had said to the angels, "Prostrate to Adam," and all prostrated except Iblis (7:11). The answer came at once: "Descend from it; it is not for you to be arrogant in it. Go out, you are of the debased" (7:13). A Muslim learns that the first sin recorded in the Qur'an was pride in one's origin.

question: After the killing between the two sons of Adam, which animal did Allah send to show how to bury the body?
explanation: Allah sent a crow that scratched the ground to show the killer how to hide his brother's body.
detail: The verse reads: "Then Allah sent a crow scratching in the ground to show him how to hide the body of his brother. He said, 'Woe to me! Have I failed to be like this crow and hide the body of my brother?' And he became of the regretful" (5:31). The two sons, unnamed in the Qur'an, had each offered a sacrifice and only one was accepted; the slain brother had refused to strike back, saying, "I fear Allah, Lord of the worlds" (5:28). A Muslim learns from the verse that follows that killing one soul unjustly is like killing all mankind (5:32).

question: What does the Quran say about the prophet Idris?
answers: Allah raised him to a high station
He was swallowed by a fish
explanation: "And We raised him to a high station."
detail: Surah Maryam introduces him with the words it uses for Ibrahim and Musa: "And mention in the Book Idris. He was a man of truth and a prophet. And We raised him to a high station" (19:56-57), the raising being verse 19:57. The surah then gathers these prophets in one verse: those on whom Allah bestowed favour, who fell down prostrating and weeping when the verses of the Most Merciful were recited to them (19:58). Elsewhere Idris is named among the patient (21:85). A Muslim learns that truthfulness and patience are what Allah recorded about this prophet.

question: What did Nuh's son do when his father called him into the ark?
answers: He refused and said he would shelter on a mountain
explanation: He said: "I will take refuge on a mountain"; the waves overwhelmed him.
detail: Surah Hud tells it on the water: "It sailed with them through waves like mountains, and Nuh called to his son: 'O my son, come aboard with us and do not be with the disbelievers.' He said, 'I will take refuge on a mountain that will protect me from the water.' Nuh said, 'There is no protector today from the command of Allah except for whom He gives mercy'" (11:42-43). Nuh then pleaded for his son as one of his family, and was told he was not, for his conduct was not righteous (11:45-46). A Muslim learns that being a prophet's child saves no one; only faith does.

question: On which mount did Nuh's ark come to rest, according to the Quran?
explanation: "And the ark came to rest on al-Judi."
detail: The end of the flood is told in one verse: "And it was said, 'O earth, swallow your water, and O sky, withhold.' And the water subsided, the matter was accomplished, and it came to rest on al-Judi. And it was said, 'Away with the wrongdoing people'" (11:44). This follows the drowning of Nuh's son, who had refused to board (11:42-43). Nuh was then told, "Disembark in security from Us and blessings upon you" (11:48). A Muslim sees in this verse earth and sky obeying a single command, and the believers settling in peace where Allah chose.

question: What did Allah command Nuh to load into the ark?
answers: A pair of every kind, and the believers
explanation: "Load into it a pair of every kind, and your family… and whoever has believed."
detail: Surah Hud gives the command at the moment the flood began: "When Our command came and the oven overflowed, We said, 'Load into it of each kind two mates, and your family, except those against whom the word has gone forth, and whoever has believed.' But none had believed with him except a few" (11:40). Nuh had built the ship "under Our eyes and Our inspiration" (11:37), and as they boarded he said, "In the name of Allah is its sailing and its anchoring" (11:41). A Muslim learns that Allah preserved every creature in pairs together with the few believers.

question: What did the chiefs of Nuh's people do when they saw him building the ark?
explanation: Whenever chiefs of his people passed by, they ridiculed him.
detail: The verse reads: "And he constructed the ship, and whenever an assembly of the eminent of his people passed by him, they ridiculed him. He said, 'If you ridicule us, then we will ridicule you just as you ridicule'" (11:38). He added that they would soon know who receives a disgracing punishment (11:39). Nuh was building on dry land, after Allah had told him that none of his people would believe except those who already had (11:36). A Muslim learns to keep doing what Allah commands, calmly, even when the powerful laugh.

question: How does the Quran describe Nuh in Surah Al-Isra?
explanation: "Indeed, he was a grateful servant."
detail: Surah Al-Isra opens with the Night Journey of the Prophet ﷺ (17:1), turns to the Book given to Musa (17:2), then addresses the Children of Israel through their ancestor: "O descendants of those We carried with Nuh. Indeed, he was a grateful servant" (17:3). Those spoken to are reminded that they exist because their forefathers were carried in the ark, and that the man who led them there is remembered by Allah for one quality above all. A Muslim learns that gratitude is the mark Allah set beside the name of Nuh, who preached so long and was saved.

question: How were the people of 'Ad, to whom Hud was sent, destroyed?
explanation: "As for 'Ad, they were destroyed by a screaming, violent wind."
detail: Surah Al-Haqqa describes their end in detail: "As for 'Ad, they were destroyed by a screaming, violent wind, which He imposed upon them for seven nights and eight days in succession, so you would see the people there fallen as if they were hollow trunks of palm trees" (69:6-7). The surah then asks, "Do you see any remains of them?" (69:8). The Qur'an also records what 'Ad used to say: "Who is greater than us in strength?" (41:15). A Muslim learns that a people proud of their strength were removed by moving air, commanded for exactly eight days.

question: What seized Thamud, the people of Salih?
explanation: "And the blast seized those who had wronged."
detail: The verse continues: "And the blast seized those who had wronged, and they became within their homes fallen prone, as if they had never lived there" (11:67-68). Salih had presented them the she-camel of Allah as a sign and warned, "Do not touch her with harm, lest a near punishment seize you" (11:64). They hamstrung her, and Salih said, "Enjoy yourselves in your homes for three days; that is a promise not to be belied" (11:65). A Muslim learns that a sign from Allah is to be respected, and that a prophet's warning is fulfilled to the day.

question: What is the name of Ibrahim's father mentioned in the Quran?
explanation: "Ibrahim said to his father Azar: do you take idols as gods?"
detail: The verse reads: "And when Ibrahim said to his father Azar, 'Do you take idols as gods? Indeed, I see you and your people in manifest error'" (6:74). Right after, the Qur'an says, "Thus did We show Ibrahim the realm of the heavens and the earth, that he would be among the certain" (6:75), and then tells of his looking at the star, the moon and the sun (6:76-78). In Surah Maryam each of his words to his father begins "O my father" (19:42-45). A Muslim learns from Ibrahim to speak the truth to family plainly, yet with tenderness.

question: After breaking the idols, which one did Ibrahim leave intact?
explanation: He broke them to pieces, except the biggest, so that his people would question it.
detail: The verse reads: "So he made them into fragments, except a large one among them, that they might return to it" (21:58). Ibrahim had promised, "By Allah, I will surely plan against your idols after you have turned away" (21:57). When his people asked who had done this to their gods (21:59), he was brought before them and said, "Rather, this one, the largest of them, did it, so ask them, if they can speak" (21:63). They turned to themselves and admitted, "You are the wrongdoers" (21:64). A Muslim learns from Ibrahim to make people see the truth for themselves.

question: After watching the star, the moon and then the sun set, what did Ibrahim declare?
answers: "I do not love those that set"
explanation: As each one set he said: "I do not love those that set," then turned to the Creator.
detail: The three verses trace his reasoning: "When the night covered him, he saw a star. He said, 'This is my lord.' But when it set, he said, 'I do not love those that set'" (6:76). When the moon set, he said, "If my Lord does not guide me, I will surely be among the people gone astray" (6:77). When the sun set too, he told his people, "I am free of what you associate with Allah" (6:78), and turned his face to the Creator of the heavens and the earth (6:79). A Muslim learns that whatever rises and disappears cannot be worshipped.

question: How many birds did Allah tell Ibrahim to take, to show him how He brings the dead to life?
explanation: "Take four birds… then call them: they will come to you in haste."
detail: Surah Al-Baqara gives the full request: "And when Ibrahim said, 'My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead.' He said, 'Have you not believed?' He said, 'Yes, but so that my heart may be at rest.' He said, 'Take four birds and draw them to yourself; then put a portion of them on each hill; then call them, they will come to you in haste'" (2:260). The verse before tells of a man made dead for a hundred years and then raised (2:259). A Muslim learns that asking to see is not doubt when it comes from a heart that already believes.

question: What did Ibrahim serve his guests, the angels who came with good news?
explanation: "He did not delay in bringing a roasted calf."
detail: Surah Hud records the visit: "Our messengers came to Ibrahim with good tidings; they said, 'Peace.' He said, 'Peace,' and did not delay in bringing a roasted calf" (11:69). When he saw that their hands did not reach for it, he grew wary, and they told him, "Do not fear; we have been sent to the people of Lut" (11:70). Surah Adh-Dhariyat adds that he went quietly to his family, brought a fat calf and asked, "Will you not eat?" (51:26-27). A Muslim learns from Ibrahim to return a greeting of peace and to serve a guest quickly, unasked.

question: What good news did the angels bring to Ibrahim's wife?
explanation: "We gave her good tidings of Ishaq, and after Ishaq, Ya'qub."
detail: The verse reads: "And his wife was standing, and she laughed. Then We gave her good tidings of Ishaq, and after Ishaq, Ya'qub" (11:71). She answered, "Woe to me! Shall I give birth while I am an old woman and this, my husband, is an old man?" (11:72), and the angels replied, "Are you amazed at the command of Allah? The mercy of Allah and His blessings be upon you, people of the house" (11:73). A Muslim learns that Allah's gift can arrive long after a person has stopped expecting it.

question: How did Ibrahim's son react when his father told him the dream of sacrificing him?
answers: He accepted: "Do what you are commanded"
explanation: He said: "O my father, do as you are commanded." And Allah ransomed him with a great sacrifice.
detail: Surah As-Saffat tells it from the father's side: "When he reached with him the age of striving, he said, 'O my son, I have seen in a dream that I sacrifice you, so see what you think'" (37:102). The son, unnamed in these verses, answered that his father would find him, if Allah willed, among the steadfast (37:102). "When they had both submitted and he laid him down on his forehead, We called to him, 'O Ibrahim, you have fulfilled the vision'" (37:103-105). A Muslim learns that submission is "if Allah wills" on the lips and steadiness in the heart.

question: In his prayer, where does Ibrahim say he settled some of his family?
answers: In a valley without cultivation, near the Sacred House
explanation: "I have settled some of my descendants in an uncultivated valley near Your Sacred House."
detail: The verse in full: "Our Lord, I have settled some of my descendants in a valley without cultivation near Your Sacred House, our Lord, that they may establish the prayer. So make hearts among the people incline toward them and provide them with fruits, that they may be grateful" (14:37). The prayer had begun, "My Lord, make this city secure and keep me and my sons away from worshipping idols" (14:35). A Muslim notices the order of Ibrahim's asking: first that his family pray, then that people love them, then food.

question: What did Ibrahim ask for the city of Makkah in his prayer?
answers: That it be a secure city and its people be given fruits
explanation: "My Lord, make this a secure city and provide its people with fruits."
detail: The verse continues with Allah's reply: "And when Ibrahim said, 'My Lord, make this a secure city and provide its people with fruits, whoever of them believes in Allah and the Last Day.' He said, 'And whoever disbelieves, I will grant him enjoyment for a little; then I will force him to the punishment of the Fire'" (2:126). Just before, Allah had made the House "a place of return for the people and a place of security" (2:125). A Muslim learns that Allah's provision in this world reaches everyone; the difference appears in the Hereafter.

question: While raising the Ka'ba, Ibrahim and Isma'il asked Allah to send among their descendants… ?
answers: A messenger from among them, reciting His verses
explanation: "Our Lord, send among them a messenger from themselves who will recite to them Your verses."
detail: The prayer is the last of three spoken at the building of the House: "Our Lord, and send among them a messenger from themselves who will recite to them Your verses and teach them the Book and wisdom and purify them" (2:129). Before it, "when Ibrahim was raising the foundations of the House, and Isma'il," they said, "Our Lord, accept from us" (2:127). The Qur'an later describes the sending of Muhammad ﷺ in these very words (62:2). A Muslim sees the Prophet ﷺ as the answer to a prayer made beside the Ka'ba.

question: The Quran says one prophet was, by himself, "a nation (umma)". Which one?
explanation: "Indeed, Ibrahim was a nation, devoutly obedient to Allah, upright."
detail: Surah An-Nahl gives several qualities in one breath: "Indeed, Ibrahim was a nation, devoutly obedient to Allah, inclining toward truth, and he was not of those who associate others with Allah; grateful for His favours, He chose him and guided him to a straight path" (16:120-121). Allah gave him good in this world and a place among the righteous in the Hereafter (16:122). Then comes the command to the Prophet ﷺ: "Follow the religion of Ibrahim, inclining toward truth" (16:123). A Muslim learns that one person alone on the truth can weigh as much as a whole community.

question: For which quality does the Quran praise Isma'il in Surah Maryam?
answers: He was true to his promise
explanation: "Indeed, he was true to his promise, and he was a messenger and a prophet."
detail: Surah Maryam continues past the verse: "And mention in the Book Isma'il. Indeed, he was true to his promise, and he was a messenger and a prophet. And he used to enjoin on his people prayer and zakat, and he was pleasing to his Lord" (19:54-55). The surah names Isma'il in his own right, as a prophet with a message and a people. Elsewhere the Qur'an shows him raising the foundations of the House with his father and praying, "Our Lord, accept from us" (2:127). A Muslim learns that keeping one's word is a quality Allah praises by name.

question: What punishment struck the people of Lut?
answers: A rain of stones of baked clay
explanation: "We turned the city upside down and rained upon it stones of baked clay."
detail: Surah Hud describes the morning: "When Our command came, We made the highest part of the city its lowest and rained upon it stones of hard clay, layered, marked from your Lord" (11:82-83). The night before, the angels had told Lut to leave with his family in the last part of the night, letting none look back except his wife, who would be struck with the rest, and had said, "Their appointed time is the morning. Is not the morning near?" (11:81). A Muslim learns that the punishment was measured and marked, and came at the hour the angels named.

question: The wives of which two prophets does the Quran give as an example of disbelief?
explanation: "Allah presents an example of those who disbelieved: the wife of Nuh and the wife of Lut."
detail: The verse reads: "Allah presents an example of those who disbelieved: the wife of Nuh and the wife of Lut. They were under two of Our righteous servants but betrayed them, so those two did not avail them from Allah at all, and it was said, 'Enter the Fire with those who enter'" (66:10). The next two verses give the opposite example, believing women in houses of disbelief: the wife of Pharaoh, and Maryam (66:11-12). A Muslim learns that each soul answers for its own faith, and that living beside a prophet does not replace believing in him.

question: Who was Ya'qub's father?
explanation: The angels announced to Ibrahim's wife "Ishaq, and after Ishaq, Ya'qub".
detail: Ya'qub is named before his birth in the good news to Ibrahim's wife: "Then We gave her good tidings of Ishaq, and after Ishaq, Ya'qub" (11:71). The Qur'an keeps the line together: "And We gave him Ishaq and Ya'qub in addition, and all of them We made righteous" (21:72). Yusuf in prison said, "I have followed the religion of my fathers, Ibrahim and Ishaq and Ya'qub" (12:38). A Muslim learns that one faith passed from Ibrahim to his son Ishaq, to his grandson Ya'qub, and on to Yusuf.

question: What happened to Ya'qub's eyesight from weeping over Yusuf?
explanation: "His eyes became white from grief, and he was suppressing it."
detail: The verse reads: "And he turned away from them and said, 'Oh, my sorrow over Yusuf,' and his eyes became white from grief, for he was holding it in" (12:84). His sons had just returned from Egypt without their younger brother, saying, "Your son has stolen" (12:81). They told their father he would go on remembering Yusuf until he fell ill or died (12:85), and he answered, "I only complain of my suffering and my grief to Allah" (12:86). A Muslim learns that grief may be deep and still be carried to Allah alone, with hope intact.

question: What restored Ya'qub's sight?
answers: Yusuf's shirt cast over his face
explanation: Yusuf said: "Cast my shirt over my father's face; he will regain his sight."
detail: When Yusuf had made himself known, he said: "Take this shirt of mine and cast it over the face of my father; he will become seeing. And bring me your whole family" (12:93). As the caravan left Egypt, Ya'qub said, "I find the smell of Yusuf" (12:94). Then "when the bearer of good news arrived, he cast it over his face, and he returned to seeing," and Ya'qub said, "Did I not tell you that I know from Allah what you do not know?" (12:96). A Muslim learns that the relief Ya'qub hoped for came from the very son he had wept over.

question: What did Yusuf prefer rather than giving in to what he was wrongly invited to?
explanation: "My Lord, prison is dearer to me than what they invite me to."
detail: The verse is a prayer: "My Lord, prison is dearer to me than that to which they invite me. And if You do not turn their plot away from me, I might incline toward them and be of the ignorant" (12:33), and "his Lord answered him and turned their plot away from him" (12:34). Just before, the wife of al-'Aziz had declared before the women of the city that if he did not obey her he would be imprisoned (12:32). A Muslim learns from Yusuf to choose hardship over sin, and to ask Allah for protection rather than trust his own strength.

question: In prison, two young men told Yusuf their dreams. What did one of them see?
explanation: One saw himself pressing wine, the other carrying bread on his head that birds ate from.
detail: The verse reads: "Two young men entered the prison with him. One of them said, 'I saw myself pressing wine.' The other said, 'I saw myself carrying bread on my head, from which the birds were eating. Tell us its interpretation; we see that you are a doer of good'" (12:36). Before answering, Yusuf spoke to them about the one God and the religion of his fathers (12:37-40). Then he told them: one would serve his master wine, the other would be crucified (12:41). A Muslim learns from Yusuf to put the call to Allah before every other service.

question: How many years of plenty and then of drought did Yusuf foretell to the king?
explanation: "You will sow for seven years… then will come seven difficult years."
detail: Yusuf's answer gave both a reading and a plan: "You will sow for seven years as usual, and what you harvest leave in its ears, except a little from which you eat. Then will come after that seven hard years which will eat up what you stored for them, except a little you keep" (12:47-48). The king had dreamt of seven fat cows eaten by seven lean ones, and seven green ears of grain and others dry (12:43). A Muslim learns from Yusuf that true knowledge serves people: he told them what to do.

question: Which office did Yusuf ask the king of Egypt for?
explanation: "Appoint me over the storehouses of the land: I am a knowing guardian."
detail: The verse reads: "He said, 'Appoint me over the storehouses of the land; indeed, I am a knowing guardian'" (12:55). The king had said, "Bring him to me; I will appoint him exclusively for myself," and after speaking with him, "You are today established and trusted with us" (12:54). The next verse explains: "Thus We established Yusuf in the land, to settle in it wherever he willed" (12:56). A Muslim learns that Yusuf asked for the post where his honesty and knowledge would protect people through the famine, and that Allah counted it among his good deeds.

question: What did Yusuf have placed in his younger brother's baggage to keep him by his side?
explanation: "He put the drinking cup into his brother's bag."
detail: The verse reads: "When he had furnished them with their supplies, he put the drinking cup into the bag of his brother. Then a crier called out, 'O caravan, you are thieves'" (12:70). Yusuf had already taken his brother aside and told him, "I am your brother, so do not grieve over what they used to do" (12:69). The brothers themselves named the penalty (12:75), and the Qur'an then says, "Thus did We plan for Yusuf" (12:76). A Muslim learns that Allah's arrangement worked through Yusuf's wisdom to bring the family together.

question: What advice did Ya'qub give his sons before they entered Egypt?
explanation: "Do not enter through one gate, but enter through different gates."
detail: The verse gives the advice and its limit: "O my sons, do not enter through one gate, but enter through different gates. And I cannot avail you against Allah at all. The decision is only for Allah; upon Him I have relied" (12:67). The next verse says that entering as their father instructed availed them nothing against Allah, but satisfied a need in Ya'qub's soul, "and he was a possessor of knowledge because of what We had taught him" (12:68). A Muslim learns from Ya'qub to take sensible precautions while placing all trust in Allah.

question: Why did Yusuf's brothers come to Egypt when he was in charge there?
answers: To get provisions during the famine
explanation: His brothers came for grain; they entered upon him and did not recognise him.
detail: The verse reads: "And the brothers of Yusuf came and entered upon him; and he recognised them, but they did not know him" (12:58). The hard years Yusuf had foretold had begun (12:48). Having given them their measure, he said, "Bring me a brother of yours from your father. Do you not see that I give full measure and that I am the best of hosts?" (12:59). The boy thrown into the well now stood over the men who did it, and served them. A Muslim learns from Yusuf that power is a chance to do good, not to settle scores.

question: In whose house was baby Musa taken in after being placed in the river?
explanation: Pharaoh's household picked him up, that he might one day be an enemy and a grief to them.
detail: The verse reads: "And the family of Pharaoh picked him up, that he might become to them an enemy and a grief. Indeed, Pharaoh and Haman and their soldiers were sinners" (28:8). Allah had inspired Musa's mother: "Suckle him; but when you fear for him, cast him into the river and do not fear and do not grieve. We will return him to you and make him one of the messengers" (28:7). Pharaoh's wife then said, "Do not kill him" (28:9). A Muslim learns that no plan stands against Allah's: the hunted child was raised in the hunter's house.

question: How did baby Musa finally return to his mother?
answers: He refused every wet nurse, and his sister suggested his mother
Pharaoh returned him out of pity
His mother stole him by night
explanation: Allah made him refuse the wet nurses; his sister suggested a household: it was his mother, who nursed him.
detail: The verses read: "And We had forbidden to him all wet nurses before, so she said, 'Shall I direct you to a household that will take care of him for you and be sincere to him?' So We returned him to his mother, that her eye might be comforted and she might not grieve, and that she might know that the promise of Allah is true" (28:12-13). The sister was there because her mother had told her, "Follow him" (28:11). A Muslim learns that the promise of 28:7 was kept exactly, through a baby's refusal and a girl's quick word.

question: Why did Musa have to leave Egypt in haste, before his mission?
answers: He had killed a man unintentionally with a blow
He had stolen from the palace
explanation: He struck an Egyptian who was fighting a man of his people and killed him; he regretted it at once.
detail: The verse reads: "He entered the city while its people were unaware and found two men fighting, one of his own people and one of his enemies. The one of his people called him for help against his enemy, so Musa struck him and killed him. He said, 'This is of the work of Shaytan; he is a clear, misleading enemy'" (28:15). At once he prayed, "My Lord, I have wronged myself, so forgive me," and Allah forgave him (28:16). A Muslim learns from Musa to name a wrong for what it is and turn to Allah without delay.

question: Who warned Musa that the chiefs were plotting to kill him?
answers: A man who came running from the far end of the city
explanation: "A man came running from the farthest part of the city: they are conspiring to kill you, so leave!"
detail: The verse reads: "And a man came running from the farthest end of the city. He said, 'O Musa, the chiefs are conferring about you to kill you, so leave; I am one of your sincere advisers'" (28:20). The Qur'an does not name him. Musa left the city fearful and watchful, praying, "My Lord, save me from the wrongdoing people" (28:21), and set out toward Madyan hoping his Lord would guide him to the right way (28:22). A Muslim learns that a sincere warning is a mercy, and that leaving in fear can still be done with trust in Allah.

question: Arriving at Madyan, what did Musa do for two women at the watering place?
explanation: He watered their flock, then withdrew to the shade calling on Allah.
detail: The verses read: "He found a crowd of people watering, and apart from them two women holding back their flock. He said, 'What is the matter with you?' They said, 'We cannot water until the shepherds move away, and our father is an old man.' So he watered for them, then turned back to the shade and said, 'My Lord, I am in need of whatever good You send down to me'" (28:23-24). One of the two then came shyly to say that her father invited him (28:25). A Muslim learns from Musa to help the weak unasked, then turn to Allah with his own need.

question: How many years did the old man of Madyan ask Musa to work in order to marry his daughter?
answers: Eight, and ten if he wished
explanation: "You will serve me for eight years; if you complete ten, it will be of your own accord."
detail: The verse reads: "I wish to marry you to one of these two daughters of mine, on condition that you work for me eight years; and if you complete ten, that is from you. I do not want to make it hard for you" (28:27). The Qur'an does not name the old man. One daughter had said, "O my father, hire him; the best you can hire is the strong and the trustworthy" (28:26). Musa accepted, adding, "Allah is witness over what we say" (28:28). A Muslim learns that a fair agreement is stated clearly, made with ease, and sealed with Allah as witness.

question: What did Allah command Musa to remove in the sacred valley of Tuwa?
explanation: "Remove your sandals: you are in the sacred valley of Tuwa."
detail: The verse reads: "Indeed, I am your Lord, so remove your sandals; you are in the sacred valley of Tuwa" (20:12). Musa had seen a fire and gone toward it, and when he came near he was called by name (20:10-11). What follows is the first message he received: "I have chosen you, so listen to what is revealed. Indeed, I am Allah; there is no god but Me, so worship Me and establish the prayer for My remembrance" (20:13-14). A Muslim learns that Musa's mission began with the oneness of Allah and the prayer.

question: What was the second sign given to Musa, after the staff?
answers: His hand came out white, without harm
explanation: "Draw your hand to your side: it will come out white, without disease."
detail: The verse reads: "And draw your hand to your side; it will come out white, without disease, another sign, that We may show you some of Our greatest signs" (20:22-23). It follows the first sign: asked "What is that in your right hand, O Musa?" he described his staff and its everyday uses (20:17-18); told to throw it, he saw it become a moving snake (20:19-20). Then came the command: "Go to Pharaoh; indeed, he has transgressed" (20:24). A Muslim learns that both signs came from ordinary things, a shepherd's staff and his own hand.

question: What did Musa ask Allah for before going to Pharaoh?
answers: To expand his chest and loosen his tongue
explanation: "My Lord, expand for me my chest, ease my task, and untie the knot from my tongue."
detail: The four verses form one prayer: "My Lord, expand for me my chest, and ease for me my task, and untie the knot from my tongue, that they may understand my speech" (20:25-28). Musa said it immediately after being told, "Go to Pharaoh; indeed, he has transgressed" (20:24). He went on to ask for his brother Harun as a helper (20:29-34), and Allah answered, "You have been granted your request, O Musa" (20:36). A Muslim learns from Musa to ask, before any hard task, for an open heart and clear words.

question: Whom did Musa ask Allah to give him as a helper in his mission?
explanation: "Appoint for me a helper from my family: Harun, my brother."
detail: The verses read: "And appoint for me a helper from my family, Harun, my brother. Strengthen me through him and let him share my task, that we may glorify You much and remember You much" (20:29-34). Allah replied, "You have been granted your request, O Musa" (20:36). In Surah Al-Qasas Musa gives his reason: "My brother Harun is more fluent than me in speech, so send him with me as a support" (28:34). The two were then sent to Pharaoh together (20:43). A Muslim learns that asking for help is part of doing a task well.

question: What did Pharaoh's magicians do when Musa's staff swallowed their illusions?
answers: They fell in prostration and believed
explanation: The magicians fell down in prostration: "We believe in the Lord of the worlds, the Lord of Musa and Harun."
detail: The verses read: "And We inspired Musa, 'Throw your staff,' and at once it swallowed up what they were faking. So the truth was established, and what they were doing came to nothing. They were defeated there and turned back humbled. And the magicians fell down in prostration" (7:117-120). These were men who had asked Pharaoh for a reward if they won (7:113-114). Threatened with crucifixion, they answered, "To our Lord we will return" (7:124-125). A Muslim learns that those who knew the craft best were the first to see that this was no craft.

question: Which of these plagues does the Quran list among those sent against Pharaoh's people?
explanation: "We sent upon them the flood, locusts, lice, frogs and blood."
detail: The verse reads: "So We sent upon them the flood and locusts and lice and frogs and blood, as distinct signs, but they were arrogant and were a criminal people" (7:133). Before this, Allah had seized Pharaoh's people with years of drought and shortage of fruits so that they might take heed (7:130). Each time a plague fell they promised to believe if Musa asked his Lord to remove it (7:134), and each time it was lifted they broke their word (7:135). A Muslim learns that signs alone do not change a heart that has decided not to see.

question: According to the Quran, what did Allah do with Pharaoh's body after he drowned?
explanation: "Today We will save your body, so that you may be a sign to those who come after you."
detail: The verse reads: "So today We will save you in body, that you may be a sign to those who come after you. And indeed, many among the people are heedless of Our signs" (10:92). Pharaoh had pursued the Children of Israel into the sea "in tyranny and enmity" until, as he drowned, he said, "I believe that there is no god except the One in whom the Children of Israel believe" (10:90). The answer was, "Now? When you disobeyed before and were of the corrupters?" (10:91). A Muslim learns that faith declared only when death is certain is not accepted.

question: According to the Quran, what did Pharaoh's believing wife ask of Allah?
answers: A house near Him in Paradise
explanation: "My Lord, build for me near You a house in Paradise, and save me from Pharaoh."
detail: The verse reads: "And Allah presents an example of those who believed: the wife of Pharaoh, when she said, 'My Lord, build for me near You a house in Paradise, and save me from Pharaoh and his deeds, and save me from the wrongdoing people'" (66:11). The Qur'an does not give her name. She is set against the wives of Nuh and Lut (66:10), and earlier she was the one who said of the infant Musa, "Do not kill him" (28:9). A Muslim notices that she asked first for nearness, "near You", and only then for the house.

question: How many nights did Allah's appointment with Musa on the mount last?
explanation: "We appointed for Musa thirty nights and completed them with ten: forty nights."
detail: The verse reads: "And We appointed for Musa thirty nights and completed them with ten, so the term of his Lord was completed as forty nights. And Musa said to his brother Harun, 'Take my place among my people, do right, and do not follow the way of the corrupters'" (7:142). Surah Al-Baqara mentions the same forty nights and adds, "then you took the calf after him" (2:51). A Muslim learns that Musa did not leave his people without a guide, and that a people's test often comes while their teacher is away.

question: What happened when Musa asked to see Allah?
answers: Allah manifested to the mount, which crumbled, and Musa fell unconscious
The mount rose into the sky
explanation: "Look at the mount: if it stays in place, you will see Me." The mount was levelled and Musa fell unconscious.
detail: The verse reads: "He said, 'My Lord, show me, that I may look at You.' He said, 'You will not see Me, but look at the mountain; if it remains in its place, then you will see Me.' But when his Lord revealed Himself to the mountain, He made it level, and Musa fell unconscious. When he recovered, he said, 'Glory be to You! I turn to You in repentance, and I am the first of the believers'" (7:143). The next verse tells him he was chosen over the people with Allah's messages and words (7:144). A Muslim learns from Musa that awe before Allah ends in glorifying Him.

question: On what did Allah write admonitions and explanations for Musa?
explanation: "We wrote for him on the Tablets an admonition concerning all things."
detail: The verse reads: "And We wrote for him on the Tablets of all things, an admonition and explanation for all things: 'Take them with firmness and order your people to take the best of it'" (7:145). This came at the meeting where Allah told Musa He had chosen him with His messages and His words (7:144). When Musa found his people with the calf, he threw the Tablets down in anger (7:150), and when the anger subsided he took them up again, "and in their inscription was guidance and mercy" (7:154). A Muslim learns that what Allah writes is to be held firmly and acted on at its best.

question: Who made the calf that the Children of Israel worshipped while Musa was away?
explanation: "As-Samiri has led them astray": from their ornaments he produced a calf that made a lowing sound.
detail: Allah told Musa on the mount: "We have tested your people after you, and as-Samiri has led them astray" (20:85). Musa returned angry and grieved (20:86), and his people said they had thrown in the people's ornaments, "and thus did as-Samiri throw" (20:87). "And he brought out for them a calf, a body with a lowing sound, and they said, 'This is your god and the god of Musa'" (20:88). Harun had already told them, "You are only being tested by it, so follow me" (20:90). A Muslim learns that a crowd can be led into plain falsehood by one man, and that the warner among them was right.

question: How many springs gushed from the rock Musa struck with his staff?
explanation: "Strike the rock with your staff": twelve springs gushed forth, one for each tribe.
detail: The verse reads: "And when Musa prayed for water for his people, We said, 'Strike the rock with your staff.' And twelve springs gushed forth from it; every people knew its drinking place. 'Eat and drink from the provision of Allah, and do not go about the earth spreading corruption'" (2:60). Surah Al-A'raf tells the same event and explains the number: Allah had divided them into twelve tribes, and each tribe knew its own spring (7:160). A Muslim learns that provision from Allah comes joined to a command not to spread corruption on the earth.

question: What food did Allah send down to the Children of Israel in the desert?
explanation: "We sent down upon you manna and quails."
detail: The verse reads: "And We shaded you with clouds and sent down to you manna and quails: 'Eat of the good things We have provided you.' And they did not wrong Us, but they were wronging themselves" (2:57). It comes among the favours listed to the Children of Israel after the rescue from Pharaoh (2:49-50). Later they asked for herbs, cucumbers, garlic, lentils and onions, and were asked, "Would you exchange what is better for what is less?" (2:61). A Muslim learns that food sent from the sky was still met with complaint, and that gratitude is what Allah asks for.

question: What colour was the cow Musa told the Children of Israel to sacrifice?
explanation: "It is a yellow cow, bright in colour, pleasing to those who see."
detail: The verse reads: "They said, 'Call upon your Lord to make clear to us what her colour is.' He said, 'He says it is a yellow cow, bright in colour, pleasing to those who look'" (2:69). Musa had told them, "Allah commands you to slaughter a cow," and they asked whether he was mocking them (2:67). They asked what kind (2:68), then, after the colour, asked yet again (2:70). "So they slaughtered her, though they almost did not" (2:71). A Muslim learns that a simple command grows heavy when met with endless questions.

question: Who, from Musa's people, was swallowed by the earth with his house for his arrogance and wealth?
explanation: Qarun owned vast treasures; "We caused the earth to swallow him and his home."
detail: The passage begins: "Qarun was from the people of Musa, but he oppressed them. And We gave him treasures whose keys would weigh down a band of strong men" (28:76). His people told him not to exult and to seek the Hereafter with what Allah had given him (28:77); he answered, "I was only given it because of knowledge I have" (28:78). "So We caused the earth to swallow him and his home, and he had no company to help him against Allah" (28:81). A Muslim learns that wealth credited to oneself rather than to Allah is a burden, not a gift.

question: Which metal did Allah make soft for Dawud?
explanation: "And We made iron pliable for him."
detail: The verse opens the account of Dawud's favours in Surah Saba: "And We certainly gave Dawud from Us bounty: O mountains, echo praises with him, and the birds. And We made iron pliable for him" (34:10). The next verse tells him what the gift is for: "Make full coats of mail and measure the links precisely, and work righteousness; indeed I see what you do" (34:11). A Muslim learns that a skill is a favour from Allah, to be used for good and under His sight.

question: What did Allah teach Dawud to make, to protect people in battle?
explanation: "We taught him the fashioning of coats of armour to protect you."
detail: Surah Al-Anbiya says: "And We taught him the fashioning of coats of armour for you, to protect you in your battles. So will you be grateful?" (21:80). It follows the verse in which the mountains and the birds glorify Allah with Dawud (21:79), and leads into the wind subjected to Sulayman (21:81). The armour is a gift to the people it protects as much as to Dawud, and the verse ends by asking them for thanks. A Muslim learns to see useful knowledge as a favour that calls for gratitude.

question: Which giant did Dawud kill in battle, according to the Quran?
explanation: "And Dawud killed Jalut, and Allah gave him the kingship and wisdom."
detail: The verse closes the story of Talut's army: "So they defeated them by permission of Allah, and Dawud killed Jalut, and Allah gave him the kingship and wisdom and taught him from what He willed" (2:251). Just before, the small company had prayed: "Our Lord, pour upon us patience, plant firmly our feet and give us victory over the disbelieving people" (2:250). The victory is credited to Allah's permission, and the young Dawud receives both rule and knowledge. A Muslim learns that success comes by Allah's leave, not by numbers.

question: How did King Talut test his army before facing Jalut?
answers: A river: not to drink from it, except a handful
explanation: "Allah will test you with a river: whoever drinks from it is not of me, except one who scoops a handful."
detail: Talut said as he set out with the army: "Allah will test you with a river: whoever drinks from it is not of me, except one who takes a handful with his hand. But they drank from it, except a few" (2:249). He was the king the Children of Israel had asked for (2:247). The few who stayed firm said: "How many a small company has overcome a large company by permission of Allah" (2:249). A Muslim learns that a small act of obedience shows who will hold firm later.

question: What did Allah make glorify Him together with Dawud?
explanation: "And We subjected the mountains to exalt Us, along with Dawud, and the birds."
detail: The verse reads: "And We subjected the mountains to glorify Us along with Dawud, and the birds; and We were the doers" (21:79). It follows the judgement of Dawud and Sulayman on the field (21:78). Surah Sad shows the same scene: the mountains glorifying with him in the evening and at sunrise, and the birds gathered, all turning to him (38:18-19). A Muslim learns that all creation praises Allah, and that a servant who praises Him joins a chorus far larger than himself.

question: Which element did Allah subject to Sulayman to carry him wherever he wished?
explanation: "And to Sulayman, the wind, blowing forcefully by his command towards the blessed land."
detail: The verse reads: "And to Sulayman We subjected the wind, blowing forcefully, running by his command towards the land We had blessed; and We know all things" (21:81). Surah Saba gives its measure: "its morning course was a month and its evening course was a month" (34:12), and Surah Sad says the wind blew gently by his command wherever he directed (38:36). A Muslim learns that even a king's greatest power is a loan from Allah, given for a time and under His knowledge.

question: Which bird brought Sulayman news of the kingdom of Saba?
explanation: The hoopoe returned and said: "I have learned something you do not know, and I bring you sure news from Saba."
detail: Sulayman inspected the birds and asked: "Why do I not see the hoopoe, or is he among the absent?", promising to punish him unless he brought a clear excuse (27:20-21). The hoopoe returned and said: "I have encompassed what you have not encompassed, and I bring you from Saba certain news" (27:22). He reported a queen with a great throne, and a people prostrating to the sun (27:23-24). A Muslim learns that Sulayman listened to a small bird, because true news matters whoever carries it.

question: Which small creature warned its kind to go inside as Sulayman's army approached?
explanation: An ant said: "O ants, enter your dwellings, lest Sulayman and his soldiers crush you unaware."
detail: The verse reads: "When they came upon the valley of the ants, an ant said: O ants, enter your dwellings, lest Sulayman and his soldiers crush you while they do not perceive" (27:18). Sulayman understood her: "He smiled, laughing at her words, and said: My Lord, enable me to be grateful for Your favour upon me and upon my parents, and to do righteousness that pleases You" (27:19). A Muslim learns that a moment of wonder at Allah's creation should turn at once into gratitude.

question: How quickly was the throne of the Queen of Saba brought to Sulayman?
answers: Before his glance returned to him
explanation: The one who had knowledge of the Book said: "I will bring it to you before your glance returns to you."
detail: Sulayman asked his assembly: "Which of you will bring me her throne before they come to me in submission?" (27:38). Then "one who had knowledge of the Book said: I will bring it to you before your glance returns to you. When he saw it placed before him, he said: This is from the favour of my Lord, to test me whether I am grateful or ungrateful" (27:40). A Muslim learns that a great gift is a test answered by thanks.

question: According to the Quran, what did the jinn make for Sulayman?
explanation: "They made for him what he willed: elevated chambers, statues, bowls like reservoirs and fixed cauldrons."
detail: The jinn worked for Sulayman by the permission of his Lord (34:12): "They made for him what he willed of elevated chambers, statues, basins like reservoirs and fixed cauldrons. Work, O family of Dawud, in gratitude; and few of My servants are grateful" (34:13). The same passage warns that any jinn who turned from Allah's command would taste the punishment of the Blaze (34:12). A Muslim learns that abundance is a call to gratitude, and that few answer it.

question: How did the jinn learn of Sulayman's death?
answers: A creature of the earth gnawed his staff and he fell
explanation: Only the "creature of the earth" eating his staff revealed his death; the jinn realised they did not know the unseen.
detail: The verse reads: "When We decreed death for him, nothing showed them his death except a creature of the earth eating his staff. When he fell, it became clear to the jinn that had they known the unseen, they would not have remained in humiliating punishment" (34:14). The jinn had been building and diving for him under his command (34:12-13), and they kept working while he stood. A Muslim learns that the unseen belongs to Allah alone, and that no one else, jinn or human, can see it.

question: What particular prayer did Sulayman make to Allah?
answers: A kingdom no one after him would have
explanation: "My Lord, forgive me and grant me a kingdom such as will not belong to anyone after me."
detail: The prayer reads: "He said: My Lord, forgive me and grant me a kingdom such as will not belong to anyone after me; indeed, You are the Bestower" (38:35). The verse comes right after the Qur'an says that Sulayman was tried and then turned back to his Lord (38:34). Allah answered by subjecting the wind to him and the devils, builders and divers (38:36-37), and said: "This is Our gift, so grant or withhold without account" (38:39). A Muslim notices that Sulayman asked for forgiveness before anything else.

question: What did Allah command Ayyub to do to recover his health?
answers: Strike the ground with his foot: a cool spring gushed
explanation: "Strike with your foot: here is a cool spring to wash with, and to drink."
detail: Ayyub called to his Lord: "Satan has touched me with hardship and torment" (38:41). The answer came: "Strike the ground with your foot; here is a cool spring to wash with and to drink" (38:42). Allah then gave him back his family and their like with them, as a mercy and a reminder (38:43), and said: "We found him patient; an excellent servant, ever turning back to Us" (38:44). A Muslim learns that Ayyub turned to Allah alone in his illness, and that relief came through an act of obedience.

question: What supplication did Yunus make in the darkness of the fish's belly?
answers: "There is no god but You! Glory be to You, I have been among the wrongdoers"
explanation: "He called out in the darkness: there is no deity except You! Exalted are You; I have been of the wrongdoers."
detail: The verse reads: "And the man of the fish, when he went off in anger; then he called out in the darkness: There is no god but You, glory be to You, I have been among the wrongdoers" (21:87). The next verse answers: "So We responded to him and saved him from the distress; and thus do We save the believers" (21:88). A Muslim learns this call for his own distress, because the Qur'an promises that this is how Allah saves the believers.

question: Which plant did Allah make grow over Yunus after the fish cast him out?
explanation: "And We caused to grow over him a gourd vine."
detail: Surah As-Saffat tells the story: Yunus fled to the laden ship, drew lots and lost, and the fish swallowed him while he was blameworthy (37:140-142). "Had he not been of those who glorify Allah, he would have remained in its belly until the Day they are resurrected" (37:143-144). "We cast him onto the open shore while he was ill" (37:145), "and We caused to grow over him a gourd plant" (37:146). A Muslim learns that Allah's care continues after forgiveness, down to the shade over a sick man's head.

question: To how many people was Yunus sent, according to the Quran?
explanation: "And We sent him to a hundred thousand, or more."
detail: The verse reads: "And We sent him to a hundred thousand or more, and they believed, so We gave them enjoyment for a time" (37:147-148). It closes the story of Yunus (37:139-146). Surah Yunus recalls them: no town's faith benefited it when punishment came except the people of Yunus, from whom Allah removed the punishment of disgrace when they believed (10:98). A Muslim learns that a whole people can turn back to Allah together, and that His mercy meets them when they do.

question: What sign did Allah give Zakariyya to confirm the coming of his son?
answers: Not speaking to people for three nights, though sound
explanation: "Your sign is that you will not speak to people for three nights, though sound."
detail: Zakariyya had asked how he could have a son in old age, and was told: "It is easy for Me" (19:8-9). He then asked for a sign: "Your sign is that you will not speak to people for three nights, though sound" (19:10). He then came out to his people and signalled to them to glorify Allah morning and evening (19:11). A Muslim learns that his sign was silence, and that even without speech he kept calling others to praise.

question: What does Allah say about the name Yahya?
answers: No one before him had been given that name
explanation: "We give you good tidings of a boy whose name will be Yahya; We have not given this name to anyone before."
detail: The good news reads: "O Zakariyya, We give you good tidings of a boy whose name will be Yahya; We have not given this name to anyone before" (19:7). It answers the quiet prayer at the surah's opening, where Zakariyya said his bones had weakened and his head was white with age, and asked for an heir pleasing to Allah (19:3-6). Allah chose the name before the child was born. A Muslim learns that Allah answers a private prayer more completely than what was asked.

question: What did Allah grant Yahya while he was still a child?
explanation: "O Yahya, take the Scripture with determination." And We gave him judgement while yet a boy.
detail: The verse reads: "O Yahya, take the Scripture with determination. And We gave him judgement while yet a boy" (19:12). The following verses describe him: tenderness from Allah and purity, fear of Allah, dutiful to his parents, neither a tyrant nor disobedient, and "peace be upon him the day he was born, the day he dies and the day he is raised alive" (19:13-15). Wisdom in childhood came together with kindness to parents. A Muslim learns that true understanding shows in good character, whatever one's age.

question: What had Maryam's mother vowed for the child she was carrying?
answers: To dedicate it to Allah's service
To entrust it to a shepherd
explanation: "My Lord, I have vowed to You what is in my womb, consecrated to Your service."
detail: The verse reads: "When the wife of 'Imran said: My Lord, I have vowed to You what is in my womb, consecrated to Your service, so accept it from me; You are the Hearing, the Knowing" (3:35). When she gave birth she said: "My Lord, I have delivered a female", named her Maryam, and sought refuge with Allah for her and her offspring from Satan (3:36). A Muslim learns from this mother that a child can be offered to Allah before birth, and that Allah accepts.

question: Which prophet took charge of Maryam after her birth?
explanation: "And He put her in the care of Zakariyya," who found with her provision from Allah.
detail: "Her Lord accepted her with good acceptance and put her in the care of Zakariyya. Whenever Zakariyya entered upon her in the prayer chamber, he found with her provision. He said: O Maryam, where does this come from? She said: It is from Allah; Allah provides for whom He wills without account" (3:37). The next verse says that Zakariyya then called on his Lord for a good offspring (3:38). A Muslim learns that seeing Allah's provision to another moved a prophet to ask, with hope, for his own.

question: According to the Quran, Allah chose Maryam above whom?
explanation: "O Maryam, Allah has chosen you and purified you, and chosen you above the women of the worlds."
detail: The verse reads: "When the angels said: O Maryam, Allah has chosen you and purified you, and chosen you above the women of the worlds" (3:42). The angels then told her what to do with that rank: "O Maryam, be devoutly obedient to your Lord, prostrate and bow with those who bow" (3:43). The Qur'an calls this news of the unseen revealed to the Prophet ﷺ (3:44). A Muslim learns that being chosen by Allah leads to more worship, not less.

question: What fell for Maryam when she shook the trunk of the palm tree?
explanation: "Shake the trunk of the palm tree towards you: it will drop upon you fresh, ripe dates."
detail: "The pains of childbirth drove her to the trunk of a palm tree; she said: I wish I had died before this and been forgotten" (19:23). A voice called from below her: "Do not grieve; your Lord has placed beneath you a stream" (19:24), "and shake towards you the trunk of the palm tree: it will drop upon you fresh, ripe dates" (19:25). A Muslim learns that Allah's provision often asks a small effort, and that comfort comes in the hardest hour.

question: What word does the Quran use for Maryam in Surah Al-Ma'ida?
explanation: "The Messiah, son of Maryam, was only a messenger… and his mother was a supporter of truth."
detail: The verse reads: "The Messiah, son of Maryam, was only a messenger; messengers had passed away before him. His mother was a woman of truth. They both used to eat food" (5:75). It answers those in the same passage who said that Allah is the Messiah, or one of three (5:72-73). The same word of truth is given to Yusuf, addressed in prison as "O Yusuf, man of truth" (12:46). A Muslim learns to honour Maryam highly and to worship Allah alone.

question: What title does the Quran give to Isa, son of Maryam?
explanation: "His name will be the Messiah, Isa son of Maryam, distinguished in this world and the Hereafter."
detail: The angels said: "O Maryam, Allah gives you good tidings of a word from Him, whose name is the Messiah, Isa son of Maryam, distinguished in this world and the Hereafter" (3:45). When she asked how she could have a child untouched by any man, she was told: "Thus Allah creates what He wills; when He decrees a matter, He only says to it, Be, and it is" (3:47). A Muslim learns Isa's names and rank from the angels' own words.

question: What did Isa fashion from clay, by Allah's permission?
answers: The shape of a bird, which became alive
explanation: "I design for you from clay the form of a bird, then I breathe into it and it becomes a bird by Allah's permission."
detail: Isa told the Children of Israel: "I have come to you with a sign from your Lord: I design for you from clay the form of a bird, then I breathe into it and it becomes a bird by Allah's permission; I give life to the dead by Allah's permission" (3:49). Twice in one verse the words "by Allah's permission" appear, and Surah Al-Ma'ida repeats them (5:110). A Muslim learns that every miracle of a prophet is Allah's act, and that the prophet is His servant.

question: What are Isa's close companions called, who declared themselves "Allah's helpers"?
explanation: "The disciples said: we are supporters of Allah."
detail: The verse reads: "When Isa sensed disbelief from them, he said: Who are my helpers for Allah? The disciples said: We are the helpers of Allah; we believe in Allah, and bear witness that we are Muslims" (3:52). They asked to be written among the witnesses (3:53). Surah As-Saff calls the believers to be helpers of Allah as the disciples were when Isa asked them (61:14). A Muslim learns that answering a prophet's call means standing with him when others turn away.

question: What did the disciples ask Isa for, which gave Surah Al-Ma'ida its name?
answers: A table spread with food sent down from heaven
explanation: "Can your Lord send down to us a table spread with food from heaven?"
detail: The disciples asked Isa whether his Lord could send down to them a table spread with food from heaven, and he answered: "Fear Allah, if you are believers" (5:112). Isa prayed: "O Allah, our Lord, send down to us a table from heaven, to be a feast for the first of us and the last of us, and a sign from You" (5:114). Allah promised to send it, warning whoever disbelieved after it (5:115). A Muslim learns that a sign given is a trust, not a spectacle.

question: What does the Quran say about the end of Isa's mission on earth?
answers: He was neither killed nor crucified: Allah raised him to Himself
explanation: "They did not kill him, nor did they crucify him… rather, Allah raised him to Himself."
detail: The verses answer a claim: "And for their saying: We killed the Messiah, Isa son of Maryam, the messenger of Allah. They did not kill him, nor did they crucify him, but it was made to appear so to them. They certainly did not kill him. Rather, Allah raised him to Himself" (4:157-158). The passage lists earlier wrongs of the same people, including a grave slander against Maryam (4:156). A Muslim learns to say of Isa's end what the Qur'an says: not killed, not crucified, raised by Allah.

question: By what name did Isa announce a messenger who would come after him?
explanation: "…bringing good tidings of a messenger to come after me, whose name is Ahmad."
detail: Isa said: "O Children of Israel, I am the messenger of Allah to you, confirming the Torah that came before me and bringing good tidings of a messenger to come after me, whose name is Ahmad" (61:6). The verse before records Musa asking his people why they harmed him though they knew he was Allah's messenger (61:5). Each messenger confirms the one before and announces the one after. A Muslim learns that Ahmad is a name of the Prophet ﷺ, announced by Isa long before his birth.

question: Which idol did the prophet Ilyas rebuke his people for worshipping?
explanation: "Do you call upon Ba'l and leave the best of creators?"
detail: Surah As-Saffat says: "Ilyas was among the messengers. When he said to his people: Will you not fear Allah?" (37:123-124), "Do you call upon Ba'l and leave the best of creators, Allah, your Lord and the Lord of your first forefathers?" (37:125-126). They denied him, and will be brought for judgement, except Allah's chosen servants (37:127-128). Allah left him a good name among later generations: "Peace be upon Ilyasin" (37:129-130). A Muslim learns that a prophet's whole argument is that only the Creator deserves to be called upon.

question: Which three prophets does the Quran mention together as "among the patient"?
explanation: "And Isma'il, Idris and Dhul-Kifl: all were of the patient."
detail: The verse reads: "And Isma'il, Idris and Dhul-Kifl: all were of the patient. We admitted them into Our mercy; they were among the righteous" (21:85-86). Surah Al-Anbiya passes from one prophet to the next: just before come Ayyub, whose harm Allah removed (21:83-84), and just after comes Yunus calling out in the darkness (21:87). A Muslim learns that patience is the trait the Qur'an chooses to remember these three by, and that patience leads into Allah's mercy.

question: Which prophet is named in Surah Sad alongside Isma'il and Dhul-Kifl?
explanation: "And remember Isma'il, Al-Yasa' and Dhul-Kifl: all are among the outstanding."
detail: The verse reads: "And remember Isma'il, Al-Yasa' and Dhul-Kifl: all are among the outstanding" (38:48). It follows the mention of Ibrahim, Ishaq and Ya'qub, men of strength and vision whom Allah chose for a special quality, the remembrance of the Hereafter (38:45-47). Al-Yasa' is named once more in Surah Al-An'am, alongside Isma'il, Yunus and Lut, among those Allah preferred over the worlds (6:86). The Qur'an gives him no story, only a rank. A Muslim learns to honour every prophet the Qur'an names, even without a story.

question: What title does the Quran give the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ in verse 33:40?
explanation: "Muhammad… is the Messenger of Allah and the Seal of the Prophets."
detail: The verse reads: "Muhammad is not the father of any of your men, but he is the Messenger of Allah and the Seal of the Prophets; and Allah knows all things" (33:40). It closes the passage about Zayd, whom the Prophet ﷺ had raised as a son (33:37), after the surah stated that adopted sons are not true sons (33:4-5). A seal comes last and closes what went before. A Muslim learns from this verse that no prophet comes after Muhammad ﷺ, and that his message is the last.

question: According to the Quran, as what was the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ sent?
explanation: "We have not sent you except as a mercy to the worlds."
detail: The verse reads: "And We have not sent you except as a mercy to the worlds" (21:107). It stands near the end of Surah Al-Anbiya, which has recounted many prophets, and the next verse gives the heart of his message: "Say: It is only revealed to me that your God is one God, so will you submit?" (21:108). The mercy is not for one people or one time but for the worlds. A Muslim learns that following him ﷺ is meant to carry mercy to everyone his message reaches.

question: According to verse 33:56, what do Allah and His angels do for the Prophet ﷺ?
explanation: "Allah and His angels send blessings upon the Prophet. O believers, send blessings upon him and greet him with peace."
detail: The verse reads: "Allah and His angels send blessings upon the Prophet. O you who believe, send blessings upon him and greet him with peace" (33:56). It follows a description of the Prophet ﷺ as a witness, a bringer of good tidings, a warner, a caller to Allah and a shining lamp (33:45-46). The believers are asked to do on earth what Allah and His angels do above. A Muslim takes from it the habit of asking blessings on him whenever his name is mentioned.

question: How does the Quran describe the Prophet's ﷺ character in Surah Al-Qalam?
answers: "You are of a great moral character"
explanation: "And indeed, you are of a great moral character."
detail: The verse reads: "And indeed, you are of a great moral character" (68:4). It comes at the opening of Surah Al-Qalam, after Allah swears by the pen and what they write that the Prophet ﷺ is not mad by the favour of his Lord, and that his reward is unending (68:1-3). Surah Al-Ahzab adds that in the Messenger of Allah is an excellent example for those who hope in Allah (33:21). A Muslim learns that the Prophet's ﷺ conduct is itself proof of his truth, and a model to follow.

question: What does verse 3:144 remind us about Muhammad ﷺ?
answers: He is only a messenger, and messengers have passed before him
explanation: "Muhammad is not but a messenger; messengers have passed on before him."
detail: The verse reads: "Muhammad is only a messenger; messengers have passed away before him. If he dies or is killed, will you turn back on your heels? Whoever turns back will not harm Allah, and Allah will reward the grateful" (3:144). It belongs to the verses on the battle in which the believers were wounded (3:140). A Muslim learns that faith rests on Allah, who never dies, and that loving the Prophet ﷺ means holding to his message.

question: Which five prophets does verse 33:7 name together for the solemn covenant?
answers: Nuh, Ibrahim, Musa, Isa and Muhammad ﷺ
Adam, Nuh, Hud, Salih and Lut
Dawud, Sulayman, Ayyub, Yunus and Idris
Isma'il, Ishaq, Ya'qub, Yusuf and Musa
explanation: "We took from the prophets their covenant: from you, from Nuh, Ibrahim, Musa and Isa son of Maryam."
detail: The verse reads: "When We took from the prophets their covenant, and from you, and from Nuh, Ibrahim, Musa and Isa son of Maryam; and We took from them a solemn covenant" (33:7). Its purpose follows: "that He may question the truthful about their truthfulness" (33:8). Surah Ash-Shura names the same five: the religion enjoined on Nuh, Ibrahim, Musa and Isa is the one revealed to the Prophet ﷺ (42:13). A Muslim learns that these messengers carried one covenant and one religion.

question: According to a hadith in al-Bukhari, which job did every prophet do?
explanation: "Allah did not send any prophet but that he tended sheep," and the Prophet ﷺ tended them for the people of Makkah.
detail: Abu Hurayra narrates in Sahih al-Bukhari 2262 that the Prophet ﷺ said Allah sent no prophet who had not tended sheep; asked whether he had too, he said he had tended them for the people of Makkah for a small payment. The Qur'an shows Musa in the same work: his staff beat down leaves for his sheep (20:18), and he watered the flocks of the two women of Madyan (28:23-24). A Muslim learns that the prophets earned their living with their hands, and that no honest work is beneath anyone.

question: According to a hadith in Muslim, which prophet worked as a carpenter?
explanation: The Prophet ﷺ said: "Zakariyya was a carpenter."
detail: The hadith is narrated by Abu Hurayra in Sahih Muslim 2379: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that Zakariyya was a carpenter. The Qur'an shows the same prophet in the prayer chamber, caring for Maryam and asking where her provision came from (3:37), and calling on his Lord for a son in his old age (19:3-6). The hadith adds that between these moments he worked with wood for his bread. A Muslim learns that prophethood and a humble trade went together, and that working with the hands carries no shame.

question: Of which prophet did the Prophet ﷺ say he was "the nearest of people", in this world and the next?
explanation: "I am the nearest of all people to Isa son of Maryam in this world and the Hereafter; the prophets are brothers."
detail: The hadith is narrated by Abu Hurayra in Sahih al-Bukhari 3442. The Prophet ﷺ said that in this world and the Hereafter he is the nearest of all people to Isa son of Maryam, that the prophets are brothers from one father, their mothers differ, and their religion is one. The Qur'an records Isa announcing a messenger after him named Ahmad (61:6), and it names no prophet between them. A Muslim learns to love Isa as the Prophet ﷺ loved him, and to see all the prophets as one family.

question: How many surahs of the Quran are named after a prophet?
explanation: Yunus (10), Hud (11), Yusuf (12), Ibrahim (14), Muhammad (47) and Nuh (71).
detail: Six surahs carry a prophet's name, as the list of surah names shows: Yunus (10), Hud (11), Yusuf (12), Ibrahim (14), Muhammad (47) and Nuh (71). Surah Yusuf tells his story and calls it the best of stories (12:3); Surah Nuh is given entirely to his call to his people; Surah Ibrahim holds his prayer for Makkah and his descendants (14:35-41); Surah Muhammad names him in its second verse (47:2). Surah Al-Anbiya is named for the prophets all together. A Muslim learns his way around the Qur'an by these names.

question: With which three words does the Quran describe Ibrahim in verse 11:75?
explanation: "Indeed, Ibrahim was forbearing, grieving and ever-returning to Allah."
detail: The verse reads: "Indeed, Ibrahim was forbearing, tender-hearted and ever-returning to Allah" (11:75). When fear left Ibrahim and the good news reached him, he began to plead with Allah for the people of Lut (11:74), until he was told: "O Ibrahim, leave this; the command of your Lord has come, and a punishment that cannot be turned back is coming to them" (11:76). A Muslim learns that a tender heart pleads even for the astray, while bowing to Allah's decree.

question: What did Shu'ayb rebuke his people for, besides idolatry?
explanation: "Give full measure and weight, and do not deprive people of their due."
detail: Shu'ayb said to the people of Madyan: "O my people, worship Allah; you have no god other than Him. A clear proof has come to you from your Lord, so give full measure and weight, do not deprive people of their due, and do not spread corruption in the land after it has been set right" (7:85). Surah Ash-Shu'ara records the same call to weigh with a straight balance (26:181-182). A Muslim learns that honesty in trade is part of worship, not separate from it.

question: What seized Shu'ayb's people after they rejected his message?
explanation: "So the earthquake seized them, and they became within their home corpses fallen prone."
detail: The verse reads: "So the earthquake seized them, and they lay lifeless in their homes. Those who denied Shu'ayb were as if they had never lived there" (7:91-92). The chiefs had threatened to expel him and the believers (7:88). Then Shu'ayb turned away: "O my people, I conveyed to you the messages of my Lord and advised you; how could I grieve for a disbelieving people?" (7:93). A Muslim learns that a warner who has delivered his message is clear of what follows.

question: What news did the angels give Ibrahim after calming his fear?
answers: That they were sent to the people of Lut
That the Ka'ba would be destroyed
explanation: "Fear not: we have been sent to the people of Lut."
detail: Guests came to Ibrahim with good news and greeted him with peace, and he brought a roasted calf (11:69). "When he saw their hands not reaching for it, he found them strange and felt fear of them. They said: Do not fear; we have been sent to the people of Lut" (11:70). His wife laughed, and was given the good news of Ishaq and, after Ishaq, of Ya'qub (11:71). A Muslim learns that the angels' errand held both mercy for one house and justice for another.

question: What did Ibrahim ask for himself and his descendants in verse 14:40?
explanation: "My Lord, make me an establisher of prayer, and from my descendants."
detail: The verse reads: "My Lord, make me an establisher of prayer, and from my descendants; our Lord, and accept my supplication" (14:40). It belongs to the long prayer Ibrahim made after settling his family by the sacred House: he asked for a secure city and protection from idols (14:35), and said he had placed his descendants in a valley without crops so that they might establish prayer (14:37). A Muslim learns to ask for prayer not only for himself but for his children after him.

question: At the end of Yusuf's story, whom did he raise onto the throne before all bowed down to him?
explanation: "He raised his parents upon the throne, and they fell before him in prostration": the childhood dream came true.
detail: The verse reads: "He raised his parents upon the throne, and they fell down before him in prostration. He said: O my father, this is the meaning of my vision of old; my Lord has made it true. He was good to me when He took me out of prison" (12:100). The vision was the eleven stars, the sun and the moon that Yusuf had seen prostrating to him as a boy (12:4). A Muslim learns that Yusuf, at the height of his honour, gave the credit to Allah.

question: Why did Yusuf's brothers want to get rid of him?
answers: Out of jealousy: their father loved him more
explanation: "Yusuf and his brother are more beloved to our father than we are… Kill Yusuf or cast him out to some land."
detail: The brothers said: "Yusuf and his brother are more beloved to our father than we are, though we are a group; our father is clearly mistaken.
