The verse before it records what the deniers had said: "O Allah, if this should be the truth from You, then rain down upon us stones from the sky or bring us a painful punishment" (8:32). Two shields held the punishment back: the Prophet ﷺ among them, and the seeking of forgiveness. A Muslim learns that asking Allah's forgiveness is a protection for a whole community.

question: To which tribe did the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ belong?
explanation: A whole surah bears the name of his tribe: Quraysh.
detail: The surah opens: "For the accustomed security of Quraysh, their security in the caravan of winter and summer" (106:1-2), then calls on the tribe: "So let them worship the Lord of this House, who has fed them against hunger and made them safe from fear" (106:3-4). Quraysh lived beside the Ka'ba and traded in two yearly journeys, and the Qur'an reminds them that both come from Allah. A Muslim learns that the Prophet ﷺ was sent first to his own tribe, and that honour carries a duty to worship.

question: From which clan of Quraysh did the Prophet ﷺ come?
explanation: The Prophet ﷺ belonged to Banu Hashim, the clan of his great-grandfather Hashim.
detail: Every standard biography records the lineage as Muhammad, son of 'Abdullah, son of 'Abd al-Muttalib, son of Hashim, and the clan takes its name from Hashim. Banu Hashim was one of the clans of Quraysh settled around the Ka'ba, and its head, Abu Talib, sheltered his nephew through the Makkan years. When Quraysh boycotted the Muslims, all of Banu Hashim were shut out with him. A Muslim learns that the Prophet ﷺ grew up inside a clan that protected him before it believed him.

question: What was the name of the wet nurse who nursed the Prophet ﷺ in the desert?
explanation: Following Makkan custom, the infant was entrusted to a Bedouin wet nurse: Halima as-Sa'diyya.
detail: Halima came from Banu Sa'd, and every standard biography tells how she arrived in Makkah with the women of her tribe seeking infants to nurse, took the orphan whose father had died, and carried him to the desert, where Makkan families sent their children for clean air and pure Arabic. The biographies record that her household's flocks increased while he was with them, and that she kept him beyond the usual term before returning him to his mother Amina. A Muslim learns that the Prophet's ﷺ first years were spent simply, among ordinary people.

question: Which uncle of the Prophet ﷺ, a hero of Badr, fell as a martyr at Uhud?
explanation: Hamza ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib fought at Badr and was killed at the battle of Uhud.
detail: Hamza was the son of 'Abd al-Muttalib and so the Prophet's ﷺ uncle, though close to him in age; the biographies record that both were nursed by the same woman, Thuwayba. He accepted Islam in Makkah after standing up to Abu Jahl, who had insulted his nephew, and at Badr he fought in the single combat that opened the battle. At Uhud he was killed by Wahshi, an Abyssinian slave who later accepted Islam and told the story himself. A Muslim remembers Hamza as a man who defended the Prophet ﷺ before believing and gave his life after believing.

question: Which cousin of the Prophet ﷺ, raised in his home, became the fourth caliph?
explanation: 'Ali, son of Abu Talib, grew up with the Prophet ﷺ and was the fourth rightly guided caliph.
detail: The biographies record that Abu Talib had many children and little means, so the Prophet ﷺ took his young cousin 'Ali into his own home to ease his uncle's burden. 'Ali was a boy when revelation came and accepted Islam among the very first; he married Fatima, slept in the Prophet's ﷺ bed on the night of the Hijra and carried the banner at Khaybar. After 'Uthman he received the pledge of allegiance in Madinah. A Muslim learns that for 'Ali, closeness to the Prophet ﷺ was a matter of upbringing and of faith together.

question: Who was the first caliph after the Prophet's ﷺ death?
explanation: Abu Bakr as-Siddiq was chosen as the first caliph.
detail: Every standard biography records that on the day the Prophet ﷺ died, the companions gathered at the meeting-place of Banu Sa'ida in Madinah and gave Abu Bakr the pledge of allegiance, 'Umar being the first to take his hand. During his final illness the Prophet ﷺ had ordered Abu Bakr to lead the prayer in his place, which the companions took as a sign of his standing. The Qur'an speaks of him, unnamed, as the second of two in the cave (9:40). A Muslim learns that leadership after the Prophet ﷺ went to the man closest to him in faith and in trial.

question: What title does Abu Bakr carry, for believing the Prophet ﷺ without hesitation?
explanation: Abu Bakr is called as-Siddiq, the one who affirms and believes the truth.
detail: The biographies link the title to the morning after the Night Journey, when the Prophet ﷺ told the Makkans he had travelled to Jerusalem and back in one night. Quraysh ran to Abu Bakr expecting him to doubt, and he answered that if the Prophet ﷺ had said it, it was true, since he already believed him about news from heaven every morning and evening. The Qur'an speaks of him as the second of two in the cave, told not to grieve (9:40). A Muslim learns that believing the Prophet ﷺ without hesitation is itself a mark of honour.

question: What title does 'Umar ibn al-Khattab carry?
explanation: 'Umar is called al-Faruq, the one who separates truth from falsehood.
detail: The biographies record that when 'Umar accepted Islam in Makkah, the Muslims, who had prayed in hiding, went out and prayed openly at the Ka'ba, and that from this came his title: through him truth was set apart from falsehood in the open. Sahih al-Bukhari records the companions saying that they had been strong since 'Umar embraced Islam. He later became the second caliph, named by Abu Bakr before his death. A Muslim learns that courage in showing the truth openly is a gift others draw strength from.

question: Why is 'Uthman ibn 'Affan called "Dhun-Nurayn", the possessor of two lights?
answers: He married two daughters of the Prophet ﷺ, one after the other
explanation: 'Uthman married Ruqayya and, after her death, Umm Kulthum, both daughters of the Prophet ﷺ.
detail: The biographies record that 'Uthman emigrated with Ruqayya to Abyssinia during the persecution in Makkah, and later to Madinah. When the Muslims marched to Badr she was ill, and the Prophet ﷺ told him to stay and care for her; she died while the army was away, and the Prophet ﷺ still counted him among the men of Badr. He then married her sister Umm Kulthum, who also died in his lifetime. A Muslim learns that 'Uthman's honour came from his closeness to the Prophet's ﷺ household.

question: In which order did the four rightly guided caliphs succeed one another?
explanation: Abu Bakr, then 'Umar, then 'Uthman, then 'Ali.
detail: Every standard biography records how each caliph came to lead. Abu Bakr received the pledge of allegiance on the day the Prophet ﷺ died, and before his own death named 'Umar to follow him; 'Umar, mortally wounded, entrusted the choice to a council of six companions, who chose 'Uthman; after 'Uthman was killed in Madinah, its people gave their pledge to 'Ali. The four are called rightly guided because they governed by the Qur'an and the Prophet's ﷺ example. A Muslim learns their order as the first chapter of the community's history after its Prophet ﷺ.

question: Who was the first person to believe in the Prophet's ﷺ message?
explanation: Khadija believed in him from the first revelation and supported him.
detail: Every standard biography records that when the Prophet ﷺ came home trembling from the cave of Hira after the first revelation, Khadija covered him and said that Allah would never disgrace him, because he kept ties with his kin, carried the burdens of the weak, gave to the poor and honoured guests. She then took him to her cousin Waraqa ibn Nawfal, who knew the earlier scriptures and told him that this was the angel who had come to Musa. A Muslim learns that the first to say yes to the message was the one who knew the Messenger ﷺ best.

question: Who bought Bilal to free him from his master's torture?
explanation: Abu Bakr bought Bilal and set him free.
detail: The biographies record that Bilal was an Abyssinian slave in Makkah whose master, Umayya ibn Khalaf, laid him on the burning sand at midday with a heavy rock on his chest to make him renounce his faith, and that Bilal answered only "Ahad, Ahad", One, One. Abu Bakr, who had wealth from trade, paid the master his price and freed him for the sake of Allah. Bilal later became the Prophet's ﷺ caller to prayer in Madinah. A Muslim learns that Abu Bakr spent his money to free the oppressed.

question: Who was the first martyr of Islam, killed in Makkah for her faith?
explanation: Sumayya bint Khayyat, mother of 'Ammar ibn Yasir, was killed by Abu Jahl.
detail: The biographies record that Yasir, his wife Sumayya and their son 'Ammar were among the weak of Makkah with no clan to protect them, and that Abu Jahl and others tortured the family in the heat to make them abandon Islam. The Prophet ﷺ passed by them and said: "Patience, family of Yasir, your appointed meeting is Paradise." Abu Jahl killed Sumayya with a spear; he himself fell at Badr, while 'Ammar lived on as a companion. A Muslim learns that the first martyr of Islam was a woman who chose her faith over her life.

question: To which land did the first emigration of Muslims persecuted in Makkah take place?
explanation: The first emigrants went to Abyssinia, to a just king.
detail: Every standard biography records that when the persecution in Makkah became unbearable, the Prophet ﷺ told his companions that in Abyssinia there was a king under whom no one was wronged, and sent them to seek refuge with him. They crossed the Red Sea in two groups; among them were 'Uthman and his wife Ruqayya, the Prophet's ﷺ daughter. Quraysh sent envoys with gifts asking the king to hand the Muslims back, and he refused. A Muslim learns that seeking safety in a just land, even one not yet Muslim, was the Prophet's ﷺ own counsel.

question: What was the king of Abyssinia called, who protected the Muslims and for whom the Prophet ﷺ prayed the funeral prayer in absence?
explanation: The Prophet ﷺ announced the Negus's death the day it happened and prayed over him with the companions.
detail: The hadith is narrated by Abu Hurayra and recorded in Sahih al-Bukhari 1245: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ announced the death of the Negus on the very day he died, went out with the companions to the place of prayer, arranged them in rows and said four takbirs. No news had reached Madinah from Abyssinia, so the announcement was itself a sign of prophethood. The Negus had sheltered the Muslims who fled Makkah and refused to surrender them to Quraysh. A Muslim learns that the Prophet ﷺ honoured the king who protected the weak.

question: Which companion spoke before the Negus to explain Islam?
explanation: Ja'far explained to the king what the Prophet ﷺ taught, and recited verses of Surah Maryam to him.
detail: The biographies preserve the scene as told by Umm Salama, one of the emigrants. Ja'far, 'Ali's elder brother, told the king that his people had lived in ignorance, worshipping idols and wronging the weak, until Allah sent them a messenger who called them to worship Allah alone, speak the truth, keep ties of kinship and protect their neighbours. When the king asked to hear the revelation, Ja'far recited from Surah Maryam, the Negus wept, and he refused to hand the Muslims over. A Muslim learns that Islam was first explained abroad in plain words and verses of the Qur'an.

question: Which uncle of the Prophet ﷺ is condemned by name in the Quran?
explanation: "May the hands of Abu Lahab perish, and may he perish."
detail: The surah reads: "May the hands of Abu Lahab be ruined, and ruined is he. His wealth will not avail him, nor what he gained. He will burn in a Fire of flame, and his wife, the carrier of firewood, upon her neck a rope of twisted fibre" (111:1-5). Sahih al-Bukhari records the occasion: when the Prophet ﷺ climbed the hill of Safa and called Quraysh to warn them, his uncle Abu Lahab answered that he hoped he would perish, and the surah came down. A Muslim learns that kinship with the Prophet ﷺ was no protection for a man who fought his message.

question: What is the year called in which the Prophet ﷺ lost his wife Khadija and his uncle Abu Talib?
explanation: The Prophet's ﷺ two great supporters died in the same year, known as the Year of Sorrow.
detail: Every standard biography records that Abu Talib and Khadija died within a short span in the tenth year of the mission. Abu Talib, though he never entered Islam, had used his standing as head of Banu Hashim to keep Quraysh from harming his nephew; the Qur'an speaks of him when it says that the Prophet ﷺ cannot guide whom he loves (28:56). With both gone, Quraysh treated him more harshly, and he went to Ta'if to seek support. A Muslim learns that even the Prophet ﷺ grieved, and that grief is no failing of faith.

question: In which town was the Prophet ﷺ driven out and hurt after calling to Islam, before refusing to let the angel of the mountains crush its people?
explanation: Rejected at Ta'if, he refused to destroy its people, hoping their descendants would worship Allah.
detail: The hadith is narrated by 'Aisha and recorded in Sahih al-Bukhari 3231. She asked the Prophet ﷺ whether any day had been harder for him than Uhud, and he answered that the hardest was when he presented himself to the chiefs of Ta'if and was refused, then walked away in grief until a cloud shaded him and Jibril called with the angel of the mountains, who offered to crush the people between the two mountains of Makkah. The Prophet ﷺ replied that he hoped Allah would bring out of their descendants people who worship Him alone. A Muslim learns to answer cruelty with hope.

question: During the Night Journey and Ascension (Isra and Mi'raj), which obligation was prescribed for Muslims?
explanation: The prayers were prescribed that night, reduced from fifty to five, with the reward of fifty.
detail: The hadith is narrated by Anas from Abu Dharr and recorded in Sahih al-Bukhari 349: Jibril washed his chest with Zamzam water, filled it from a golden tray of wisdom and faith, and took him up through the heavens, where he met Adam, Idris, Musa, 'Isa and Ibrahim. There Allah made fifty prayers a day obligatory; Musa told him his community could not bear it, and he returned again and again until they were five, counted as fifty in reward. A Muslim learns that the daily prayer was given in the highest place and lightened out of mercy.

question: Which tree, at the farthest boundary, did the Prophet ﷺ see during the Ascension, according to Surah An-Najm?
explanation: "Near Sidrat al-Muntaha", the lote tree of the utmost boundary.
detail: Surah An-Najm describes the vision: "And he certainly saw him in another descent" (53:13), "near the Lote Tree of the Utmost Boundary" (53:14), "near which is the Garden of Refuge, when there covered the Lote Tree that which covered it. The sight did not swerve, nor did it exceed" (53:15-17). The surah opens by swearing by the star that the Prophet ﷺ has not gone astray and speaks only what is revealed to him (53:1-4). A Muslim learns that what the Prophet ﷺ reported of the Ascension is confirmed by the Qur'an itself.

question: What are the pledges of allegiance called that people of Yathrib gave the Prophet ﷺ before the Hijra?
explanation: People of Yathrib pledged allegiance to the Prophet ﷺ at Al-'Aqaba, near Mina, before the Hijra.
detail: Every standard biography records two pledges, given in successive pilgrimage seasons at the pass of Al-'Aqaba, where the Prophet ﷺ met the men of Yathrib by night, away from Quraysh. At the first, twelve men pledged, as Sahih al-Bukhari records from 'Ubada ibn as-Samit, not to associate anything with Allah, not to steal, not to commit adultery and not to kill their children. At the second, more than seventy men and two women pledged to defend him as they defended their own families. A Muslim learns that the community of Madinah began with a promise given quietly in the dark.

question: Which companion did the Prophet ﷺ send to Yathrib, before the Hijra, to teach Islam?
explanation: Mus'ab ibn 'Umayr was the first envoy to Yathrib, teaching the Quran to the new Muslims.
detail: The biographies record that after the first pledge at Al-'Aqaba the people of Yathrib asked for a teacher, and the Prophet ﷺ sent Mus'ab ibn 'Umayr, a young man of Quraysh who had left a life of ease for Islam. He lodged with As'ad ibn Zurara, recited the Qur'an to whoever would listen, and through him the chiefs Sa'd ibn Mu'adh and Usayd ibn Hudayr entered Islam. He was killed at Uhud carrying the banner, with only a cloak for a shroud. A Muslim learns that the faith reached Madinah through one patient teacher.

question: Who slept in the Prophet's ﷺ bed on the night he left for the Hijra?
explanation: 'Ali took his place in the bed to mislead those watching, then returned the deposits to the Makkans.
detail: Every standard biography records that the clans of Quraysh agreed to send a young man from each to strike the Prophet ﷺ together; the Qur'an recalls it: "when those who disbelieved plotted against you to confine you or kill you or drive you out; they plan, and Allah plans" (8:30). The Prophet ﷺ told 'Ali to lie in his bed under his green cloak and left unseen, charging 'Ali to return the goods that Makkans had left in his safekeeping. A Muslim learns that the Prophet ﷺ kept his trusts even to those who plotted his death.

question: In which cave did the Prophet ﷺ and Abu Bakr hide during the Hijra?
explanation: They hid for three days in the cave of Thawr, south of Makkah.
detail: Thawr lies south of Makkah while Madinah lies north; the two men went the opposite way first to throw off the search. The Qur'an speaks of this moment: "the second of two, when they were in the cave, when he said to his companion, 'Do not grieve, indeed Allah is with us'" (9:40). Sahih al-Bukhari records Abu Bakr's fear that a searcher looking under his feet would see them, and the Prophet's ﷺ answer asking what he thought of two whose third was Allah. A Muslim learns that trust in Allah stays calm even in danger.

question: Which daughter of Abu Bakr brought provisions to the cave and was nicknamed "she of the two belts"?
explanation: Asma tore her belt in two to tie up the provisions: hence "Dhat an-Nitaqayn".
detail: The long account of the Hijra narrated by 'Aisha in Sahih al-Bukhari 3905 tells how the two men hid in the cave of Thawr for three nights, how Abu Bakr's son 'Abdullah brought news each evening, and how 'Amir ibn Fuhayra brought sheep for milk. Asma prepared the provisions, and finding nothing to tie the food bag, cut her waist-belt in two and used one half; from that she was named Dhat an-Nitaqayn. A Muslim learns that the Hijra succeeded through the quiet service of a whole family.

question: What happened to Suraqa, who pursued the Prophet ﷺ during the Hijra?
answers: His horse sank into the ground, and he asked for safety
He caught up with the Prophet ﷺ
He got lost in the desert
explanation: His horse's legs sank into the earth; Suraqa asked for safe conduct and left without harm.
detail: Suraqa ibn Malik tells the story himself in Sahih al-Bukhari 3906. When a man mentioned seeing riders on the coast, Suraqa, hoping for the reward Quraysh had offered, rode after them; as he drew close, his horse's forelegs sank into the ground up to the knees. He called out for safety, and the Prophet ﷺ had 'Amir ibn Fuhayra write him a guarantee on a piece of leather. A Muslim learns that Allah protected His Messenger ﷺ on the open road as He had in the cave.

question: What was the old name of Madinah, mentioned in the Quran?
explanation: "O people of Yathrib…", says the Quran, recalling the battle of the confederates.
detail: The verse records the hypocrites during the siege of Madinah: "And when a faction of them said, 'O people of Yathrib, there is no place for you here, so return', and a party of them asked permission of the Prophet, saying, 'Our houses are exposed', while they were not exposed; they wanted only to flee" (33:13). Sahih al-Bukhari records the Prophet ﷺ saying that people called it Yathrib but it was Madinah. A Muslim learns that the old name survives in the Qur'an in the mouths of those who wished to abandon the city.

question: What was the name of the Prophet's ﷺ she-camel, which knelt at Hudaybiyya?
explanation: At Hudaybiyya, Al-Qaswa knelt; the Prophet ﷺ said: "The One who held back the elephant has held her back."
detail: The long hadith of Hudaybiyya in Sahih al-Bukhari 2731 tells that the Prophet ﷺ set out with more than a thousand companions to perform 'umra, and that at the pass near Makkah Al-Qaswa knelt and would not rise. The people said she had become stubborn, and the Prophet ﷺ answered that stubbornness was not her nature, but that the One who had held back the elephant from Makkah had held her back. He then swore to grant Quraysh any request that honoured the sanctity of Allah's House. A Muslim learns that the Prophet ﷺ read Allah's will even in the halting of his camel.

question: What did the Prophet ﷺ establish between the Muhajirun and the Ansar on arriving in Madinah?
explanation: He made the emigrants and the helpers brothers, each Muhajir paired with a brother from the Ansar.
detail: Every standard biography records that soon after arriving in Madinah the Prophet ﷺ gathered the emigrants and the helpers in the house of Anas ibn Malik and joined them as brothers two by two. The Qur'an praises the Ansar for this: "those who settled in the home and in faith before them love those who emigrated to them, and find no need in their breasts for what the emigrants were given, and give them preference over themselves even though they are in need" (59:9). Sahih al-Bukhari records that Sa'd ibn ar-Rabi' offered his brother 'Abd ar-Rahman ibn 'Awf half his wealth. A Muslim learns that brotherhood in faith was made real by sharing.

question: What is the document called by which the Prophet ﷺ organised relations between the communities of Madinah?
explanation: The Sahifa set out the rights and duties of the Muslims and the other tribes of Madinah.
detail: Every standard biography preserves the text of the document the Prophet ﷺ drew up on arriving in Madinah. It declares that the believers of Quraysh and of Yathrib, and whoever joins them, are one community apart from all other people; that the Jewish tribes who enter the pact are a community alongside the believers, the Jews having their religion and the Muslims theirs; that Yathrib is inviolable and will be defended together; and that any dispute is referred to Allah and to Muhammad ﷺ. A Muslim learns that the first Muslim city was founded on written obligations shared with its non-Muslim neighbours.

question: What were the poor companions called who lived in the Prophet's ﷺ mosque?
answers: Ahl as-Suffa (the people of the bench)
explanation: Abu Hurayra relates that he was among the people of the Suffa, fed by the Prophet ﷺ.
detail: Sahih al-Bukhari 6452 records Abu Hurayra's account of his hunger: he would tie a stone to his belly, and once sat on the road hoping to be fed; Abu Bakr and 'Umar passed by without noticing. Then the Prophet ﷺ came, smiled and took him home, where a cup of milk had been sent as a gift. He told Abu Hurayra to call the people of the Suffa, the guests of Islam with no family or wealth, and to serve each until all had drunk their fill, then drank what remained himself. A Muslim learns that the poorest companions were the Prophet's ﷺ own guests.

question: How many years after the Hijra did the battle of Badr take place?
explanation: Badr was fought in 2 AH, during Ramadan.
detail: Every standard biography places the battle in Ramadan of the second year after the Hijra, when the Prophet ﷺ set out with a little over three hundred men to intercept a Quraysh caravan and instead met an army of about a thousand from Makkah. The Qur'an calls that day the day of the criterion, the day the two armies met (8:41), and reminds the believers: "Allah had already given you victory at Badr when you were few" (3:123). A Muslim learns that Badr was the first proof that the small community in Madinah would survive.

question: How many angels did Allah promise to send as reinforcement to the believers at Badr?
explanation: "I will reinforce you with a thousand angels, following one another."
detail: The verse belongs to the account of Badr in Surah Al-Anfal: "When you asked help of your Lord, and He answered you, 'Indeed, I will reinforce you with a thousand of the angels, following one another'" (8:9). The next verse explains their purpose: "Allah made it only as good tidings and so that your hearts would be assured; victory is only from Allah" (8:10). The surah then recalls the drowsiness that calmed the believers and the rain that steadied their feet (8:11). A Muslim learns that help from Allah may come unseen, and that it is Allah, not numbers, who gives victory.

question: At Uhud, which mistake by the archers turned the battle?
answers: They left the hill despite the Prophet's ﷺ order
explanation: The Prophet ﷺ had ordered the archers not to move; most came down for the spoils and the enemy cavalry went round them.
detail: The hadith is narrated by al-Bara' ibn 'Azib in Sahih al-Bukhari 3039. The Prophet ﷺ placed 'Abdullah ibn Jubayr over fifty archers and told them not to leave their position, whether they saw the Muslims defeated or victorious, until he sent for them. When Quraysh broke and their women fled up the hillside, the archers said the spoils were there for the taking; Ibn Jubayr reminded them of the order, but they went down anyway, and their faces were then turned about. A Muslim learns that obeying the Prophet's ﷺ command mattered more than any gain of the moment.

question: Near which city is Mount Uhud?
explanation: Mount Uhud lies north of Madinah; the battle took place at its foot.
detail: Every standard biography places Mount Uhud a short ride north of Madinah, so that the Muslims marched out from the city and camped with the mountain at their backs. The Qur'an speaks of that morning: "when you left your household to post the believers at their stations for the battle" (3:121). Sahih al-Bukhari records the Prophet ﷺ saying that it is a mountain that loves us and we love it, and Hamza and the other martyrs were buried at its foot. A Muslim learns that a mountain of Madinah is remembered with affection because of who died beneath it.

question: Which companion suggested digging a trench to defend Madinah against the confederates?
explanation: Salman the Persian suggested the trench, a tactic known in Persia.
detail: Every standard biography records Salman's long journey: born in Persia, he left his father's fire-worship, served Christian monks in several towns, was told that a prophet would appear in a land of date palms, and reached Madinah as a slave, where the Prophet ﷺ helped him buy his freedom. When the confederates marched on Madinah, Salman proposed digging a trench across the open side of the city, a defence he had seen in Persia, and the Prophet ﷺ carried earth alongside the companions. A Muslim learns that good counsel is welcome whatever land it comes from.

question: By what other name is the battle of the Trench known, after the surah that speaks of it?
explanation: Surah Al-Ahzab recalls the allied armies that besieged Madinah and the wind sent against them.
detail: The surah recalls the siege: "O you who believe, remember the favour of Allah upon you when armies came to you and We sent upon them a wind and armies you did not see" (33:9), "when they came at you from above you and from below you, and when eyes shifted and hearts reached the throats" (33:10). The believers, seeing the confederates, said this was what Allah and His Messenger had promised them (33:22), and Allah turned the disbelievers back having gained nothing (33:25). A Muslim learns that the siege was broken by a wind and by faith, not by a sword.

question: What is the pledge called that was given under a tree at Hudaybiyya, with which Allah says He was pleased?
explanation: "Allah was pleased with the believers when they pledged allegiance to you under the tree."
detail: The verse reads: "Certainly Allah was pleased with the believers when they pledged allegiance to you under the tree, and He knew what was in their hearts, so He sent down tranquillity upon them and rewarded them with an imminent conquest" (48:18). Sahih al-Bukhari records the occasion: the Prophet ﷺ had sent 'Uthman into Makkah as his envoy, and when word came that he had been killed, the Prophet ﷺ called the companions to pledge themselves to him under a tree at Hudaybiyya. A Muslim learns that Allah Himself recorded His approval of those who stood by His Messenger ﷺ.

question: Which surah opens with "We have given you a clear victory", revealed after the treaty of Hudaybiyya?
explanation: "Indeed, We have given you a clear victory": Surah Al-Fath.
detail: The surah begins: "Indeed, We have given you a clear conquest, that Allah may forgive you what preceded of your sin and what will follow" (48:1-2). Sahih al-Bukhari records that it came down on the road back from Hudaybiyya, and that the Prophet ﷺ said a surah had been revealed to him dearer than everything on which the sun rises. The companions had felt the treaty as a setback; the revelation named it a conquest. A Muslim learns that Allah's judgement of an event may be the reverse of what it looks like on the day.

question: In which year of the Hijra was the treaty of Hudaybiyya concluded?
explanation: The treaty of Hudaybiyya was concluded in 6 AH between the Muslims and Quraysh.
detail: Every standard biography places the treaty in Dhul-Qa'da of the sixth year after the Hijra, when the Prophet ﷺ had come to perform 'umra and Quraysh barred the way. Sahih al-Bukhari preserves its terms: the Muslims would return that year and come back the next for three days; there would be no fighting for ten years; and anyone who came from Quraysh to the Prophet ﷺ without permission would be sent back. The next year the Prophet ﷺ performed the 'umra as agreed. A Muslim learns that a hard peace, kept faithfully, opened the way to Makkah.

question: Which Byzantine emperor received the Prophet's ﷺ letter inviting him to Islam and questioned Abu Sufyan about him?
explanation: Heraclius questioned Abu Sufyan about the Prophet ﷺ after receiving his letter.
detail: Sahih al-Bukhari 7 records, from Ibn 'Abbas, how Heraclius summoned Abu Sufyan and the Makkan traders in Syria and questioned him about the man claiming prophethood: his lineage, who followed him, whether he had ever lied or broken a pact, and what he commanded. Abu Sufyan, still an enemy, answered truthfully, and Heraclius concluded that if this was so, the man would one day rule the ground beneath his feet. The letter, then read out, quoted the call to the People of the Scripture to a common word (3:64). A Muslim learns that even an enemy's honest testimony bore witness to the Prophet ﷺ.

question: To whom did the Prophet ﷺ hand the banner at Khaybar, after saying: "Tomorrow I will give it to a man whom Allah and His Messenger love"?
explanation: He called 'Ali, who had sore eyes; he applied his saliva, cured him and gave him the banner.
detail: The hadith is narrated by Sahl ibn Sa'd in Sahih al-Bukhari 3701. The companions spent the night wondering who would receive the banner, and in the morning each hoped for it, but the Prophet ﷺ asked for 'Ali, who was suffering from his eyes; he applied his saliva, prayed for him, and 'Ali was healed as if nothing had troubled him. Handing him the banner, he told him to advance calmly and invite the people to Islam first, for Allah to guide one man through him was better than red camels. A Muslim learns that the aim of the banner was guidance before conquest.

question: Which three commanders fell one after another at the battle of Mu'ta?
answers: Zayd ibn Haritha, Ja'far ibn Abi Talib and 'Abdullah ibn Rawaha
explanation: The Prophet ﷺ announced in Madinah: "Zayd took the banner and fell, then Ja'far, then Ibn Rawaha… then a sword of Allah took it."
detail: The hadith is narrated by Anas in Sahih al-Bukhari 4262. Before any messenger had arrived from the battlefield, the Prophet ﷺ told the people in Madinah that Zayd had taken the banner and been struck down, then Ja'far, then Ibn Rawaha, his eyes flowing with tears as he spoke, until a sword among the swords of Allah took it and Allah granted them victory. Zayd ibn Haritha is the only companion named in the Qur'an (33:37). A Muslim learns that the Prophet ﷺ wept for his companions and honoured them in the order they fell.

question: Which companion did the Prophet ﷺ call "a sword among the swords of Allah"?
explanation: At Mu'ta, "a sword among the swords of Allah", Khalid ibn al-Walid, took the banner and saved the army.
detail: The words come from the hadith of Anas in Sahih al-Bukhari 4262, in which the Prophet ﷺ said that the banner was then taken by a sword among the swords of Allah, through whom Allah gave the Muslims victory. Every standard biography identifies him as Khalid ibn al-Walid, who had led the Quraysh cavalry against the Muslims at Uhud and accepted Islam after the treaty of Hudaybiyya; at Mu'ta he drew the army back to safety. A Muslim learns that a title given by the Prophet ﷺ can outlast a man's earlier enmity.

question: What did the Prophet ﷺ do with the idols around the Ka'ba at the conquest of Makkah?
answers: He knocked them down reciting "Truth has come and falsehood has vanished"
explanation: He struck the idols with his stick saying: "Truth has come and falsehood has vanished."
detail: The hadith is narrated by Ibn Mas'ud in Sahih al-Bukhari 4287: when the Prophet ﷺ entered Makkah on the day of the conquest, there were three hundred and sixty idols around the Ka'ba, and he went among them striking them with a stick and reciting: "Truth has come and falsehood has vanished; indeed falsehood is ever bound to vanish" (17:81), together with a verse of Surah Saba (34:49). The first verse had been revealed years earlier in Makkah, while the idols still stood. A Muslim learns that the House built for the worship of Allah alone was cleared in the words of the Qur'an itself.

question: Who gave the call to prayer from the top of the Ka'ba on the day Makkah was conquered?
explanation: The Prophet ﷺ ordered Bilal to climb onto the Ka'ba and call to prayer.
detail: Every standard biography records that on the day Makkah was conquered, after the idols had been cleared from the Ka'ba, the Prophet ﷺ ordered Bilal to climb onto its roof and give the call to prayer, and the voice of the former slave rang out over the city where he had once been tortured for saying that Allah is One. Bilal had been the Prophet's ﷺ caller to prayer since the adhan was instituted in Madinah, as Sahih al-Bukhari records. A Muslim learns that in Islam, standing comes from faith and not from birth.

question: What did the Prophet ﷺ tell the defeated Makkans who had persecuted him, on the day of the conquest?
explanation: He forgave them: "Go, you are free."
detail: Every standard biography records that on the day of the conquest the Prophet ﷺ stood at the door of the Ka'ba before the assembled Quraysh, who had fought him for years, and asked them what they thought he would do with them. They answered that he was a noble brother and the son of a noble brother. He replied with the words of Yusuf to his brothers: "No blame upon you today; Allah will forgive you" (12:92), and then told them to go, for they were free. A Muslim learns that the greatest victory of the Prophet ﷺ was sealed with forgiveness.

question: At which battle, named in the Quran, were the Muslims at first caught off guard despite their large numbers?
explanation: "On the day of Hunayn, your great number pleased you, but it availed you nothing."
detail: The verses read: "...and on the day of Hunayn, when your great number pleased you, but it availed you nothing, and the earth, vast as it is, was straitened for you; then you turned back, fleeing. Then Allah sent down His tranquillity upon His Messenger and upon the believers, and sent down soldiers you did not see" (9:25-26). Every standard biography places the battle soon after the conquest of Makkah, against Hawazin and Thaqif; the Prophet ﷺ held his ground on his mule until the companions rallied. A Muslim learns that reliance on numbers is a weakness, and reliance on Allah a strength.

question: Which companion, who stayed behind from the expedition to Tabuk, confessed honestly and was forgiven by a revelation?
explanation: Ka'b ibn Malik told the truth, endured fifty days of being shunned, then Allah revealed his forgiveness (9:118).
detail: Ka'b tells his own story in Sahih al-Bukhari 4418. He kept putting off his departure for Tabuk until the army was gone. When the Prophet ﷺ returned, the hypocrites came with excuses and oaths and were let go, but Ka'b said he had no excuse at all; the Prophet ﷺ answered that this man had spoken the truth, and ordered the Muslims not to speak to him. On the fiftieth morning the verse came down: "And upon the three who were left behind" (9:118). A Muslim learns that a hard truth told to the Prophet ﷺ was better than any easy lie.

question: What is 9 AH called, when many tribes came to Madinah to embrace Islam?
explanation: After the conquest of Makkah, delegations of Arab tribes streamed into Madinah.
detail: Every standard biography records that once Makkah had entered Islam, the tribes of Arabia sent delegations to Madinah to declare their Islam before the Prophet ﷺ; among them came Thaqif of Ta'if, the town that had driven him out. The Qur'an speaks of this season: "When the victory of Allah has come and the conquest, and you see the people entering the religion of Allah in multitudes, then glorify your Lord with praise and ask His forgiveness" (110:1-3). A Muslim learns that the answer to a flood of new believers was praise and humility.

question: Where did the Prophet ﷺ deliver his Farewell Sermon?
explanation: The Farewell Sermon was delivered at Arafat, during the Farewell Pilgrimage.
detail: Every standard biography records that during his only pilgrimage the Prophet ﷺ addressed the pilgrims at Arafat, telling them that their blood and property were as sacred to one another as that day, that month and that city, and that he was leaving among them the Book of Allah, which whoever held fast to would never go astray. When they affirmed that he had conveyed the message, he called on Allah to bear witness, three times. The verse announcing the perfection of the religion was revealed at Arafat that same day (5:3). A Muslim learns that the Prophet's ﷺ last public words were about the sanctity of life and the keeping of the Qur'an.

question: Which verse, revealed during the Farewell Pilgrimage, announces that the religion is perfected?
answers: "This day I have perfected for you your religion"
"Read, in the name of your Lord"
explanation: "This day I have perfected for you your religion and completed My favour upon you."
detail: The full passage reads: "This day those who disbelieve have despaired of your religion. This day I have perfected for you your religion and completed My favour upon you, and I have approved for you Islam as religion" (5:3). Sahih al-Bukhari records that a Jewish man said to 'Umar that had this verse come to the Jews they would have made that day a festival, and 'Umar replied that it came down while the Prophet ﷺ stood at Arafat on a Friday. A Muslim learns that the religion was declared complete during the Farewell Pilgrimage, with nothing left to be added.

question: In which city did the Prophet ﷺ die and get buried?
explanation: He died in Madinah in 11 AH and was buried there.
detail: Every standard biography records that after the Farewell Pilgrimage the Prophet ﷺ returned to Madinah, fell ill some months later in the eleventh year after the Hijra, and died on a Monday in the room of his wife 'Aisha beside his mosque. Sahih al-Bukhari records that his last words were a prayer for the highest companionship. He was buried in the room where he died, and Abu Bakr and 'Umar were later laid beside him. A Muslim learns that the city that welcomed the Prophet ﷺ in the Hijra is the city that keeps his grave.

question: In which wife's room was the Prophet ﷺ buried?
explanation: He was buried where he died, in 'Aisha's room, now inside the Prophet's Mosque.
detail: Sahih al-Bukhari records 'Aisha's account of the last day: the Prophet ﷺ died resting against her chest, and she counted it a favour from Allah that it happened in her house and on her day. He was buried in that room, and every standard biography records that Abu Bakr and then 'Umar were buried beside him. When the mosque was later enlarged the room was enclosed within it, so his grave now lies inside the Prophet's Mosque. A Muslim learns that the Prophet ﷺ died in a small room among his family, with nothing of a king's ceremony.

question: Who declared, at the Prophet's ﷺ death: "Whoever worshipped Muhammad, Muhammad has died; whoever worships Allah, Allah is Ever-Living"?
explanation: Abu Bakr calmed the companions and recited: "Muhammad is not but a messenger…" (3:144).
detail: The hadith is narrated by 'Aisha and recorded in Sahih al-Bukhari 3667. Abu Bakr came in, uncovered the Prophet's ﷺ face, kissed him and wept. He then went out to the mosque, where 'Umar was telling the people that the Prophet ﷺ had not died, told him to sit, spoke the words the question quotes, and recited: "Muhammad is not but a messenger; messengers have passed on before him. If he dies or is killed, will you turn back on your heels?" (3:144). A Muslim learns that grief for the Prophet ﷺ is right, but that worship belongs to Allah alone.

question: What were the names of the Prophet's ﷺ two grandsons, the sons of Fatima and 'Ali?
explanation: Al-Hasan and Al-Husayn, whom the Prophet ﷺ loved dearly.
detail: Every standard biography records that al-Hasan and al-Husayn were born in Madinah to Fatima, the Prophet's ﷺ daughter, and 'Ali, and that their grandfather carried them on his shoulders, sat them on his lap and let them climb on his back. Sahih al-Bukhari records him saying of al-Hasan, "O Allah, I love him, so love him, and love whoever loves him," and calling the two of them his two sweet-scented flowers of this world. A Muslim learns that the Prophet ﷺ showed his tenderness for children openly and asked others to love them.

question: Which wife of the Prophet ﷺ was the daughter of Abu Bakr?
explanation: 'Aisha, daughter of Abu Bakr, transmitted a very large number of hadiths.
detail: Every standard biography records that the Prophet ﷺ married 'Aisha, daughter of his closest companion Abu Bakr, after the death of Khadija, and that she lived with him in the room beside the mosque where he later died. Sahih al-Bukhari records that when he was asked whom he loved most, he answered 'Aisha, and when asked among men, her father. After his death she lived on for many years in Madinah, and companions and their students came to her to learn. A Muslim learns that much of what is known of the Prophet's ﷺ home life comes from the wife who remembered it.

question: Which wife of the Prophet ﷺ was the daughter of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab?
explanation: Hafsa bint 'Umar; the first collected copy of the Quran was kept with her.
detail: Every standard biography records that Hafsa's first husband died after Badr, and that her father 'Umar offered her in marriage to Abu Bakr and to 'Uthman, who both declined, before the Prophet ﷺ himself asked for her. Sahih al-Bukhari records that after 'Umar's death the sheets on which the Qur'an had been collected in Abu Bakr's time were kept with Hafsa, and that 'Uthman borrowed them to make the copies he sent to the cities, returning them to her afterwards. A Muslim learns that the text of the Qur'an passed through the keeping of a wife of the Prophet ﷺ.

question: Which companion narrated the largest number of hadiths from the Prophet ﷺ?
explanation: Abu Hurayra, who kept close company with the Prophet ﷺ, is the companion who narrated the most hadiths.
detail: Every standard biography records that Abu Hurayra came to the Prophet ﷺ in the year of Khaybar, lived among the poor of the Suffa and stayed constantly at his side. Sahih al-Bukhari records his own explanation: the Muhajirun were busy in the markets and the Ansar with their land, while he followed the Prophet ﷺ on an empty stomach; and when he complained of forgetting, the Prophet ﷺ had him spread out his cloak and hold it to his chest, after which he forgot nothing. A Muslim learns that the largest store of hadith was kept by a man who chose company over trade.

question: Which young companion served the Prophet ﷺ for ten years without ever hearing a reproach?
explanation: Anas said: "I served the Prophet ﷺ for ten years; he never said 'uff' to me, nor 'why did you do that?'"
detail: Anas ibn Malik reports in Sahih al-Bukhari 6038 that in ten years of service the Prophet ﷺ never said "uff" to him, never asked of something done "why did you do it?", nor of something left undone "why did you not do it?". "Uff" is the smallest sound of impatience, the very word the Qur'an forbids a child to say to ageing parents (17:23). A Muslim takes from it how to treat those who help at home: with patience, without small reproaches.

question: For which young cousin did the Prophet ﷺ pray: "O Allah, teach him the Book"?
explanation: The Prophet ﷺ embraced Ibn 'Abbas and said: "O Allah, teach him the Book."
detail: Ibn 'Abbas narrates the moment in Sahih al-Bukhari 75: the Prophet ﷺ pressed him to his chest and said, "O Allah, teach him the Book." The Book is the Qur'an, sent down "as clarification for all things and as guidance and mercy and good tidings for the Muslims" (16:89). Ibn 'Abbas was a boy, and the prayer came with an embrace. A Muslim learns to join affection with prayer for a child, and to ask Allah first for understanding of the Qur'an.

question: Which companion did the Prophet ﷺ send to Yemen, telling him to call first to the oneness of Allah?
explanation: "You are going to a people of the Book: first call them to testify that there is no god but Allah…"
detail: Ibn 'Abbas relates in Sahih al-Bukhari 1395 the instructions the Prophet ﷺ gave Mu'adh ibn Jabal: he was going to a people of the Book and should first call them to testify that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is His Messenger. If they accepted, he should teach them the five daily prayers Allah had made a duty; then, that a charity was due from their rich to their poor. A Muslim learns that the call begins with Allah's oneness and moves step by step.

question: Which companion did the Prophet ﷺ call "the trustworthy one (amin) of this nation"?
explanation: "Every nation has a trustworthy one, and the trustworthy one of this nation is Abu 'Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah."
detail: Anas reports in Sahih al-Bukhari 3744 that the Prophet ﷺ said every nation has a trustworthy one, and that the trustworthy one of this nation is Abu 'Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah. Amin was the title Makkah had given the Prophet ﷺ before his mission, and here he gives it to a companion publicly. The Qur'an counts among the successful "those who are to their trusts and their promises attentive" (23:8). A Muslim takes from it that being trusted is a rank, one a leader honours in public.

question: Which companion, a scribe of the revelation, was tasked by Abu Bakr with collecting the Quran?
explanation: After the battle of al-Yamama, Abu Bakr tasked Zayd ibn Thabit with collecting the Quran.
detail: Zayd ibn Thabit tells it in Sahih al-Bukhari 4986. After losses among the reciters at al-Yamama, 'Umar urged Abu Bakr to gather the Qur'an before more was lost, and Abu Bakr, unwilling at first to do what the Prophet ﷺ had not done, agreed. He told Zayd he was a wise young man who had written the revelation. Zayd said moving a mountain would have been lighter, and gathered the Qur'an from parchments, palm stalks and the memories of men. A Muslim learns how carefully his Book was preserved.

question: Under which caliph were official copies of the Quran sent to the provinces?
explanation: 'Uthman had the mushaf copied and sent a copy to every province.
detail: Anas ibn Malik relates in Sahih al-Bukhari 4987 how the official copies came about. Hudhayfa, alarmed by differences in recitation among Muslims of Syria and Iraq, asked 'Uthman to save the community before it differed over its Book as earlier communities had. 'Uthman borrowed from Hafsa the sheets gathered under Abu Bakr, had Zayd ibn Thabit and three men of Quraysh copy them, and sent a copy to every province. A Muslim learns that the unity of the Qur'an's text was guarded by the companions themselves.

question: From which land did the companion Salman, called "al-Farisi", come?
explanation: Salman al-Farisi, "the Persian", came from Persia in search of the truth.
detail: Every biography records that Salman was born in Persia and left his home in search of the true religion, serving Christian monks before being sold as a slave and carried to Yathrib. There, after the Hijra, he watched the Prophet ﷺ for the signs he expected, embraced Islam, and gained his freedom. At the siege of Madinah it was Salman who proposed the trench. A Muslim learns that truth is worth a long journey, and that Islam made Persian, Arab and Abyssinian one family.

question: Which companion, who came from the Byzantine lands, is called "ar-Rumi"?
explanation: Suhayb ar-Rumi grew up among the Byzantines before embracing Islam in Makkah.
detail: The biographies agree that Suhayb was born an Arab, taken captive as a child and raised among the Byzantines, and came to Makkah, where he gained his freedom and embraced Islam. When he set out for Madinah, Quraysh pursued him, and he bought his way through by handing over all the wealth he had earned. The Prophet ﷺ greeted him saying that Suhayb's trade had been profitable. A Muslim learns that a believer counts faith and the Prophet's ﷺ company as worth more than all he owns.

question: What is the Prophet's ﷺ mosque in Madinah called?
explanation: The mosque he founded in Madinah is called the Prophet's Mosque, al-Masjid an-Nabawi.
detail: Al-Masjid an-Nabawi is the mosque the Prophet ﷺ founded on arriving in Madinah; every biography records that he built it with his companions from mud brick and palm trunks, carrying bricks himself. His wives' rooms opened onto it, the poor of the Suffa sheltered in it, and there he taught, judged and led the prayer for ten years. He was buried in 'Aisha's room beside it, within the mosque today. A Muslim sees in it the heart of the first community, where prayer and daily life were one.

question: How many times does the name "Muhammad" appear in the Quran?
explanation: In verses 3:144, 33:40, 47:2 and 48:29; the name "Ahmad" appears in 61:6.
detail: The name stands in four verses: "Muhammad is not but a messenger; messengers have passed on before him" (3:144); "Muhammad is not the father of any one of your men, but the Messenger of Allah and the Seal of the Prophets" (33:40); belief "in what has been sent down upon Muhammad" (47:2); and "Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah" (48:29). In 61:6 'Isa announces a messenger "whose name is Ahmad". A Muslim learns to find his Prophet ﷺ named in the Book he recites.

question: How does the Quran describe the Prophet ﷺ for the believers, in verse 33:21?
explanation: "There has certainly been for you in the Messenger of Allah an excellent example."
detail: The verse reads: "There has certainly been for you in the Messenger of Allah an excellent example for anyone whose hope is in Allah and the Last Day and who remembers Allah often" (33:21). It belongs to the siege of Madinah in Surah al-Ahzab, when the enemy came "from above you and from below you" (33:10), and the believers, seeing the armies, said this was what Allah had promised (33:22). A Muslim takes from it that following the Prophet ﷺ means copying his conduct, especially in hardship.

question: What was the Prophet's ﷺ kunya (paternal nickname)?
explanation: He was called Abu al-Qasim, after his eldest son Al-Qasim.
detail: Every biography records that the Prophet's ﷺ first child by Khadija was a son, al-Qasim, born before the revelation, and that by Arab custom the father was thereafter called Abu al-Qasim. The boy died while still small, as did the other son born to Khadija, 'Abdullah, yet the kunya stayed with the Prophet ﷺ all his life. A kunya in Arab usage marks honour and closeness. A Muslim learns that behind this familiar title stands a father who buried his children and bore it with patience.

question: What was the name of the Prophet's ﷺ son born in Madinah, who died as a small child?
explanation: Ibrahim, born in Madinah, died as an infant; the Prophet ﷺ wept and said the heart grieves without saying what displeases Allah.
detail: The biographies agree that Ibrahim was born in Madinah to Mariya and nursed in a home the Prophet ﷺ often visited. The child died as an infant, and the Prophet ﷺ held him as he was dying and wept. That day the sun was eclipsed, and people said it was for Ibrahim; the Prophet ﷺ told them the sun and moon are two signs of Allah, not eclipsed for anyone's death. A Muslim learns that tears are allowed, and that nature's signs are tied to no man.

question: For whom did the Prophet ﷺ lead a trade caravan to Syria before the revelation?
explanation: Khadija, a wealthy merchant, entrusted him with her caravan to Syria, then proposed marriage.
detail: All the biographies record that Khadija was a merchant, and that having heard of the honesty of Muhammad ﷺ she sent him with her caravan to Syria with her servant Maysara, who came back praising him. The trade prospered, and she sent word proposing marriage. When the first revelation came she was the first to believe and calmed him, saying Allah would never disgrace a man who kept ties of kinship and helped the weak. A Muslim learns that his mission began in a marriage built on trust.

question: How did the young Muhammad ﷺ settle the clans' dispute over replacing the Black Stone?
answers: He laid it on a cloth that every clan lifted, then set it himself
He entrusted it to Abu Bakr
explanation: He spread a cloak, placed the Stone on it, had the clan chiefs lift the cloth together, then set it in place with his own hand.
detail: Every biography records the rebuilding of the Ka'ba. When the walls reached the height of the Black Stone, each clan claimed to set it, and the dispute neared bloodshed until they agreed that the first man through the gate would decide. It was Muhammad ﷺ, and they accepted al-Amin's judgement. He spread his cloak, laid the Stone on it, had a chief of each clan lift an edge, and set it himself. A Muslim learns that a fair solution giving everyone a share ends a quarrel.

question: At what age did the Prophet ﷺ receive the first revelation?
explanation: The revelation began when he was forty years old, in the cave of Hira.
detail: The biographies agree that the Prophet ﷺ was forty when the revelation began, and that he had taken to withdrawing to the cave of Hira to worship alone. The Qur'an names the month: "the month of Ramadan in which the Qur'an was sent down" (2:185). Jibril came to him there with "Read in the name of your Lord who created" (96:1). Forty is the age the Qur'an describes as full maturity (46:15). A Muslim learns that the mission began in solitude and reflection.

question: To which cousin of Khadija, learned in the Scriptures, was the Prophet ﷺ taken after the first revelation?
explanation: Waraqa said: "This is the Namus (the angel) whom Allah sent to Musa."
detail: Sahih al-Bukhari 3 describes Waraqa ibn Nawfal as Khadija's cousin, a Christian before Islam who wrote from the Gospel in Hebrew. Khadija said, "Listen to your nephew," and after hearing of Hira Waraqa said this was the Namus Allah had sent down to Musa, and wished he were young for the day his people would drive him out. Asked if they would, Waraqa answered that no man had ever brought what he brought without meeting hostility. A Muslim learns that a man of the earlier Scriptures recognised his mission.

question: On which hill did the Prophet ﷺ climb to call Quraysh publicly, after the verse "Warn your closest kin"?
explanation: He climbed as-Safa, called the clans of Quraysh and warned them of a severe punishment.
detail: Ibn 'Abbas relates in Sahih al-Bukhari 4770 that when "And warn your closest kindred" (26:214) was revealed, the Prophet ﷺ climbed as-Safa and called the clans of Quraysh. He asked whether they would believe him if he said horsemen were about to attack, and they said they had known only truth from him. He said he warned them of a severe punishment. Abu Lahab wished him ruin, and "May the hands of Abu Lahab be ruined" (111:1) came down. A Muslim learns that his message rested on proven honesty.

question: Which caliph established the Muslim calendar starting from the year of the Hijra?
explanation: Under 'Umar, the Hijra was chosen as the starting point of the calendar.
detail: Every account of the caliphate of 'Umar records that, when dated records made a fixed calendar necessary, he gathered the companions to decide from which event the years should be counted. They chose the Hijra over the Prophet's ﷺ birth or death, and made the year begin with Muharram. The Qur'an had already fixed the months: "Indeed, the number of months with Allah is twelve months in the register of Allah" (9:36). A Muslim learns that his calendar counts from the founding of the community.

question: How many years did the Prophet ﷺ live in Madinah after the Hijra?
explanation: He lived ten years in Madinah, from the Hijra to his death in 11 AH.
detail: All the biographies agree that the Prophet ﷺ entered Madinah in Rabi' al-Awwal and died in the same month of the eleventh year, ten years apart. Into them fall the great events: Badr in the second year, Uhud in the third, the siege of Madinah in the fifth, Hudaybiyya in the sixth, the conquest of Makkah in the eighth and the Farewell Pilgrimage in the tenth. The Qur'an calls the city by its old name, Yathrib (33:13). A Muslim learns that a whole community was built in one decade.

question: For how many years did the Prophet ﷺ preach in Makkah before the Hijra?
explanation: Thirteen years in Makkah, then ten in Madinah: twenty-three years of mission.
detail: The biographies agree that from the first revelation to the Hijra the Prophet ﷺ preached in Makkah for thirteen years: three calling people quietly, the rest in public, through the emigration to Abyssinia, the boycott of his clan, the deaths of Khadija and Abu Talib and the pledges of 'Aqaba. The Qur'an describes its revelation as "a Qur'an which We have separated, that you might recite it to the people over a prolonged period" (17:106). A Muslim learns that the Qur'an's teaching was given in years of patience.

question: Which companion, a poet, defended the Prophet ﷺ with his verses and for whom he asked Jibril's support?
explanation: The Prophet ﷺ told Hassan: "Answer them, and Jibril is with you."
detail: Al-Bara' reports in Sahih al-Bukhari 3212 that the Prophet ﷺ said to Hassan, "Satirise them, and Jibril is with you." Hassan ibn Thabit was a poet of the Ansar, and the poets of Quraysh were attacking the Prophet ﷺ in verse. The Qur'an condemns poets followed by the misguided but excepts "those who believe and do righteous deeds and remember Allah often and defend themselves after they were wronged" (26:227). A Muslim learns that a gift for words is honoured when placed in the service of truth.

question: Of which companion did the Prophet ﷺ say he had been given "one of the flutes of the family of Dawud" for his beautiful recitation?
explanation: Hearing him recite, the Prophet ﷺ said Abu Musa had been given one of the flutes of the family of Dawud.
detail: Abu Musa al-Ash'ari narrates in Sahih al-Bukhari 5048 that the Prophet ﷺ said to him, "O Abu Musa, you have been given one of the flutes of the family of Dawud." The Qur'an tells that Allah gave Dawud the Zabur (4:163) and made the mountains and the birds join him in praise (21:79), the model of a praising voice. Abu Musa was reciting the Qur'an when the Prophet ﷺ heard him. A Muslim learns that a beautiful recitation is a gift the Prophet ﷺ admired.

question: The Prophet ﷺ recommended learning the Quran from four companions. Which of these was one of them?
explanation: "Learn the Quran from four: Ibn Mas'ud, Salim, Mu'adh ibn Jabal and Ubayy ibn Ka'b."
detail: 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr reports in Sahih al-Bukhari 3758 that he heard the Prophet ﷺ say, "Take the Qur'an from four," beginning with 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, then Salim the freed slave of Abu Hudhayfa, Mu'adh ibn Jabal and Ubayy ibn Ka'b. Ibn Mas'ud and Salim were emigrants from Makkah, Mu'adh and Ubayy were of the Ansar, so the Qur'an's teachers came from both halves of the community. A Muslim learns that the Qur'an was passed on by named teachers the Prophet ﷺ trusted, in a chain reaching back to him.

question: At which battle was the Prophet ﷺ wounded in the face and lost a tooth?
explanation: At Uhud, his tooth was broken and his face wounded.
detail: Sahih al-Bukhari 4073 records that on the day of Uhud the Prophet's ﷺ face was wounded and a front tooth was broken. The Qur'an speaks of that day, when the Muslims fled "while the Messenger was calling you from behind" (3:153), and consoles the wounded: "If a wound should touch you, there has already touched the opposing people a wound similar to it" (3:140). He stayed on the field with his companions. A Muslim learns that the Prophet ﷺ shared his community's pain in his own body.

question: To which companion, an archer at Uhud, did the Prophet ﷺ say: "Shoot! May my father and mother be your ransom"?
explanation: The Prophet ﷺ handed him arrows saying: "Shoot, may my father and mother be sacrificed for you."
detail: 'Ali reports in Sahih al-Bukhari 4055 that he never heard the Prophet ﷺ say to anyone "may my father and mother be sacrificed for you" except to Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, on the day of Uhud, when he told him to shoot. Sa'd was firing arrows to keep the enemy from the Prophet ﷺ. Among Arabs, offering one's parents as ransom was the strongest expression of love. A Muslim learns that courage in defending the Prophet ﷺ earned words he gave to no one else.

question: Which caravan did the Muslims set out to intercept, which led to the battle of Badr?
explanation: The Quraysh caravan led by Abu Sufyan escaped, but the Makkan army came to Badr.
detail: The biographies agree that the Muslims marched to meet a Quraysh caravan under Abu Sufyan returning from Syria, but that he turned along the coast and sent to Makkah for help, so an army came out instead. The Qur'an recalls it: "And when Allah promised you one of the two groups, that it would be yours, and you wished that the unarmed one would be yours" (8:7). The battle followed at Badr. A Muslim learns that what Allah chose was harder than what they wanted, and greater.

question: When did the Makkan chief Abu Sufyan embrace Islam?
explanation: Abu Sufyan converted on the eve of the Prophet's ﷺ entry into Makkah.
detail: All the biographies record that Abu Sufyan, the leader of Quraysh, went out to spy on the army approaching Makkah, was brought to the Prophet ﷺ by his uncle al-'Abbas, and embraced Islam on the night before the entry. The Prophet ﷺ then honoured him by proclaiming that whoever entered the house of Abu Sufyan was safe, as was anyone who shut his door or entered the mosque. A Muslim learns that the Prophet ﷺ met his oldest enemy with safety and honour.

question: Which spring gushed forth for Hajar and her son Isma'il in the valley of Makkah?
explanation: An angel struck the ground and the water of Zamzam gushed out; Hajar made a basin around it.
detail: Ibn 'Abbas tells it in Sahih al-Bukhari 3364. Ibrahim left Hajar and Isma'il in the valley; when she asked whether Allah had commanded this and he said yes, she answered that He would not neglect them. The water ran out, the child cried with thirst, and she saw an angel dig with his heel until water gushed. She built a basin, and the Prophet ﷺ said that had she left it, Zamzam would have flowed freely. A Muslim learns that Zamzam was given to a mother who trusted Allah.

question: What was engraved on the Prophet's ﷺ ring?
explanation: His silver ring bore "Muhammad, Messenger of Allah" in three lines.
detail: Anas reports in Sahih al-Bukhari 5872 that the Prophet ﷺ had a ring of silver made, engraved "Muhammad Rasul Allah", in the story of his letters: when he decided to write to rulers, he was told that a letter without a seal would not be read. Anas adds that the ring's whiteness still stood before his eyes. The three words are the second half of the testimony of faith. A Muslim learns that the Prophet ﷺ used the means of his time to make his message received.

question: Which foods did the Prophet ﷺ like, according to 'Aisha?
explanation: 'Aisha reports that the Prophet ﷺ loved sweet things and honey.
detail: 'Aisha reports in Sahih al-Bukhari 5431 that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ loved sweet things and honey. Her short sentence shows him taking pleasure in good food without excess. The Qur'an speaks of honey as a healing: from the bees "there emerges from their bellies a drink, varying in colours, in which there is healing for people" (16:69). His taste was for something the Qur'an names among Allah's signs. A Muslim learns that enjoying lawful food with gratitude is part of the Prophet's ﷺ way.

question: On which day of the week was the Prophet ﷺ born, a day on which he also fasted?
explanation: Asked about fasting on Monday, he said: "That is the day I was born and the day revelation came to me."
detail: Abu Qatada reports in Sahih Muslim 1162 that the Prophet ﷺ was asked about fasting on Monday and answered that it was the day he was born and the day revelation came down to him. The same hadith records that fasting the day of 'Arafa expiates the year before and the year after, and 'Ashura the year before. Birth and mission fall on the same weekday, and he honoured it not with a feast but with a fast. A Muslim learns that gratitude for a blessing is shown by worship.

question: Where was the "seal of prophethood" on the Prophet's ﷺ body?
explanation: The seal of prophethood was between his shoulders.
detail: As-Sa'ib ibn Yazid relates in Sahih al-Bukhari 3541 that as a boy he was taken by his aunt to the Prophet ﷺ; the Prophet ﷺ stroked his head, prayed for blessing and made ablution, and the boy drank from the water. Then he stood behind him and saw the seal of prophethood between his shoulders, like the button of a tent. The Qur'an calls him "the Seal of the Prophets" (33:40). A Muslim learns that even children who met the Prophet ﷺ remembered him closely.

question: From which wood was the Prophet's ﷺ minbar (pulpit) made, by a carpenter?
explanation: The Prophet ﷺ had a minbar made of tamarisk wood, from which he addressed the people.
detail: Sahl ibn Sa'd relates in Sahih al-Bukhari 917 that the Prophet ﷺ asked a woman to have her carpenter slave make him something of wood to sit on when addressing the people, made from the tamarisk of al-Ghaba. Once it stood in the mosque, the Prophet ﷺ prayed on it, stepped down backwards to prostrate at its foot, then told the people he had done this so they would learn his prayer. A Muslim learns that the Prophet ﷺ showed the prayer as well as describing it.

question: Which two great tribes of Madinah formed the Ansar?
explanation: The Aws and the Khazraj, long-time rivals, united in Islam and became the Ansar.
detail: Every biography records that the Aws and the Khazraj had fought each other for generations, and that men of the Khazraj met the Prophet ﷺ at Makkah, accepted his call, and returned with men of the Aws to pledge allegiance at 'Aqaba. The Qur'an reminds them: "Remember the favour of Allah upon you when you were enemies and He brought your hearts together and you became, by His favour, brothers" (3:103). A Muslim learns that faith turned old enemies into one people.

question: What title does the Quran give the wives of the Prophet ﷺ?
explanation: "His wives are their mothers": the Mothers of the Believers.
detail: The verse reads: "The Prophet is more worthy of the believers than themselves, and his wives are their mothers" (33:6). Surah al-Ahzab addresses them directly, "O wives of the Prophet, you are not like any other women" (33:32), and forbids the believers ever to marry them after him, calling that "in the sight of Allah an enormity" (33:53). A Muslim learns to speak of Khadija and 'Aisha as his mothers, and to receive what they passed on from the Prophet's ﷺ home as a mother's teaching.

question: In which year of the Christian calendar did the Hijra take place?
explanation: The Hijra, in 622, marks the start of the Muslim calendar.
detail: All the biographies agree that the Prophet ﷺ left Makkah with Abu Bakr in the year corresponding to 622, hid three days in the cave of Thawr while Quraysh searched, and reached Madinah. The Qur'an recalls the cave: "when those who disbelieved had driven him out as one of two, when they were in the cave and he said to his companion, 'Do not grieve; indeed Allah is with us'" (9:40). A Muslim learns that his calendar began with a journey made in trust.

question: What did 'Abd ar-Rahman ibn 'Awf reply when his Ansari brother offered him half of his wealth?
explanation: He said: "May Allah bless your wealth and family; just show me the market," and prospered through trade.
detail: Anas tells it in Sahih al-Bukhari 2048. When 'Abd ar-Rahman ibn 'Awf arrived, the Prophet ﷺ made him the brother of Sa'd ibn ar-Rabi', who offered him half his property. 'Abd ar-Rahman asked only to be shown the market, and traded at a profit. Later he came with a trace of yellow perfume, having married for gold the weight of a date-stone, and the Prophet ﷺ told him to give a wedding feast, even with one sheep. A Muslim learns to accept help without living on it.

question: Which companion did the Prophet ﷺ ask which verse of the Quran is the greatest, before congratulating him on his answer (the Throne Verse)?
explanation: Ubayy answered: "Allah, there is no god but He, the Ever-Living…"; the Prophet ﷺ said: "May knowledge delight you, Abu al-Mundhir!"
detail: Ubayy ibn Ka'b relates in Sahih Muslim 810 that the Prophet ﷺ asked him, "O Abu al-Mundhir, do you know which verse of the Book of Allah is the greatest?" Ubayy answered with the Throne Verse, "Allah, there is no god but He, the Ever-Living, the Sustainer of existence" (2:255), which goes on to say that His Kursi extends over the heavens and the earth. The Prophet ﷺ struck his chest and said, "May knowledge delight you, Abu al-Mundhir." A Muslim learns to know this verse and its place.

question: How was the site of the Prophet's ﷺ mosque in Madinah chosen?
answers: In the centre of the market
explanation: He let his she-camel walk freely: where she knelt, the mosque was built.
detail: Every biography records that when the Prophet ﷺ entered Madinah the Ansar begged him to lodge with them, and he told them to let his she-camel go, for she was under command. She walked on until she knelt at a drying-place belonging to two orphan boys of Banu an-Najjar. Though they offered it as a gift, he insisted on paying, and there the mosque was built. A Muslim learns that the Prophet ﷺ favoured no clan and paid a fair price even to orphans who wished to give.

question: How many sons did the Prophet ﷺ have, all of whom died young?
explanation: Al-Qasim and 'Abdullah, born to Khadija, and Ibrahim, born in Madinah.
detail: The biographies record three sons: al-Qasim and 'Abdullah, both born to Khadija, and Ibrahim, born in Madinah to Mariya; each died in early childhood. His four daughters, Zaynab, Ruqayya, Umm Kulthum and Fatima, grew up. The Qur'an states the outcome: "Muhammad is not the father of any one of your men, but the Messenger of Allah and the Seal of the Prophets" (33:40). A Muslim learns that the Prophet ﷺ knew the grief of burying children, and that his message was carried on without a son.

question: Which companion, freed by the Prophet ﷺ and raised like a son, was the father of Usama?
explanation: Zayd ibn Haritha, beloved of the Prophet ﷺ, was the father of Usama ibn Zayd.
detail: All the biographies agree that Zayd ibn Haritha was taken captive as a boy, was given by Khadija to the Prophet ﷺ, and that when his father came for him, Zayd chose to stay. The Prophet ﷺ freed and adopted him; he was called Zayd ibn Muhammad until the Qur'an ended such naming: "Call them by the names of their fathers" (33:5). He is the only companion named in the Qur'an (33:37) and fell commanding at Mu'ta. A Muslim learns what love between master and freed man can be.

question: Which young companion did the Prophet ﷺ appoint to lead an army shortly before his death, despite his youth?
explanation: The Prophet ﷺ gave Usama the command and answered those who criticised his age that he was worthy of it, like his father.
detail: Ibn 'Umar reports in Sahih al-Bukhari 4469 that the Prophet ﷺ sent out a force under Usama ibn Zayd, and when people criticised his command he said that those who criticised Usama had criticised his father's command before him; that his father had been worthy and among the dearest to him; and that this one was among the dearest to him after him. Usama was very young, and his father had commanded at Mu'ta. A Muslim learns that leadership is given for merit rather than age.

question: Which grandfather of the Prophet ﷺ re-dug the well of Zamzam, long filled in?
explanation: 'Abd al-Muttalib re-dug Zamzam and took charge of it for the pilgrims.
detail: Every biography records that Zamzam had been filled in long before, and that 'Abd al-Muttalib was shown its place in a dream and dug it out with his only son, al-Harith; he then held the office of watering the pilgrims. They also record his vow to sacrifice a son if Allah gave him ten, and that when the lot fell on 'Abdullah, the future father of the Prophet ﷺ, he was ransomed with a hundred camels. A Muslim learns that the Prophet's ﷺ grandfather served the pilgrims.

question: Roughly how many people accompanied the Prophet ﷺ at the battle of Badr?
explanation: The Muslims at Badr were a little over three hundred, facing a much larger army.
detail: All the biographies put the Muslims at Badr at a little over three hundred men, facing a Quraysh army of close to a thousand. The Qur'an records the imbalance: "Allah had already given you victory at Badr while you were few" (3:123), and promises help from heaven: "Is it not sufficient for you that your Lord should reinforce you with three thousand angels sent down?" (3:124). Those who were at Badr were honoured all their lives. A Muslim learns that victory is not decided by numbers.

question: In which month of the Muslim calendar was the Prophet ﷺ born?
explanation: He was born in the month of Rabi' al-Awwal, in the Year of the Elephant.
detail: Every biography records that the Prophet ﷺ was born in Makkah in Rabi' al-Awwal in the Year of the Elephant, the year Abraha marched with an elephant to destroy the Ka'ba. The Qur'an recalls it: "Have you not considered how your Lord dealt with the companions of the elephant?" (105:1). His father 'Abdullah had died before his birth, his mother was Amina, and he was nursed by Halima. A Muslim learns that Allah protected the House in the very year its last Prophet ﷺ was born.

question: In which month did the Prophet ﷺ arrive in Madinah during the Hijra?
explanation: He arrived in Madinah in Rabi' al-Awwal, after stopping at Quba.
detail: The biographies agree that the Prophet ﷺ reached Madinah in Rabi' al-Awwal and halted first at Quba, where he founded a mosque, and that he entered the city on a Friday, praying the first Friday prayer on the way. The Qur'an speaks of Quba as "a mosque founded on righteousness from the first day" (9:108). Every household of the Ansar wished to host him. A Muslim learns that the first thing the Prophet ﷺ built in his new home, before any house of his own, was a place of prayer.

question: What pact did Quraysh make to isolate Banu Hashim, who protected the Prophet ﷺ?
answers: A boycott: no trade or marriage with them
explanation: Quraysh signed a boycott pact, and Banu Hashim were confined to a valley for years.
detail: Every biography records that Quraysh wrote a document binding themselves not to trade or intermarry with Banu Hashim and Banu al-Muttalib until they handed over Muhammad ﷺ, and hung it inside the Ka'ba. Abu Talib withdrew with the whole clan into his valley outside Makkah, where they suffered hunger for about three years. It ended when men of Quraysh ashamed of it had the document torn up, and it was found eaten away except for the name of Allah. A Muslim learns that patience outlasted the pact.

question: How did the Prophet ﷺ begin his mission in Makkah, before the public call?
answers: By calling his close circle discreetly
explanation: He first called his relatives and friends privately, before the call became public.
detail: All the biographies agree that after the first revelation the Prophet ﷺ spoke of his message only to those closest to him, and that the first to believe were Khadija, Abu Bakr, 'Ali and Zayd ibn Haritha. For about three years the believers met quietly in the house of al-Arqam. Then the Qur'an commanded, "Then declare what you are commanded" (15:94), and "And warn your closest kindred" (26:214). A Muslim learns that the call grew step by step, from a trusted circle to the whole city.

question: Between which two hills did Hajar run looking for water for Isma'il?
explanation: She ran seven times between as-Safa and al-Marwa: the origin of the pilgrims' sa'y.
detail: Ibn 'Abbas relates in Sahih al-Bukhari 3364 that when the water was gone and Isma'il cried with thirst, Hajar climbed as-Safa to look for anyone, came down, and in the valley lifted her garment and ran like a person in distress, then climbed al-Marwa. She did this seven times, and the Prophet ﷺ said that this is why pilgrims go between them. The Qur'an says: "Indeed, as-Safa and al-Marwa are among the symbols of Allah" (2:158). A Muslim learns that every pilgrim's sa'y retraces a mother's search.

question: Of which grandson did the Prophet ﷺ say: "This son of mine is a sayyid; Allah will reconcile two groups of Muslims through him"?
explanation: Al-Hasan ibn 'Ali later reconciled two large groups of Muslims, as the Prophet ﷺ had foretold.
detail: Abu Bakra relates in Sahih al-Bukhari 2704 that he saw the Prophet ﷺ on the minbar with al-Hasan beside him, saying, "This son of mine is a sayyid, and it may be that Allah will reconcile through him two great groups of Muslims." Al-Hasan was the son of 'Ali and Fatima, and the words were said before the whole congregation. The Qur'an makes peace between believers the duty of all (49:10). A Muslim learns that the Prophet ﷺ prized peace among Muslims above rule.

question: What was the name of the Prophet's ﷺ daughter, mother of Al-Hasan and Al-Husayn?
explanation: Fatima, wife of 'Ali, was the mother of Al-Hasan and Al-Husayn.
