detail: Every biography records that Fatima was the youngest of the Prophet's ﷺ daughters, that she married 'Ali in Madinah, and that from that marriage came al-Hasan and al-Husayn, the grandsons he carried and played with. They also record his words that Fatima was a part of him, and that she was the only one of his children to outlive him, dying about six months after him. A Muslim learns that the Prophet's ﷺ family life was one of tenderness, and that his descendants come through a daughter.

question: Who was the eldest daughter of the Prophet ﷺ?
explanation: Zaynab was the eldest of the Prophet's ﷺ four daughters.
detail: All the biographies agree that Zaynab was married to her cousin Abu al-'As ibn ar-Rabi' and stayed with him in Makkah after the Hijra. When he was captured at Badr, she sent as ransom a necklace Khadija had given her; the Prophet ﷺ recognised it, was moved, and returned it and released her husband on condition that Zaynab join her father. She emigrated to Madinah, and Abu al-'As later embraced Islam. A Muslim learns how the Prophet ﷺ loved his daughter and honoured Khadija's memory.

question: Which companion, a former slave of Abyssinian origin, was chosen as muezzin for his beautiful voice?
explanation: Bilal, freed by Abu Bakr, became the Prophet's ﷺ muezzin.
detail: Every biography records that Bilal ibn Rabah was a slave in Makkah tortured by his master for embracing Islam, who kept repeating "Ahad, Ahad" until Abu Bakr bought and freed him. In Madinah the Prophet ﷺ chose him to give the call to prayer, and on the day Makkah was conquered Bilal climbed onto the roof of the Ka'ba and called the adhan from there. A Muslim learns that the former slave rose to call the community to prayer, and that rank is measured by faith.

question: Of which companion did the Prophet ﷺ say: "If I were to take a bosom friend (khalil) from among men, it would be him"?
explanation: "If I were to take a bosom friend from my nation, I would take Abu Bakr, but he is my brother and companion."
detail: Sahih al-Bukhari 3661 records the Prophet's ﷺ words that had he taken a bosom friend among men it would have been Abu Bakr, his brother and companion. The Qur'an reserves the word khalil for the bond between Ibrahim and his Lord, "And Allah took Ibrahim as a khalil" (4:125), and recalls Abu Bakr as "the second of two, when they were in the cave" (9:40). A Muslim learns that no one ranked closer to the Prophet ﷺ than Abu Bakr, and that the heart's deepest bond is kept for Allah.

question: Which city, together with Makkah, is called "al-Haramayn", the two sanctuaries?
explanation: Makkah and Madinah are the two holy cities, al-Haramayn.
detail: Every biography records that as Ibrahim had declared Makkah a sanctuary, the Prophet ﷺ declared Madinah a sanctuary between its two tracts of black stone, and prayed for its blessing. The Qur'an calls Makkah "a secure sanctuary" (28:57) and names Madinah by its old name, Yathrib (33:13); the Prophet ﷺ called it Taybah. Makkah holds the Ka'ba, Madinah his mosque and grave, and together they are al-Haramayn. A Muslim learns to revere both: where the Qur'an began and where the community was built.

question: How many times did the Prophet ﷺ perform Hajj after the Hijra?
explanation: He performed only one Hajj after the Hijra: the Farewell Pilgrimage, in 10 AH.
detail: All the biographies agree that after the Hijra the Prophet ﷺ made the pilgrimage once, in the tenth year, and that it was called the Farewell Pilgrimage because he died months later. At 'Arafat he addressed the people, reminding them that their lives and property were sacred, and there the verse came down: "This day I have perfected for you your religion and completed My favour upon you" (5:3). A Muslim learns that the Hajj he performs today follows the one Hajj the Prophet ﷺ led.

question: According to Anas, what did the Prophet ﷺ do when a Bedouin pulled hard on his cloak demanding goods?
answers: He smiled and ordered that he be given something
explanation: The Prophet ﷺ turned to him, laughed, and ordered that he be given something.
detail: Anas relates in Sahih al-Bukhari 3149 that walking with the Prophet ﷺ, who wore a cloak with a rough border, a Bedouin seized it and pulled so hard that it marked the Prophet's ﷺ shoulder. The man said, "O Muhammad, order for me some of the wealth of Allah." The Prophet ﷺ turned, laughed, and ordered him a gift. The Qur'an says: "And indeed, you are of a great moral character" (68:4). A Muslim learns that the Prophet ﷺ answered rudeness with a smile and generosity.

question: Which city, home to al-Aqsa Mosque, was the destination of the Night Journey?
explanation: The Night Journey took the Prophet ﷺ from Makkah to al-Aqsa Mosque in Jerusalem.
detail: The Qur'an opens Surah al-Isra with the journey: "Exalted is He who took His Servant by night from al-Masjid al-Haram to al-Masjid al-Aqsa, whose surroundings We have blessed, to show him of Our signs" (17:1). Every biography records that the Prophet ﷺ was carried that night from Makkah to Jerusalem and raised through the heavens, where the five prayers were prescribed. Quraysh mocked him, and Abu Bakr believed him at once. A Muslim learns that Jerusalem is bound to his prayer from the start.

question: How old was the Prophet ﷺ when he died?
explanation: He died at the age of sixty-three, in 11 AH.
detail: All the biographies agree that the Prophet ﷺ died at sixty-three: forty before the revelation, thirteen in Makkah, ten in Madinah. He died in Rabi' al-Awwal in the room of 'Aisha. Abu Bakr steadied the community by reciting, "Muhammad is not but a messenger; messengers have passed on before him. So if he was to die or be killed, would you turn back on your heels?" (3:144). A Muslim learns that his love for the Prophet ﷺ rests on worship of Allah, who does not die.

question: Which uncle of the Prophet ﷺ accepted Islam and became one of his staunchest defenders in Makkah?
explanation: Hamza, the Prophet's ﷺ uncle and foster brother, accepted Islam in Makkah and was called "the lion of Allah".
detail: Every standard biography records that Hamza and the Prophet ﷺ were nursed by the same woman, so the uncle was also a foster brother close in age. Hamza declared his Islam after hearing that Abu Jahl had insulted his nephew at the Ka'bah; from that day Quraysh knew the Prophet ﷺ had a protector who would not bend. He fought at Badr and was killed at Uhud, where the Prophet ﷺ stood over his body in grief. A Muslim remembers Hamza as courage placed at the service of faith.

question: In whose house did the first Muslims meet secretly in Makkah?
explanation: The house of al-Arqam ibn Abi al-Arqam, on the hill of Safa, was the first gathering and teaching place.
detail: The sira records that al-Arqam ibn Abi al-Arqam, one of the earliest converts, opened his house to the Prophet ﷺ when open teaching in Makkah was impossible. There the Prophet ﷺ read the revelation to the small band of believers and prayed with them out of sight of Quraysh. It was to this house that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab came to declare his Islam, after which the Muslims went out to pray at the Ka'bah openly. A Muslim learns that the community grew from patient teaching in a single room.

question: Which companion, who accepted Islam in Makkah, was later sent as the first teacher to Yathrib?
explanation: Mus'ab ibn 'Umayr, a young Makkan of noble family, was sent to Yathrib after the pledge of 'Aqabah to teach the Quran.
detail: Every standard biography records that Mus'ab ibn 'Umayr grew up in comfort and left it all when he accepted Islam, his family cutting him off. In Yathrib he taught the Qur'an house by house and was called the reader, al-muqri'; through him Islam entered nearly every household of the city before the Hijra. At Uhud he carried the banner and was killed, and his shroud was too short to cover both his head and his feet. A Muslim learns that one patient teacher can prepare a whole city.

question: With what command does Surah Al-Muddaththir, which began the public call, open?
answers: "O you who covers himself! Arise and warn"
"Read, in the name of your Lord"
explanation: "O you who covers himself with a garment! Arise and warn."
detail: The surah continues: "O you who covers himself, arise and warn, and your Lord glorify, and your clothing purify, and uncleanliness avoid" (74:1-5). The one addressed is the Prophet ﷺ, who had wrapped himself in a garment after the first encounter with the angel; the Qur'an now calls him out of that covering to a task. The first revelation, "Read" (96:1), made him a prophet; these verses made him a messenger to others. A Muslim learns that receiving the truth is followed by carrying it to people.

question: Which verse ordered the Prophet ﷺ to proclaim openly what he was commanded?
answers: "So declare openly what you are commanded"
explanation: "So declare openly what you are commanded and turn away from the polytheists."
detail: The verse and the one after it read: "So declare openly what you are commanded and turn away from the polytheists. Indeed, We are sufficient for you against the mockers" (15:94-95). It belongs to Surah al-Hijr, revealed in Makkah while the call was still quiet, and the promise that follows answers the fear of what open preaching would bring. Another verse told him to begin with his nearest relatives (26:214). A Muslim learns that speaking the truth openly comes with a promise of Allah's protection.

question: Where did Quraysh hang the document of the boycott against Banu Hashim?
explanation: The text of the boycott was hung inside the Ka'bah, until the pact was broken and the document abandoned.
detail: The sira records that Quraysh swore neither to marry into nor to trade with Banu Hashim and Banu al-Muttalib until they surrendered the Prophet ﷺ, and the whole clan withdrew with Abu Talib into their valley, where hunger pressed them for years. The Prophet ﷺ then told Abu Talib that termites had eaten the document except the name of Allah written in it; when the sheet was taken down, it was found as he had said. A Muslim learns that Allah brings an unjust pact to nothing.

question: In whose garden at Ta'if did the Prophet ﷺ take shelter and receive a bunch of grapes after being driven out?
answers: The garden of 'Utba and Shayba, where the slave 'Addas served him
explanation: Wounded and driven from Ta'if, he took shelter in a garden where he was offered grapes, brought by a Christian slave named 'Addas.
detail: Every standard biography records that 'Addas, a Christian from Nineveh, heard the Prophet ﷺ say "In the name of Allah" before eating, words he had never heard from the people of that land. When the Prophet ﷺ learned his city, he said 'Addas came from the town of the righteous man Yunus, son of Matta, his brother in prophethood; 'Addas kissed his head and hands. On the road back the Prophet ﷺ was consoled that his message was heard. A Muslim learns that kindness reaches a stranger before argument does.

question: Which companion, at first a fierce opponent, accepted Islam and was named "the one who distinguishes truth from falsehood"?
explanation: 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, hostile at first, accepted Islam in Makkah and was given the title al-Faruq.
detail: The sira records that 'Umar set out sword in hand intending to kill the Prophet ﷺ, and on the way was told that his own sister Fatima and her husband Sa'id ibn Zayd had become Muslims. He went to their house, heard the beginning of Surah Ta-Ha, and asked to be taken to the Prophet ﷺ, then in the house of al-Arqam. After his Islam the Muslims prayed at the Ka'bah openly. A Muslim learns that a hard heart can turn in a single hour of listening to the Qur'an.

question: With which family did the Prophet ﷺ stay on reaching Madinah, where his camel knelt?
explanation: The camel knelt near the house of Abu Ayyub al-Ansari, who hosted the Prophet ﷺ on his arrival.
detail: Every standard biography records that as the Prophet ﷺ entered Madinah, the Ansar begged him to stay with them, and he said to let the camel go, for she was commanded. She knelt on land belonging to two orphan boys, where the mosque was afterwards built, and the nearest house was that of Abu Ayyub, who carried the Prophet's ﷺ saddle inside. A Muslim learns that the Prophet ﷺ let Allah choose his host, not rank.

question: What is the cemetery of Madinah called, where many companions are buried?
explanation: Baqi' al-Gharqad, beside the Prophet's ﷺ mosque, is the burial ground of Madinah.
detail: The name Baqi' al-Gharqad comes from the thorn trees, gharqad, that once grew on the ground beside the Prophet's ﷺ mosque. The Prophet ﷺ used to go out to al-Baqi' at night, greet its people as believers, and pray for their forgiveness, saying the living would soon join them. His infant son Ibrahim, several of his wives, and companions of every rank were laid there. A Muslim visiting Madinah greets the people of al-Baqi' in the words the Prophet ﷺ used and remembers that death gathers everyone.

question: Which mosque does the Quran describe as "founded on piety from the first day"?
explanation: "A mosque founded on righteousness from the first day is more worthy for you to stand in."
detail: The verse reads: "A mosque founded on righteousness from the first day is more worthy for you to stand in. Within it are men who love to purify themselves, and Allah loves those who purify themselves" (9:108). It follows the condemnation of a mosque the hypocrites built for harm (9:107), which the Prophet ﷺ is forbidden to stand in. Quba is where he stopped and laid a foundation on arriving at Madinah. A Muslim learns that a place of prayer is honoured by the intention it was built with.

question: In which mosque was the Prophet ﷺ praying when the command to change the qibla was revealed?
answers: The mosque of the two qiblas (Masjid al-Qiblatayn)
explanation: The command came during prayer; the worshippers turned toward the Ka'bah, hence the name "mosque of the two qiblas".
detail: Every standard biography records that the Muslims had prayed facing Jerusalem while the Prophet ﷺ longed to face the Ka'bah. The Qur'an answered: "We have certainly seen the turning of your face toward the heaven, and We will surely turn you to a qiblah with which you will be pleased. So turn your face toward al-Masjid al-Haram" (2:144). The prayer in that mosque began facing one direction and ended facing the other. A Muslim learns that a command is obeyed the moment it is heard.

question: Which obligation was prescribed to the Muslims in the second year of the Hijra?
explanation: Fasting Ramadan was made obligatory in Madinah, in the second year after the Hijra.
detail: The Qur'an gives the command: "O you who have believed, decreed upon you is fasting as it was decreed upon those before you, that you may become righteous" (2:183), and names the month: "The month of Ramadan in which was revealed the Qur'an" (2:185). Every standard biography records that this first Ramadan of fasting was also the month in which the battle of Badr was fought. A Muslim learns that Ramadan was given as a month of self-restraint and of the Qur'an together.

question: Which companion saw the words of the call to prayer in a dream, which the Prophet ﷺ then adopted?
explanation: 'Abdullah ibn Zayd reported the dream of the adhan; the Prophet ﷺ approved it and told Bilal to call it.
detail: The sira records that the Muslims, lacking a way to gather for prayer, discussed a bell or a horn, and neither pleased the Prophet ﷺ. 'Abdullah ibn Zayd then saw in a dream a man teaching him the words of the call; the Prophet ﷺ declared it a true dream and had him teach it to Bilal, whose voice carried further. 'Umar came and said he had seen the same. A Muslim learns that the adhan heard five times a day began with a dream confirmed by the Prophet ﷺ.

question: What does the Quran say of the handful of dust the Prophet ﷺ threw at Badr?
answers: "You did not throw when you threw, but it was Allah who threw"
explanation: "And you did not throw when you threw, but it was Allah who threw."
detail: The verse reads in full: "And you did not kill them, but it was Allah who killed them. And you threw not when you threw, but it was Allah who threw, that He might test the believers with a good test from Him" (8:17). Surah al-Anfal was revealed about Badr, and the verse addresses the Prophet ﷺ after he cast a handful of dust toward the enemy lines. A Muslim learns to work with effort and to credit victory to Allah alone.

question: How does the Quran describe some believers' state as they set out for Badr?
answers: They disputed about it as though being driven toward death
explanation: "Arguing with you concerning the truth after it had become clear, as if they were being driven toward death."
detail: The passage reads: "As your Lord brought you out of your home in truth, while a party of the believers were unwilling, arguing with you concerning the truth after it had become clear, as if they were being driven toward death while they were looking on" (8:5-6). The next verse gives the cause: they had hoped for the unarmed caravan, and Allah wished to establish the truth instead (8:7). A Muslim learns that reluctance before a hard duty is human, and obedience through it is faith.

question: How does the Quran remind the believers of their state before victory?
answers: They were few and oppressed in the land, then Allah sheltered and supported them
explanation: "And remember when you were few and oppressed in the land… then He sheltered you and supported you with His victory."
detail: The verse reads: "And remember when you were few and oppressed in the land, fearing that people might abduct you, but He sheltered you, supported you with His victory, and provided you with good things, that you might be grateful" (8:26). It stands in Surah al-Anfal before the warning not to betray Allah and His Messenger (8:27). The sheltering is the welcome in Madinah, the victory is Badr. A Muslim learns to look back at times of weakness so that today's strength is met with thanks.

question: Which companion at Badr suggested moving the army to the well nearest the enemy?
explanation: Al-Hubab ibn al-Mundhir asked whether the position was revelation or opinion; told it was opinion, he proposed advancing to the well, and the Prophet ﷺ agreed.
detail: Every standard biography records al-Hubab's exact question: was this a position Allah had ordered, or a matter of opinion, war and stratagem? Told it was the latter, he proposed to advance to the well nearest the enemy, fill in the other wells, and build a cistern so the Muslims would drink and their enemy would not; the Prophet ﷺ said he had spoken well and moved at once. A Muslim learns that the Prophet ﷺ welcomed sound counsel in matters not settled by revelation.

question: What was the name of the watering place at which the battle of Badr took place?
answers: Badr, a well on the caravan road
explanation: Badr was a watering place on the caravan road between Makkah and Syria; the battle took its name from it.
detail: The Qur'an names the place itself: "And already had Allah given you victory at Badr while you were few in number" (3:123). Surah al-Anfal describes the ground: "when you were on the near side of the valley, and they were on the farther side, and the caravan was lower than you" (8:42). The caravan under Abu Sufyan had escaped by the coast, so the Muslims met the army of Makkah instead. A Muslim learns that Badr, the first great test, is remembered in the Qur'an by its own name.

question: What matter concerning the captives was addressed by revelation after Badr?
answers: The ransom accepted for the prisoners
explanation: The passage speaks of the captives and the ransom, then permits what was taken as lawful and good.
detail: The passage reads: "It is not for a prophet to have captives until he inflicts a massacre in the land. You desire the commodities of this world, but Allah desires the Hereafter" (8:67), then: "So consume what you have taken of war booty as being lawful and good" (8:69). The next verse tells the prisoners that if Allah knows any good in their hearts He will give them better than what was taken (8:70). A Muslim learns that Allah's correction came together with His forgiveness.

question: According to Surah Al-'Imran, what turned the situation at Uhud after an early success?
answers: Disobedience and disputing about the order given
explanation: "…until you lost courage and fell to disputing about the order and disobeyed."
detail: The verse reads: "And Allah had certainly fulfilled His promise to you when you were killing them by His permission until, when you lost courage and fell to disputing about the order and disobeyed after He had shown you that which you love" (3:152). It continues that some among them desired this world and some the Hereafter, and that Allah had forgiven them. The following verse recalls their flight while the Messenger ﷺ called them from behind (3:153). A Muslim learns that the promise of help stands while obedience stands.

question: What does the Quran say of those killed in the way of Allah?
answers: Do not think them dead: they are alive with their Lord
They sleep until the Last Day
explanation: "And never think of those who have been killed in the cause of Allah as dead. Rather, they are alive with their Lord, receiving provision."
detail: The verse continues: "rejoicing in what Allah has bestowed upon them of His bounty, and they receive good tidings about those after them who have not yet joined them, that there will be no fear concerning them, nor will they grieve" (3:169-170). It belongs to the part of Surah Al-'Imran revealed after Uhud, when the survivors mourned their dead. The Qur'an answers their grief with a picture of life, provision and joy with their Lord. A Muslim learns that death in Allah's cause is a passage into His keeping.

question: On which hill did the Prophet ﷺ station the archers at Uhud?
answers: The Hill of the Archers (Jabal ar-Rumat)
explanation: Fifty archers were posted on a hill later called "the hill of the archers", with orders not to leave it.
detail: Every standard biography records that the Prophet ﷺ put the archers under 'Abdullah ibn Jubayr and told them not to move whether the battle went for them or against them. When the Makkans first fled, most of the archers left the hill to gather spoils, and the cavalry of Quraysh came round it and struck the Muslims from behind. The Qur'an refers to this as disputing about the order and disobeying (3:152). A Muslim learns that a post held is worth more than a prize taken.

question: How does Surah Al-Ahzab describe the trial of the siege of Madinah?
answers: Eyes turned aside, hearts reached the throats
explanation: "When they came at you from above you and from below you, and when eyes shifted and hearts reached the throats."
detail: The verse continues: "There the believers were tested and shaken with a severe shaking" (33:10-11). The two directions are the confederate armies outside the city and the treachery within it. The Qur'an then contrasts two voices: the hypocrites said that Allah and His Messenger had promised them only delusion (33:12), while the believers, seeing the armies, said this was what Allah and His Messenger had promised them (33:22). A Muslim learns that fear itself is no sin; what matters is what the heart says under it.

question: How does the Quran describe the outcome of the Battle of the Trench?
answers: Allah turned back the confederates in their rage, having gained no good
explanation: "And Allah repelled those who disbelieved, in their rage, not having obtained any good. And sufficient was Allah for the believers in battle."
detail: The verse reads in full: "And Allah repelled those who disbelieved, in their rage, not having obtained any good. And sufficient was Allah for the believers in battle, and ever is Allah Powerful and Exalted in Might" (33:25). Earlier in the surah the means are named: "when armies came to you and We sent upon them a wind and armies you did not see" (33:9). The confederates left without a pitched battle. A Muslim learns that Allah can end a threat without a sword being raised.

question: Where is Hudaybiyya, the place of the famous treaty?
answers: On the edge of the sacred precinct, west of Makkah
explanation: Hudaybiyya is a place on the edge of the sacred precinct of Makkah, where the treaty was concluded.
detail: Every standard biography records that the Prophet ﷺ set out meaning only to perform 'umrah, and that his camel al-Qaswa knelt at Hudaybiyya and would not go on. There, under a tree, the companions gave him the pledge the Qur'an praises: "Certainly was Allah pleased with the believers when they pledged allegiance to you under the tree" (48:18). The treaty sent them home that year with a promise to return. A Muslim learns that a halt on the edge of the Haram became a door to the conquest.

question: Which vision of the Prophet ﷺ does the Quran confirm after Hudaybiyya?
answers: That they would enter the Sacred Mosque in security, heads shaved or shortened
That they would win at Khaybar
That they would build a city
That they would travel to Syria
explanation: "Certainly has Allah shown to His Messenger the vision in truth: you will surely enter the Sacred Mosque, in safety."
detail: The verse continues: "with your heads shaved and hair shortened, not fearing. He knew what you did not know and has arranged before that a conquest near at hand" (48:27). When the treaty turned the company back the vision seemed unfulfilled; the Qur'an declares it true and only delayed. The same surah opens by calling the treaty itself a clear conquest (48:1). A Muslim learns that a promise of Allah is fulfilled in His time, and a delay is not a denial.

question: What does Surah Al-Fath recall about hands withheld at Makkah?
answers: Allah withheld their hands from you and your hands from them within Makkah
explanation: "And it is He who withheld their hands from you and your hands from them within the area of Makkah, after He caused you to overcome them."
detail: The verse reads in full: "And it is He who withheld their hands from you and your hands from them within the area of Makkah after He caused you to overcome them, and Allah is Seeing of what you do" (48:24). The next verse explains the restraint: believing men and women unknown to the Muslims were in Makkah and might have been trampled had fighting begun (48:25). A Muslim learns that a battle avoided at Hudaybiyya was a mercy Allah counts among His favours.

question: In which year of the Hijra did the expedition to Khaybar take place?
explanation: Khaybar took place in 7 AH, the year after the treaty of Hudaybiyya.
detail: Every standard biography records that Khaybar followed the truce with Quraysh, and the Qur'an promises those who pledged at Hudaybiyya "much booty which you will take" (48:20). The Prophet ﷺ gave the banner to 'Ali ibn Abi Talib on the day the strongest fort fell, and the people of Khaybar were left on their land to work it for a share of the harvest. A Muslim learns that the seventh year turned a treaty many had grieved over into an opening.

question: What is the 'umrah performed the year after Hudaybiyya, under the terms of the treaty, called?
explanation: The treaty provided that the Muslims would return the following year; that 'umrah is called 'umrat al-qada.
detail: The sira records that the Muslims entered Makkah for three days as the treaty allowed, while Quraysh withdrew to the surrounding hills to watch. The Prophet ﷺ told his companions to walk briskly in the first rounds of the tawaf so that Quraysh, who said the fever of Madinah had weakened them, would see their strength. This 'umrah completed the one from which they had been turned back the year before. A Muslim learns that the Prophet ﷺ kept the treaty to the letter, even when its terms were hard.

question: Which ruler, on receiving the Prophet's ﷺ letter, tore it up?
explanation: The Prophet ﷺ sent letters to the neighbouring rulers; the one to the king of Persia was torn up.
detail: Every standard biography records that after Hudaybiyya the Prophet ﷺ sent letters calling the rulers of the surrounding lands to Islam: the Byzantine emperor, the Negus of Abyssinia, the ruler of Egypt and the king of Persia. Chosroes tore the letter to pieces on reading it, and the Prophet ﷺ, when told, asked Allah to tear his kingdom likewise. The same letters were received with respect by others. A Muslim learns that the message was offered to every ruler alike, and that each answered for himself.

question: Which companion was sent with the Prophet's ﷺ letter to the Negus of Abyssinia and to other rulers?
explanation: Messengers were chosen from among the companions; 'Amr ibn Umayya ad-Damri was sent to the Negus.
detail: The sira records that the Negus had already sheltered the first emigrants years earlier and refused to hand them over to the envoys of Quraysh. 'Amr ibn Umayya ad-Damri carried the Prophet's ﷺ letter, and the Negus received it with honour and sent the remaining emigrants, Ja'far ibn Abi Talib among them, back by ship; they reached the Prophet ﷺ at Khaybar. When the Negus died, the Prophet ﷺ led the funeral prayer for him in Madinah. A Muslim learns that a just ruler is remembered and prayed for.

question: In which direction does Khaybar lie from Madinah?
answers: To the west, on the sea
explanation: Khaybar is a fortified oasis north of Madinah, on the road toward Syria.
detail: Every standard biography records that Khaybar was a cluster of fortresses among palm groves, and that the Prophet ﷺ reached it by night and waited until morning before advancing, since he did not attack a town in which the call to prayer was heard. The forts fell one after another, and the people of Khaybar asked to stay on their land, working it in return for half of what it produced, which was granted. A Muslim learns that the campaign to the north ended in an agreement, not in expulsion.

question: What did the house of Abu Sufyan become on the day Makkah was conquered?
answers: A place of safety for whoever entered it
explanation: The Prophet ﷺ declared safety for whoever entered the Sacred Mosque, stayed in his own home, or entered the house of Abu Sufyan.
detail: The sira records that Abu Sufyan, the leader of Quraysh, came to the Muslim camp outside Makkah with al-'Abbas, saw the size of the army, and accepted Islam that night. Al-'Abbas said that Abu Sufyan was a man who loved honour and asked the Prophet ﷺ to grant him something; the Prophet ﷺ then made his house a sanctuary alongside the Sacred Mosque and every man's own home. A Muslim learns that the Prophet ﷺ won Makkah by sparing it.

question: Which year is called "the year of the conquest" ('am al-fath)?
explanation: Makkah was conquered in 8 AH, the year known as "the year of the conquest".
detail: Every standard biography records that the Prophet ﷺ entered Makkah in Ramadan with his head bowed low on his camel out of humility before Allah. He went round the Ka'bah and struck down the idols around it, reciting: "Truth has come, and falsehood has departed. Indeed is falsehood ever bound to depart" (17:81). Then he asked Quraysh what they expected of him, and told them to go, for they were free. A Muslim learns that the year of the conquest is remembered for forgiveness more than for force.

question: Which battle followed soon after the conquest of Makkah, against the tribes of Hawazin?
explanation: Hunayn took place shortly after the conquest, in a valley between Makkah and Ta'if.
detail: The Qur'an speaks of this battle by name: "and on the day of Hunayn, when your great number pleased you, but it did not avail you at all, and the earth was confining for you with its vastness; then you turned back, fleeing" (9:25). The sira records that Hawazin lay in ambush in the valley, and that the Prophet ﷺ held his ground on his mule, calling out that he was the Prophet, until his companions rallied. A Muslim learns that numbers win nothing; steadfastness does.

question: What did Allah send down upon His Messenger ﷺ and the believers after their dismay at Hunayn?
answers: His tranquillity (sakinah), and soldiers they did not see
explanation: "Then Allah sent down His tranquillity upon His Messenger and upon the believers and sent down soldiers you did not see."
detail: The verse reads in full: "Then Allah sent down His tranquillity upon His Messenger and upon the believers and sent down soldiers you did not see, and He punished those who disbelieved. And that is the recompense of the disbelievers" (9:26). The verse before it recalls the flight itself, when the Muslims' great number pleased them and the earth grew narrow (9:25). A Muslim learns that calm sent by Allah, not the size of an army, turns a rout into a victory.

question: Which town did the Muslim army move against after Hunayn?
explanation: After Hunayn the Muslims laid siege to Ta'if, whose people had shut themselves in.
detail: The sira records that Thaqif, the tribe of Ta'if, had fought beside Hawazin at Hunayn and, after the defeat, shut themselves inside the walls with provisions for a long stay. The Muslims besieged it for a time, and the Prophet ﷺ lifted the siege, praying that Allah guide Thaqif and bring them to him. Within the year a delegation from Ta'if came to Madinah and accepted Islam. A Muslim learns that the town which had stoned the Prophet ﷺ was won at last by a prayer.

question: Which expedition does the Quran call "the hour of difficulty" (sa'at al-'usrah)?
explanation: "Allah has accepted the repentance of the Prophet, the emigrants and the helpers who followed him in the hour of difficulty."
detail: The verse reads: "Allah has already forgiven the Prophet and the Muhajirun and the Ansar who followed him in the hour of difficulty after the hearts of a party of them had almost inclined to doubt, and then He forgave them" (9:117). The Qur'an explains the difficulty elsewhere: the journey was long (9:42), and those who stayed behind said not to go out in the heat (9:81). A Muslim learns that setting out when the way is hard earns Allah's mercy.

question: What does the Quran say of the three companions who stayed behind at Tabuk, before they were forgiven?
answers: The earth became narrow for them despite its vastness, then Allah accepted their repentance
explanation: "And the three who were left behind, until the earth closed in on them in spite of its vastness… then He accepted their repentance."
detail: The verse reads in full: "And the three who were left behind, until the earth closed in on them in spite of its vastness and their souls confined them and they were certain that there is no refuge from Allah except in Him. Then He turned to them so they could repent" (9:118). These three had confessed plainly that they had no excuse. The next verse commands: be with those who are true (9:119), and a Muslim learns that honest confession is the road to forgiveness.

question: In which direction lies Tabuk, the goal of the last great expedition?
answers: To the north, toward the Syrian frontier
To the west, on the Red Sea
explanation: Tabuk is north of Madinah, on the road to Syria; it was the Prophet's ﷺ last great expedition.
detail: The Qur'an records that the expedition was made in fierce heat: those who stayed behind said not to go forth in the heat, and Allah replied that the fire of Hell is more intense in heat (9:81). The Prophet ﷺ marched to Tabuk, found no army waiting, and returned without fighting. On the way back, the Qur'an exposed the mosque built by hypocrites for harm (9:107). A Muslim learns that Tabuk was a test of who would answer the call when the journey was long.

question: Which companion equipped a large part of the army of Tabuk from his own wealth?
explanation: 'Uthman ibn 'Affan provided a considerable share of the equipment of "the army of difficulty" (jaysh al-'usrah).
detail: Every standard biography records that when the Prophet ﷺ called for help to equip the expedition in a year of drought and heat, 'Uthman brought camels, mounts and money in a quantity no one else matched. The Prophet ﷺ turned the coins over in his hand and said that nothing 'Uthman did after that day would harm him. Abu Bakr brought all he owned and 'Umar half of his. A Muslim learns that giving for the community is measured by what it costs the giver.

question: Which companion was the first to shoot an arrow in the way of Allah?
explanation: Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, one of the earliest to accept Islam, is known as the first to shoot an arrow in the way of Allah.
detail: The sira records that Sa'd's mother swore to neither eat nor drink until he left the religion; the Qur'an answered her: "But if they endeavour to make you associate with Me that of which you have no knowledge, do not obey them but accompany them in this world with appropriate kindness" (31:15). At Uhud the Prophet ﷺ urged him to shoot, saying his father and mother were ransom for him. A Muslim learns that firmness in faith and kindness to parents go together.

question: Which companion is called "the disciple (hawari) of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ"?
explanation: Az-Zubayr ibn al-'Awwam, the Prophet's ﷺ cousin, was called his hawari, his close support.
detail: Every standard biography records that az-Zubayr was the son of Safiyya bint 'Abd al-Muttalib, the Prophet's ﷺ aunt, and that he accepted Islam very young in Makkah. During the siege of Madinah, when the Prophet ﷺ asked who would bring him news of the enemy, az-Zubayr volunteered three times, and the Prophet ﷺ said that every prophet has a hawari and his was az-Zubayr. A Muslim learns that the title was earned by stepping forward when others held back.

question: Which companion was entrusted with knowledge of the hypocrites, and so called "the keeper of the secret"?
explanation: Hudhayfa ibn al-Yaman is known as "sahib as-sirr", the one the Prophet ﷺ confided in about the hypocrites.
detail: The sira records that on the return from Tabuk a band of hypocrites tried to push the Prophet ﷺ from a mountain pass in the dark, and that Hudhayfa, who was driving his camel, learned who they were. The Prophet ﷺ told him their names and told him to keep them; afterwards 'Umar himself asked Hudhayfa whether his own name was among them. A Muslim learns that a trust kept in silence is a form of loyalty.

question: Where did Salman, called "al-Farisi", who proposed the trench, come from?
explanation: Salman, of Persian origin, searched long for the truth before joining the Prophet ﷺ in Madinah.
detail: Every standard biography records that Salman was born in Persia to a father devoted to fire-worship, and left home to seek the Christians' teaching in Syria. The last monk he served told him a prophet would soon appear in a land of palm trees, who would refuse charity, accept gifts and bear the seal of prophethood between his shoulders. Sold as a slave, he reached Madinah and found the three signs in the Prophet ﷺ. A Muslim learns that a sincere seeker is guided across any distance.

question: Which woman, the mother of Anas ibn Malik, offered the Prophet ﷺ her son's service?
explanation: Umm Sulaym of the Ansar presented her son Anas to the Prophet ﷺ to serve him when he reached Madinah.
detail: The sira records that Anas served the Prophet ﷺ for ten years without once being asked why he had done something or why he had not. Umm Sulaym asked the Prophet ﷺ to pray for her little servant, and he asked Allah to increase Anas's wealth and children and to bless him in what He gave, which Anas saw answered. A Muslim learns that a mother's gift of her son to the Prophet's ﷺ service was a gift to the whole community.

question: Which wife of the Prophet ﷺ was known for her great learning and narrated many hadiths?
explanation: 'Aisha, the daughter of Abu Bakr, is among the greatest narrators of hadith and a reference in religious knowledge.
detail: Every standard biography records that 'Aisha came to the Prophet's ﷺ house in Madinah as a young girl and grew up beside him, and remembered his practice at home more closely than anyone. When the hypocrites slandered her, the Qur'an itself declared her innocence: "Indeed, those who came with falsehood are a group among you" (24:11). After the Prophet's ﷺ death in her room, the elder companions brought her their questions. A Muslim learns that much of the Prophet's ﷺ daily life reaches us through her.

question: Which wife of the Prophet ﷺ was his cousin, and whose marriage is mentioned in Surah Al-Ahzab?
explanation: The marriage to Zaynab bint Jahsh is mentioned in Surah Al-Ahzab (33:37).
detail: The verse says: "So when Zayd had no longer any need for her, We married her to you in order that there not be upon the believers any discomfort concerning the wives of their adopted sons" (33:37). Zaynab, daughter of the Prophet's ﷺ aunt Umayma, had first been married to Zayd ibn Haritha, his former adopted son; Zayd is the only companion named in the Qur'an. Zaynab used to say that Allah Himself had given her in marriage. A Muslim learns that an adopted son is not a son by blood.

question: Which wife of the Prophet ﷺ advised the step that broke the deadlock at Hudaybiyya?
explanation: Umm Salama advised the Prophet ﷺ to go out and perform the sacrifice and the shaving himself: the companions at once followed.
detail: The sira records that when the treaty was signed, the companions were so grieved at turning back without 'umrah that the Prophet ﷺ told them three times to rise, sacrifice and shave, and none moved. Umm Salama, who had travelled with him, said to go out, say nothing to anyone, sacrifice his animal and call his barber; he did so, and the companions rose and did the same. A Muslim learns that example moves people where words cannot.

question: What is the Prophet's ﷺ full name, back to his grandfather?
explanation: He is Muhammad, son of 'Abdullah, son of 'Abd al-Muttalib, of the tribe of Quraysh.
detail: Every standard biography opens with this lineage: Muhammad ﷺ, son of 'Abdullah, son of 'Abd al-Muttalib, of Banu Hashim within Quraysh, the tribe that kept the Ka'bah. His father died before his birth; after his mother's death his grandfather 'Abd al-Muttalib cared for him, then his uncle Abu Talib. The Qur'an recalls it: "Did He not find you an orphan and give you shelter?" (93:6). A Muslim learns that the last Prophet ﷺ began life as an orphan in the care of his family.

question: Which other name of the Prophet ﷺ, mentioned in the Quran by 'Isa, means "most praised"?
explanation: 'Isa announced a messenger to come after him "whose name is Ahmad" (Quran 61:6).
detail: The verse is in Surah As-Saff, where 'Isa, peace be upon him, tells his people that he confirms the Torah and brings "good tidings of a messenger to come after me, whose name is Ahmad" (61:6). Ahmad and Muhammad share the Arabic root hamd, praise. The verse adds that when that messenger came with clear proofs, they called it plain magic. A Muslim learns from 61:6 that the Prophet ﷺ was announced by the prophet who came before him.

question: Over how long was the Quran revealed to the Prophet ﷺ?
explanation: The revelation spanned about twenty-three years: thirteen in Makkah and ten in Madinah.
detail: The Qur'an explains why it was not sent down at once: "a Qur'an which We have divided, that you may recite it to the people over a prolonged period" (17:106). To those who asked why it did not come in one piece, the answer was: "Thus, that We may strengthen your heart thereby" (25:32). The first words came in the cave of Hira, "Read in the name of your Lord" (96:1). A Muslim learns that the Qur'an met the community's needs as they arose, over a whole lifetime.

question: Which companion was the first free adult man to accept Islam?
explanation: Among free adult men, Abu Bakr was the first to answer the Prophet's ﷺ call.
detail: Every standard biography records that Abu Bakr accepted the call without hesitation, and that through him came several early companions, among them 'Uthman, az-Zubayr, 'Abd ar-Rahman ibn 'Awf, Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas and Talha. He spent his wealth freeing Muslims tortured for their faith, Bilal among them. The Qur'an names him as the companion in the cave: "when he said to his companion: Do not grieve; indeed Allah is with us" (9:40). A Muslim learns that the first to believe was also the first to give.

question: Which child was the first to accept Islam?
explanation: 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, raised in the Prophet's ﷺ household, was the first among the children to believe.
detail: The standard biographies record how 'Ali came to that household: in a year of hardship in Makkah, the Prophet ﷺ took his young cousin from the house of Abu Talib to ease his uncle's burden, as Abu Talib had once taken in the orphaned Muhammad ﷺ. So 'Ali saw the first revelation from inside the home and believed as a boy. On the night of the Hijra he slept in the Prophet's ﷺ bed to deceive Quraysh. A Muslim learns that faith is not measured by age.

question: Which freedman of the Prophet ﷺ was the first among freedmen to accept Islam?
explanation: Zayd ibn Haritha, freed and raised as a son by the Prophet ﷺ, was the first among freedmen to believe.
detail: Every standard biography tells how Zayd, captured as a boy and sold, came to Khadija and then to the Prophet ﷺ; when his father and uncle came to buy him back, Zayd chose to stay, and the Prophet ﷺ freed him and declared him his son. He was called Zayd ibn Muhammad until the Qur'an ordered: "Call them by the names of their fathers" (33:5). He is the only companion named in the Qur'an (33:37). A Muslim learns from Zayd's choice what the Prophet's ﷺ company was worth.

question: Which verse ended legal adoption, saying the Prophet ﷺ is not the father of any of their men?
answers: "Muhammad is not the father of any of your men, but the Messenger of Allah and the seal of the prophets"
explanation: "Muhammad is not the father of any one of your men, but he is the Messenger of Allah and the last of the prophets."
detail: The verse comes in Surah Al-Ahzab, after the account of Zayd's marriage (33:37): "Muhammad is not the father of any of your men, but he is the Messenger of Allah and the seal of the prophets; and Allah is ever, of all things, Knowing" (33:40). Earlier the surah had said, "He has not made your adopted sons your sons" (33:4), and ordered, "Call them by the names of their fathers" (33:5). A Muslim reads two truths here: an adopted child keeps his father's name, and no prophet follows Muhammad ﷺ.

question: On which day of the week do Muslims gather for the congregational prayer instituted in Madinah?
explanation: The Friday prayer (al-jumu'ah) was instituted in Madinah and gathers the community every week.
detail: Surah Al-Jumu'ah takes its name from this day: "When the call is made for the prayer on the day of Jumu'ah, hasten to the remembrance of Allah and leave trade" (62:9). The next verse releases them: "And when the prayer has ended, disperse in the land and seek from the bounty of Allah" (62:10). Jumu'ah means gathering, and the Prophet ﷺ led it in his mosque, addressing the people from the minbar first. A Muslim learns that once a week the whole community sets its business aside to pray together.

question: Which companion led the prayer during the Prophet's ﷺ final illness, by his own order?
explanation: The Prophet ﷺ ordered that Abu Bakr lead the prayer during his illness; the companions took it as a sign.
detail: Every standard biography records that when the Prophet ﷺ was too ill to come out, he told his household to have Abu Bakr lead the prayer; 'A'isha asked him to choose another, saying her father was soft-hearted and would weep, and he repeated the order. Once, supported by two men, he came out and sat beside Abu Bakr as he prayed. After his death the companions recalled that he had put Abu Bakr forward in their religion. A Muslim learns that the Prophet ﷺ prepared his community for his absence.

question: Which caliph was struck down while leading the dawn prayer?
explanation: 'Umar ibn al-Khattab was struck during the fajr prayer in Madinah and died of his wounds.
detail: The standard biographies record that 'Umar was stabbed in the mosque of Madinah as he stood to lead fajr, by a slave named Abu Lu'lu'a, and had another man complete the prayer. Before he died he named a council of six companions to choose the next caliph, and asked 'A'isha's permission to be buried beside the Prophet ﷺ and Abu Bakr, which she gave. His caliphate had lasted about ten years, in which the Muslims opened Syria, Iraq, Persia and Egypt. A Muslim learns that 'Umar died in prayer.

question: How long did the caliphate of Abu Bakr last?
explanation: Abu Bakr ruled for about two years before his death, and 'Umar succeeded him.
detail: The standard biographies record that Abu Bakr was chosen on the day the Prophet ﷺ died, in the gathering of the Ansar and Muhajirun at the hall of Banu Sa'ida. In his first address he told the people to obey him as long as he obeyed Allah and His Messenger ﷺ, and to correct him if he went wrong. In those two years he sent out the army of Usama, fought the tribes that broke away, and had the Qur'an collected. A Muslim learns how much a short time holds.

question: Which movement did Abu Bakr have to act against at the start of his caliphate?
answers: The refusal of zakat and the apostasy of some tribes
explanation: The first caliphate opened with the ridda wars, against tribes that refused zakat or left Islam.
detail: Every standard biography records Abu Bakr's answer to those who wanted to let the zakat go: he swore he would fight anyone who separated the prayer from the zakat, since the Qur'an joins the two, even over a single young goat once paid to the Messenger ﷺ. 'Umar first thought him harsh, then saw that his heart had been opened to the truth. The armies also faced Musaylima, who claimed prophethood. A Muslim learns that the community held to the whole religion, not part of it.

question: Which title did 'Umar ibn al-Khattab take as head of the community?
explanation: The title amir al-mu'minin was established under 'Umar and borne by the caliphs after him.
detail: The standard biographies record how the title arose. Abu Bakr had been called khalifat rasul Allah, the successor of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ; 'Umar would then be the successor of the successor of the Messenger, a name that would grow longer with each caliph. The companions addressed him instead as amir al-mu'minin, and it stayed. The Qur'an calls the believers al-mu'minun throughout, and speaks of "those in authority among you" (4:59). A Muslim learns that the leader's title named him by the people he served, not by a crown.

question: Which mosque in Jerusalem was the first qibla of the Muslims?
explanation: The Muslims prayed first toward Jerusalem, before the qibla was fixed toward the Ka'bah.
detail: The Qur'an names the mosque in the verse of the Night Journey: "Glory be to Him who took His servant by night from the Sacred Mosque to al-Aqsa Mosque, whose surroundings We have blessed" (17:1). The believers faced it in Makkah and in the first months in Madinah, until revelation changed the qibla: "So turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque" (2:144), after foretelling that the foolish would ask what turned them from their qibla (2:142). A Muslim learns that the direction of prayer is set by Allah's command.

question: Which three mosques are those to which travel is specially encouraged?
answers: The Sacred Mosque, the Prophet's ﷺ mosque and al-Aqsa
The Sacred Mosque, Quba and Damascus
explanation: Travel is specially encouraged to three mosques: the Sacred Mosque, the Prophet's ﷺ mosque and al-Aqsa Mosque.
detail: Every standard collection of the Prophet's ﷺ words records that he said saddles are not to be fastened for a journey to any mosque except three: the Sacred Mosque, his own mosque, and al-Aqsa Mosque. The Qur'an names the first two: the Sacred Mosque as the qibla, "turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque" (2:144), and al-Aqsa as the goal of the Night Journey (17:1). The third he built with his own hands in Madinah. A Muslim learns that these three places hold a rank no other mosque shares.

question: Where did the Prophet ﷺ deliver his farewell sermon, on the day of 'Arafah?
answers: In the valley of 'Uranah, at Mount 'Arafat
explanation: The farewell sermon was delivered on the day of 'Arafah, in the valley of 'Uranah at the foot of Mount 'Arafat.
detail: The standard biographies record that on the day of 'Arafah the Prophet ﷺ addressed the people from his camel in the valley of 'Uranah, and that on that same day and plain the verse came down: "This day I have perfected for you your religion and completed My favour upon you and have approved for you Islam as religion" (5:3). At the end he asked the crowd whether he had conveyed the message; they answered yes. A Muslim learns that the religion was declared complete at 'Arafat.

question: What did the Prophet ﷺ declare inviolable in his farewell sermon?
explanation: He declared the blood, property and honour of the Muslims sacred, as sacred as that day, that month and that city.
detail: Every standard biography records how he framed it: he asked the crowd which day, which month and which city it was, and when they answered that all three were sacred, he told them that their blood, property and honour were as inviolable as that day, month and city. He also abolished the usury of the days of ignorance. The Qur'an had said: "Whoever kills a soul, it is as if he had killed all mankind" (5:32). A Muslim learns that another Muslim's life, wealth and dignity are sacred.

question: What did the Prophet ﷺ leave his community in his farewell sermon, so that it would not go astray?
explanation: He reminded them that he was leaving among them what they should hold to so as not to go astray: the Book of Allah.
detail: Every standard biography records his words at 'Arafah: he told the crowd he had left among them that which, if they held fast to it, would keep them from ever going astray, the Book of Allah. He then asked what they would say when questioned about him, and they answered that he had conveyed the message and fulfilled his trust. The Qur'an had said: "Hold firmly to the rope of Allah all together" (3:103). A Muslim learns that the Prophet's ﷺ inheritance was not gold or land but the Book.

question: Which month of the Muslim calendar marks the pilgrimage the Prophet ﷺ performed at his farewell?
explanation: The farewell pilgrimage took place in Dhul-Hijjah of the year 10 AH.
detail: The Qur'an sets the pilgrimage in its season: "Hajj is in the well-known months" (2:197), and speaks of "the day of the greater pilgrimage" (9:3). Dhul-Hijjah is one of the four sacred months: "of them, four are sacred" (9:36). The farewell pilgrimage was the only Hajj the Prophet ﷺ performed after the Hijra; he stood at 'Arafah, spent the night at Muzdalifah, threw the pebbles at Mina, and told the people to take their rites from him. A Muslim learns that every Hajj since follows that pattern.

question: Who washed and shrouded the body of the Prophet ﷺ after his death?
answers: The people of his household, among them 'Ali and al-'Abbas
explanation: His own household saw to it, among them 'Ali ibn Abi Talib and his uncle al-'Abbas.
detail: The standard biographies record that the Prophet ﷺ died in the room of 'A'isha and that his family washed him without removing his garment, 'Ali washing while al-'Abbas, his sons al-Fadl and Qutham, and Usama ibn Zayd helped. The people then came in group after group to pray over him without an imam. Abu Bakr told them that a prophet is buried where he dies, so his grave was dug in that room. A Muslim learns that the last service to him was done within his household.

question: In which month of the Hijri year did the Prophet ﷺ die?
explanation: The Prophet ﷺ died in Madinah in the month of Rabi' al-Awwal, in the year 11 AH.
detail: The standard biographies record that Rabi' al-Awwal was also the month in which the Prophet ﷺ had reached Madinah at the Hijra, so his arrival in the city and his death in it fell in the same month, ten years apart. He died on a Monday in the room of 'A'isha, resting against her, after a fever of several days; his last words asked for the highest companion. Abu Bakr kissed his forehead and wept over him. A Muslim learns that the Prophet ﷺ was mortal.

question: Which verse did Abu Bakr recite to remind people that the Prophet ﷺ was mortal?
answers: "Muhammad is but a messenger; messengers have passed on before him"
explanation: "Muhammad is not but a messenger. Other messengers have passed on before him. So if he was to die or be killed, would you turn back on your heels?"
detail: The verse had come down after Uhud, when a rumour spread that the Prophet ﷺ was killed: "Muhammad is not but a messenger; messengers have passed on before him. So if he was to die or be killed, would you turn back on your heels?" (3:144). When 'Umar denied the death, Abu Bakr said that whoever worshipped Muhammad should know that he had died, and whoever worshipped Allah should know that Allah does not die, then recited 3:144. A Muslim learns that faith rests on Allah, not on any man.

question: Which companion is known above all for the sheer number of hadiths he memorised?
explanation: Abu Hurayra spent the Prophet's ﷺ last years at his side and became the most prolific narrator of hadith.
detail: The standard biographies record that Abu Hurayra came to Madinah in the year of Khaybar and lived among the poor of the Suffa, the covered part of the mosque, so as to stay close to the Prophet ﷺ. He told how he once complained of forgetting what he heard, and the Prophet ﷺ had him spread out his cloak and gather it to his chest, after which he forgot nothing. A Muslim learns that much of the Prophet's ﷺ words reached the world through one man.

question: Which companion, the Prophet's ﷺ cousin, became the great authority on Quranic exegesis?
explanation: 'Abdullah ibn 'Abbas, for whom the Prophet ﷺ prayed for understanding of the Book, became "the interpreter of the Quran".
detail: The standard biographies record that the Prophet ﷺ once put his arm around the boy and prayed that Allah would give him understanding of the religion and teach him the interpretation of the Book. Ibn 'Abbas, nephew of the Prophet's ﷺ wife Maymunah, was still young when the Prophet ﷺ died. Under 'Umar he sat with the elders of Badr, and when 'Umar asked about Surah An-Nasr, only he saw that it announced the Prophet's ﷺ approaching death. A Muslim learns that understanding of the Qur'an is Allah's gift.

question: Which companion was sent by the Prophet ﷺ as governor and judge to Yemen, and died young in Syria?
explanation: Mu'adh ibn Jabal, a scholar among the companions, was sent to Yemen and later died in Syria while still young.
detail: The standard biographies record the instruction the Prophet ﷺ gave Mu'adh as he sent him to Yemen: he was going to a people of the Book, so he should call them first to the testimony of faith, then to the five daily prayers, then to the zakat taken from their rich and given to their poor; and he should beware of the prayer of the wronged, for no veil stands between it and Allah. A Muslim learns from this the order in which the religion is taught.

question: Which valley lies between the two hills of Safa and Marwa, walked during the pilgrimage?
answers: The valley of Makkah, around the Ka'bah
explanation: Safa and Marwa are two small hills in the valley of Makkah, today enclosed within the Sacred Mosque.
detail: The Qur'an names the two hills: "Indeed, as-Safa and al-Marwa are among the symbols of Allah; so whoever makes Hajj to the House or performs 'Umrah, there is no blame upon him for walking between them" (2:158). Ibrahim, peace be upon him, had settled Hajar and Isma'il there, "in a valley without cultivation, near Your sacred House" (14:37). Every standard account records Hajar running between the hills in search of water for her child until Zamzam sprang up. A Muslim who walks between them follows a mother's search.

question: Which two great Arab tribes of Madinah had been at war before the Prophet ﷺ arrived?
explanation: The Aws and the Khazraj, long enemies, together formed the Ansar after the Prophet ﷺ arrived.
detail: Every standard biography records that the Aws and the Khazraj had fought for years, and that their last great battle, the day of Bu'ath, came shortly before the Hijra and left both sides weakened. Men of the Khazraj met the Prophet ﷺ at the pilgrimage season, and the next year the two tribes pledged to him together at 'Aqabah. The Qur'an then reminded them: "when you were enemies and He brought your hearts together" (3:103). A Muslim learns that Islam turned the enemies of yesterday into one people, the Ansar.

question: Which verse reminds the Ansar that they had been enemies and that Allah joined their hearts?
answers: "You were enemies and He brought your hearts together"
explanation: "And remember the favour of Allah upon you: when you were enemies and He brought your hearts together, and you became brothers by His favour."
detail: The verse of Surah Al 'Imran opens with a command: "And hold firmly to the rope of Allah all together and do not become divided. And remember the favour of Allah upon you: when you were enemies and He brought your hearts together, and you became, by His favour, brothers; and you were on the edge of a pit of the Fire, and He saved you from it" (3:103). The next verse asks for a community calling to good (3:104). A Muslim learns that unity is a favour to guard.

question: How does the Quran praise the Ansar in their welcome of the emigrants?
answers: They prefer others over themselves, even in their own need
They housed them outside the city
explanation: "And they give preference over themselves, even though they are in privation. And whoever is protected from the stinginess of his soul — those are the successful."
detail: The verse belongs to Surah Al-Hashr, revealed after the expulsion of Banu an-Nadir: "And those who settled in the home and in faith before them love those who emigrated to them, and find in their breasts no need for what they were given, and give preference over themselves, even though they are in privation" (59:9). The verse before praises the poor emigrants (59:8), and the verse after those who come later and pray for both (59:10). A Muslim learns that giving what one needs oneself is the measure of generosity.

question: What is the body of the Prophet's ﷺ sayings, actions and approvals called?
explanation: The Sunnah is what the Prophet ﷺ said, did or approved; the Sira is the account of his life.
detail: The Qur'an sends the believers to the Prophet's ﷺ example in plain words: "There has certainly been for you in the Messenger of Allah an excellent example" (33:21), and: "Whatever the Messenger gives you, take; and what he forbids you, refrain from" (59:7). It joins obedience to him with obedience to Allah: "He who obeys the Messenger has obeyed Allah" (4:80). His companions watched how he prayed, fasted, ate and judged, and passed it on. A Muslim learns that the Qur'an is followed through the Prophet's ﷺ way.

question: What is the generation after that of the companions called?
explanation: The Tabi'un are those who met the companions without having seen the Prophet ﷺ.
detail: The name comes from the Qur'an, which ranks the generations in one verse: "And the first forerunners among the Muhajirun and the Ansar and those who followed them with good conduct, Allah is pleased with them and they are pleased with Him" (9:100). Those who followed, at-tabi'un, learned the Qur'an and the Sunnah from the companions themselves in Madinah, Makkah, Kufa, Basra and Damascus, and through them the companions' reports reached the hadith collections. A Muslim learns that the religion passed from the Prophet ﷺ onward, hand to hand.

question: What is the chain of narrators of a hadith called?
explanation: The isnad is the chain of transmission; the matn is the text of the hadith itself.
detail: The word isnad comes from sanad, a support: the chain is what the text leans on. A report in Sahih al-Bukhari or Sahih Muslim is written chain first, the collector naming his teacher, who names his, back to the companion who heard the Prophet ﷺ; only then comes the matn. The Qur'an demands the same care: "if there comes to you a disobedient one with information, investigate" (49:6). A Muslim learns that a saying reaches the Prophet ﷺ only through named witnesses.

question: Which two hadith collections are held to be the most rigorous, called "the two Sahihs"?
answers: The Sunan of Abu Dawud and at-Tirmidhi
The Sunan of an-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah
explanation: Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim are together called "the two Sahihs" (as-sahihan).
detail: Sahih means sound: each compiler, Muhammad ibn Isma'il al-Bukhari and his student Muslim ibn al-Hajjaj, gathered only reports whose chains he had examined and accepted. Both arranged their books by subject, from faith and purification through prayer, zakat, fasting and pilgrimage to the life of the Prophet ﷺ, each report written with its full chain of narrators. A hadith found in both is called muttafaq 'alayh, agreed upon, and holds the highest rank among reports. A Muslim learns where to look first to know what the Prophet ﷺ said.

question: In which city are the Prophet's ﷺ mosque and his grave?
explanation: The Prophet's ﷺ mosque and his grave are in Madinah, the city of the Hijra.
detail: Every standard biography records that the Prophet ﷺ let his camel choose where it knelt when he entered the city, and that his mosque was built there. He led the prayers in it for ten years and died in 'A'isha's room, where he was buried; Abu Bakr and 'Umar were later laid beside him. The Qur'an calls the city al-Madinah: "It was not for the people of Madinah to remain behind the Messenger of Allah" (9:120). A Muslim who visits prays in his mosque.

question: What epithet does Madinah carry, referring to the light attributed to it?
explanation: Madinah is called al-Munawwarah; Makkah for its part is called al-Mukarramah.
detail: The Qur'an calls the city simply al-Madinah, the city, as in "the hypocrites of Madinah" (9:101); the epithet al-Munawwarah, the illuminated, was added by the Muslims once it became the city of the Prophet ﷺ. Its older name appears once, in the mouths of those who wanted to desert at the Trench: "O people of Yathrib, there is no place for you here, so return" (33:13). Makkah's epithet al-Mukarramah means the honoured. A Muslim learns that both cities are named for what Allah placed there.

question: What name does the Quran give Makkah, "the mother of cities"?
explanation: "…that you may warn the mother of cities (Umm al-Qura) and those around it."
detail: The verse belongs to Surah Al-An'am, revealed in Makkah: "And this is a Book which We have sent down, blessed and confirming what was before it, that you may warn the mother of cities and those around it" (6:92). The same expression returns in Surah Ash-Shura (42:7). Makkah is the mother of cities because it holds the first house built for worship: "the first House established for mankind was that at Bakkah" (3:96). A Muslim learns that the warning began at the centre and spread outward.

question: What was the trade of the Prophet's ﷺ first wife, Khadija?
explanation: Khadija bint Khuwaylid was a respected merchant of Makkah, who entrusted her caravan to the young Muhammad ﷺ.
detail: Every standard biography records that Khadija bint Khuwaylid hired the young Muhammad ﷺ to take her goods to Syria, and that her servant Maysara returned with an account of his honesty; she then proposed marriage. When the first revelation came at Hira and he returned trembling, she wrapped him in a cloak and said that Allah would never disgrace him, because he kept the ties of kinship and gave to the poor. A Muslim learns that the first believer was a working woman.

question: For how long was the Prophet ﷺ married to Khadija alone?
answers: Until her death; he married no other woman in her lifetime
explanation: The Prophet ﷺ married no other woman while Khadija lived; the later marriages came after her death.
detail: The standard biographies record that all the Prophet's ﷺ children except Ibrahim were Khadija's: al-Qasim and 'Abdullah, who died as infants, and his daughters Zaynab, Ruqayyah, Umm Kulthum and Fatimah. She died in Makkah before the Hijra, in the same year as Abu Talib, a year the biographies call the year of sorrow. Years later 'A'isha said she was never as jealous of any wife as of Khadija, because the Prophet ﷺ spoke of her so often. A Muslim learns that he never forgot his first wife.

question: What is the name of the Prophet's ﷺ uncle who protected him without accepting Islam?
explanation: Abu Talib, the father of 'Ali, protected his nephew against Quraysh until his death.
detail: Every standard biography records that Abu Talib took his nephew in after 'Abd al-Muttalib died and refused when Quraysh demanded that he hand him over. At his deathbed the Prophet ﷺ urged him to say that there is no god but Allah, while Abu Jahl pressed him to keep the religion of 'Abd al-Muttalib, and he died without saying it; then came the verse: "you do not guide whom you like, but Allah guides whom He wills" (28:56). A Muslim learns that guidance is Allah's alone.

question: Which uncle of the Prophet ﷺ was taken prisoner at Badr before accepting Islam?
explanation: Al-'Abbas, the Prophet's ﷺ uncle and forefather of the Abbasids, was captured at Badr and later accepted Islam.
detail: The standard biographies record that al-'Abbas came to Badr on the side of Quraysh and was taken prisoner; to the captives the Qur'an said: "say to whoever is in your hands of the captives: If Allah knows any good in your hearts, He will give you better than what was taken from you" (8:70). At Hunayn he held the Prophet's ﷺ mule and called the scattered men back. A Muslim learns that the uncle once on the other side became a pillar at his side.

question: What are the companions who fought at the battle of Badr called?
explanation: The companions present at Badr are known as the Badriyyun, and that merit is particular to them.
detail: The Qur'an calls the battle "the day of the criterion, the day when the two armies met" (8:41). Every standard biography records that the Muslims there were a little over three hundred, facing an army about three times their number. The Qur'an speaks of the angels sent to them: "I will reinforce you with a thousand from the angels" (8:9). When Hatib ibn Abi Balta'a later erred, the Prophet ﷺ reminded 'Umar that he had been at Badr. A Muslim learns why Badr remained the highest honour.

question: What share of the spoils does the Quran set aside for Allah, the Messenger, the near of kin, the orphans, the poor and the traveller?
explanation: "Know that whatever you take as spoils, a fifth is for Allah and for the Messenger, and for the near relatives, the orphans, the needy and the traveller."
detail: The verse comes in Surah Al-Anfal, the surah of the spoils, revealed after Badr: "And know that anything you obtain of spoils, then indeed for Allah is one fifth of it and for the Messenger and for the near relatives and the orphans and the needy and the traveller, if you have believed in Allah and in what We sent down to Our servant on the day of the criterion" (8:41). A Muslim learns that even the gains of war carry a share for the weak.

question: Which verse, often cited with the farewell sermon, grounds the equality of peoples before Allah?
answers: "The most noble of you before Allah is the most righteous"
explanation: "O mankind, We created you from a male and a female… the most noble of you in the sight of Allah is the most righteous."
detail: The verse belongs to Surah Al-Hujurat: "O mankind, indeed We have created you from male and female and made you peoples and tribes that you may know one another. Indeed, the most noble of you in the sight of Allah is the most righteous of you" (49:13). In the farewell sermon the Prophet ﷺ said that no Arab has merit over a non-Arab except by righteousness. A Muslim learns that tribe and colour are for recognition, not rank.

question: How many took part in the second pledge of 'Aqabah, the decisive meeting with the people of Yathrib?
answers: A delegation of more than seventy people
explanation: The second pledge of 'Aqabah gathered a delegation of more than seventy men and women of Yathrib.
detail: Every standard biography records that the second pledge took place at night, in secret, at the pass of 'Aqabah near Mina during the pilgrimage season; the delegation slipped away from their sleeping companions to meet the Prophet ﷺ, who came with his uncle al-'Abbas. Two women were among them, Nusayba bint Ka'b and Asma' bint 'Amr. The people of Yathrib pledged to protect him as they protected their own women and children. A Muslim learns that Madinah opened its doors to Islam through a promise made in the dark.

question: How many naqibs (responsible chiefs) did the Prophet ﷺ have appointed among the people of Yathrib at the pledge of 'Aqabah?
explanation: Twelve naqibs were chosen to represent the groups of the Yathrib delegation and answer for their pledge.
detail: Every standard biography records that the Prophet ﷺ asked the delegation to bring forward twelve chiefs, nine from the Khazraj and three from the Aws, and told them they would be guarantors over their people as the disciples had been for 'Isa, son of Maryam, while he was the guarantor for his own people. The number recalls the Children of Israel: "and We appointed among them twelve leaders" (5:12). A Muslim learns that from its first night the community had men answerable for it.

question: What name did Madinah take after the Hijra?
answers: Madinat an-Nabi, the city of the Prophet ﷺ
explanation: Yathrib took the name Madinat an-Nabi, "the city of the Prophet ﷺ", shortened to al-Madinah.
detail: The Qur'an records both names. The old one appears once, in the mouths of those who wanted to abandon the Prophet ﷺ at the battle of the Trench: "O people of Yathrib, there is no place for you here, so return" (33:13). The new one appears wherever the Qur'an speaks of the believers' city, as in "the people of Madinah" (9:120). The Prophet ﷺ also called it Taybah, the good. A Muslim learns that the city was renamed by the man it sheltered.

question: Which caliph had official copies of the Quran made and sent to the provinces?
explanation: Abu Bakr had the text collected; 'Uthman had official copies made and sent to the main cities.
detail: Every standard biography records what moved 'Uthman: Hudhayfa ibn al-Yaman, returning from the campaigns in Armenia and Azerbaijan, had heard soldiers from Syria and Iraq dispute over their recitations, and asked the caliph to act before the community differed over its Book. 'Uthman sent for the sheets that Abu Bakr had collected and that Hafsa kept, had Zayd ibn Thabit and three men of Quraysh copy them, and sent a copy to each province. A Muslim learns that the single text recited everywhere goes back to those copies.

question: In which language was the Quran revealed to the Prophet ﷺ?
explanation: The Quran was revealed in clear Arabic, the language of the Prophet's ﷺ own people.
detail: The Qur'an speaks of its own language many times: "Indeed, We have sent it down as an Arabic Qur'an that you might understand" (12:2); the trustworthy Spirit brought it down "in a clear Arabic tongue" (26:195). It also gives the rule behind this: "And We did not send any messenger except in the language of his people" (14:4). Quraysh, masters of that language, were challenged to bring one surah like it (2:23). A Muslim recites the Qur'an in Arabic wherever he lives, and reads a translation to understand its meaning.

question: Which companion did the Prophet ﷺ send to Bahrain, returning with its tribute?
explanation: Abu 'Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah, called "the trustworthy one of this community", returned from Bahrain with its tribute.
detail: Every standard biography records what happened when the wealth from Bahrain arrived: the Ansar came in numbers to the fajr prayer, and the Prophet ﷺ smiled and said that he knew they had heard of Abu 'Ubayda's return. He said that it was not poverty he feared for them, but that the world would be spread out before them as it had been for those before, and would destroy them as it had destroyed those. A Muslim learns that the day of plenty is the day to guard the heart.

question: Which event marks the start of the Muslim calendar?
answers: The Hijra from Makkah to Madinah
explanation: The Hijri calendar begins with the year of the Hijra, a decision taken during the caliphate of 'Umar.
detail: Every standard biography records that 'Umar, faced with dated documents that named no year, consulted the companions on where the Muslim years should begin, and that they chose the year of the Hijra over the year of the Prophet's ﷺ birth or of the first revelation, because the Hijra founded the community. The year begins with Muharram, the first of the twelve months the Qur'an names: "the number of months with Allah is twelve" (9:36). A Muslim counts the years from the community's first home.

question: Which surah is named after the elephant?
explanation: Surah 105, Al-Fil ("The Elephant"), recalls Abraha's army of elephants, stopped before Makkah.
detail: The surah opens with a question: "Have you not seen how your Lord dealt with the companions of the elephant? Did He not make their plan go astray?" (105:1-2). The next verses tell how He sent birds in flocks that struck them with stones of baked clay, until they were like straw eaten away (105:3-5). Five verses record one army that came against the House and never reached it. A Muslim learns that no force, however large, can overturn what Allah has decided.

question: Surah An-Nahl is named after which insect?
explanation: An-Nahl means "the bees"; in it Allah inspires the bee to build its homes (16:68).
detail: The verse reads: "And your Lord inspired the bee: take for yourself homes among the mountains and the trees and in what they build" (16:68). The next verse tells the bee to eat of every fruit and follow the ways its Lord made easy, and names its honey a drink of varying colours "in which there is healing for people" (16:69). The bee follows a guidance it was given. A Muslim learns to see the work of a small creature as a sign pointing to its Creator.

question: Which surah is named after the ant?
explanation: An-Naml ("The Ants", surah 27) tells of the ant that warned its fellows as Sulayman's army approached.
detail: The Qur'an says: "Until, when they came upon the valley of the ants, an ant said: O ants, enter your dwellings, lest Sulayman and his soldiers crush you while they do not notice" (27:18). Sulayman smiled at her words and prayed: "My Lord, enable me to be grateful for Your favour which You have bestowed upon me and upon my parents" (27:19). A tiny creature caring for its own moved a king to thanks rather than pride. A Muslim learns that every blessing calls for gratitude.

question: In Surah Al-'Ankabut, what does the Qur'an compare those who take protectors besides Allah to?
answers: A spider building a flimsy house
explanation: "The frailest of houses is the spider's house" (29:41), which gives the surah its name.
