detail: The prayer is placed in a man's mouth at a set moment of life: when he reaches full strength and forty years, the verse says, he says it (46:15), and it ends with words the explanation leaves out: "Indeed, I have repented to You, and indeed, I am of the Muslims". Before the prayer the verse recalls the mother who carried him with hardship and bore him with hardship, thirty months of pregnancy and weaning. The next verse answers: from such people the best of their deeds is accepted and their misdeeds overlooked (46:16). A Muslim learns a prayer that binds three generations: parents, himself, and his children.

question: What do "the servants of the Most Merciful" ask concerning their families?
answers: That they be a comfort to the eyes, and that they be an example for the righteous
explanation: "Our Lord, grant us from among our wives and offspring comfort to our eyes, and make us an example for the righteous."
detail: This prayer is the last trait in the portrait of "the servants of the Most Merciful" in Surah Al-Furqan, and the next verse gives their reward: "Those will be awarded the highest chamber for what they patiently endured, and they will be received there with greeting and peace" (25:75). Just before the prayer, the servants are described as those who, when reminded of their Lord's verses, do not fall over them deaf and blind (25:73); their asking for good families follows their own attentiveness to revelation (25:74). A Muslim learns to pray for his household and to want it to be righteous, not merely happy.

question: How do "the servants of the Most Merciful" behave in the face of frivolity?
explanation: "And those who do not testify to falsehood, and when they pass near ill speech, they pass by with dignity."
detail: The verse follows the gravest sins the servants of the Most Merciful avoid, associating another god with Allah, killing unjustly and unlawful intercourse (25:68), and the promise that for those who repent, believe and do good, Allah replaces their evil deeds with good ones (25:70). Then two smaller things are named: they do not bear false witness, and when they pass by what is idle, they pass on with dignity (25:72). A Muslim learns to walk past what does not deserve his attention without contempt and without joining in.

question: What does the Quran command in a gathering when room is asked for?
answers: Make room: Allah will make room for you
explanation: "O you who have believed, when you are told: 'Make room in the assemblies', then make room; Allah will make room for you."
detail: The verse goes on to a second courtesy and a promise: "And when you are told to rise, then rise; Allah will raise those who have believed among you and those who were given knowledge by degrees. And Allah is Acquainted with what you do" (58:11). The verses before it deal with private talk in a gathering, telling the believers not to confer in secret about sin and enmity but about righteousness and taqwa (58:9). Making room is answered by Allah making room, and standing when asked by Allah raising in rank. A Muslim learns that small courtesies in a gathering are noticed by Allah and rewarded in kind.

question: With whom does the Quran command one to be, in Surah At-Tawbah?
explanation: "O you who have believed, fear Allah and be with those who are true."
detail: The command comes at the end of an account of forgiveness in Surah At-Tawbah: Allah turned in mercy to the Prophet ﷺ and to those who followed him in the hour of hardship (9:117), and to three men who had been left behind, until the earth, for all its breadth, closed in on them and they knew there was no refuge from Allah except in Him (9:118). The next verse then tells the believers to fear Allah and be with the truthful (9:119). A Muslim learns to choose his company by honesty, and to be counted among those who tell the truth.

question: With whom does the Quran command the Prophet ﷺ to keep patient company, in Al-Kahf?
answers: Those who call upon their Lord morning and evening, seeking His face
explanation: "And keep yourself patient with those who call upon their Lord in the morning and the evening, seeking His face; and let not your eyes pass beyond them."
detail: The verse continues with what the Prophet ﷺ is not to do: let his eyes pass beyond these people "desiring the adornment of the worldly life", or obey one "whose heart We have made heedless of Our remembrance, who follows his desire and whose affair is ever in neglect" (18:28). The verse after leaves each person his choice: "The truth is from your Lord, so whoever wills, let him believe, and whoever wills, let him disbelieve" (18:29). A Muslim learns to seek out those who remember Allah and to stay with them, whatever their rank.

question: On what does the Quran command mutual help, and on what does it forbid it?
answers: Cooperate in righteousness and piety, not in sin and aggression
explanation: "And cooperate in righteousness and piety, but do not cooperate in sin and aggression."
detail: The command comes at the end of the second verse of Surah Al-Ma'idah, just after the believers are told not to let hatred of a people who once barred them from the Sacred Mosque push them into transgression, and just before its closing warning: "And fear Allah; indeed, Allah is severe in penalty" (5:2). The verse opens with respect for the rites of Allah and for the pilgrims heading to the Sacred House, so cooperation is asked of people who have just been reminded of an old grievance. A Muslim learns to ask, before joining any effort, whether it is righteousness or wrong that he is helping to build.

question: What does the Quran command about a covenant made and oaths confirmed?
answers: To fulfil the covenant and not break oaths after confirming them
explanation: "And fulfil the covenant of Allah when you have taken it, and do not break oaths after their confirmation."
detail: The verse gives the reason its oaths bind: "while you have made Allah a witness over you. Indeed, Allah knows what you do" (16:91). It follows the verse in which Allah commands justice, good conduct and giving to relatives, and forbids immorality, wrong and oppression (16:90), and it is followed by a picture of the oath-breaker: a woman who unravels her yarn after it was firmly spun, using oaths as a means of deceit between people (16:92). A Muslim learns that a promise sworn with Allah's name is kept because Allah was called to witness it.

question: According to a hadith reported by al-Bukhari, when is a man's faith complete?
answers: When he loves for his brother what he loves for himself
When he fasts the whole year
When he gives away all his wealth
explanation: "None of you truly believes until he loves for his brother what he loves for himself."
detail: The hadith is narrated by Anas ibn Malik and recorded in Sahih al-Bukhari 13, in the Book of Faith, under a chapter heading which states that loving for one's brother what one loves for oneself is part of faith. The wording is a denial: faith is not complete without this. The Qur'an gives the ground of that brotherhood, "the believers are but brothers" (49:10), and praises the Ansar who gave preference to others over themselves even when in need (59:9). A Muslim learns to test his faith by one question: does he want for others the good he wants for himself?

question: In which cases does the Quran see good in private conversation?
answers: Enjoining charity, a good deed, or reconciliation between people
explanation: "No good is there in much of their private conversation, except for one who enjoins charity or what is right or conciliation between people."
detail: The verse ends with a condition and a promise: "And whoever does that seeking the approval of Allah, We are going to give him a great reward" (4:114). It comes in a passage of Surah An-Nisa about people who hide from others but not from Allah, who is with them when they spend the night in talk He does not accept (4:108), and it turns their secret talk into a test: whispering is worthless except when it serves charity, kindness or peace between people. A Muslim learns to ask what a private conversation is for, and to make sure it is for people's good.

question: What is the name of the Prophet of Islam?
explanation: The Prophet of Islam is Muhammad ﷺ, son of 'Abdullah.
detail: The Qur'an itself gives the Prophet's ﷺ name: "Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah" (48:29), and again: "Muhammad is not the father of any of your men, but the Messenger of Allah and the seal of the prophets" (33:40). His name and lineage open every standard biography, and every Muslim says his name each day in the testimony of faith. A Muslim learns the name of the man who brought him the Qur'an, and honours it whenever it is spoken.

question: Isma'il and Ishaq are the sons of which prophet?
explanation: 'Praise be to Allah who granted me, despite old age, Isma'il and Ishaq' (14:39).
detail: These words close a long prayer Ibrahim makes near the end of Surah Ibrahim, after settling his family in a valley without crops beside the Sacred House (14:37). He says: "Praise be to Allah, who has granted me in old age Isma'il and Ishaq. Indeed, my Lord is the Hearer of supplication" (14:39), then asks that he and his descendants keep up the prayer (14:40). Both sons are named as gifts received late in life. A Muslim learns to thank Allah for children as a gift, not as something owed.

question: Which prophet did Allah raise up to Himself?
explanation: 'Rather, Allah raised him to Himself' (4:158).
detail: The verse answers a false claim recorded just before it. Surah An-Nisa' reports the boast of those who said they had killed the Messiah, 'Isa son of Maryam, and replies: "They did not kill him, nor did they crucify him, but it was made to appear so to them" (4:157). Then comes the truth: "Rather, Allah raised him to Himself. And Allah is ever Mighty and Wise" (4:158). A Muslim learns that 'Isa was not killed, that Allah protected His messenger, and that no scheme can defeat His plan.

question: Who is the mother of the prophet 'Isa?
explanation: Maryam, to whom a whole surah of the Qur'an is devoted.
detail: Surah Maryam tells her story: "And mention in the Book Maryam, when she withdrew from her family to a place toward the east" (19:16). Allah sent His Spirit to her in the form of a man; she sought refuge in the Most Merciful from him, and he said he was only a messenger of her Lord, come to give her a pure boy (19:17-19). When she asked how, he answered: "Your Lord says: it is easy for Me" (19:21). A Muslim learns that 'Isa was born by Allah's command alone.

question: Who is the first human being Allah created?
explanation: Adam is the first man, whom Allah taught all the names.
detail: Before Adam was created, Allah told the angels: "I am placing upon the earth a successor" (2:30). Then "He taught Adam the names, all of them" (2:31), showed the angels that this new creature knew what they did not, and commanded them to prostrate to him (2:34). The Qur'an later addresses all people as "children of Adam" (7:26), and reminds them that Allah "created you from one soul" (4:1). A Muslim learns that every human being on earth descends from this one first man, honoured with knowledge by his Creator.

question: For which prophet did the fire become coolness and peace?
explanation: "O fire, be coolness and peace upon Ibrahim."
detail: Surah Al-Anbiya tells how young Ibrahim broke his people's idols, left the largest one standing, and told them to ask it if it could speak (21:58-63). Their answer was fire: "Burn him and support your gods, if you are going to act" (21:68). Allah then commanded: "O fire, be coolness and peace upon Ibrahim" (21:69); they plotted against him, but Allah made them the losers (21:70). A Muslim learns that fire burns only by Allah's permission, and that He protects whoever stands for the truth.

question: Which prophet carried a staff that became a serpent?
explanation: Allah asked Musa: "And what is that in your right hand?"
detail: Allah asked Musa this in the sacred valley of Tuwa (20:12): "And what is that in your right hand, O Musa?" (20:17). Musa answered: "It is my staff; I lean on it, and I bring down leaves with it for my sheep" (20:18). Allah said, "Throw it down," and it became a snake moving swiftly; then He told him to take it without fear, and it returned to its former state (20:19-21). A Muslim learns that Allah can turn a shepherd's stick into a sign.

question: Which prophet dreamt of eleven stars prostrating?
explanation: "O my father, I saw eleven stars, the sun and the moon."
detail: Surah Yusuf opens with the boy telling his father: "O my father, indeed I saw eleven stars and the sun and the moon; I saw them prostrating to me" (12:4). Ya'qub told him not to tell his brothers, lest they plot against him (12:5). Long after, when his family bowed before him in Egypt, Yusuf said: "This is the explanation of my vision of before; my Lord has made it true" (12:100). A Muslim learns that what Allah shows may take long years and hard trials to come true.

question: Which bird brought news to the prophet Sulayman?
explanation: The hoopoe said: 'I bring you from Saba' sure news' (27:22).
detail: Sulayman had asked why the hoopoe was missing, threatening to punish it unless it brought a clear excuse (27:20-21). It came back with news: "I have learned something you have not learned, and I have come to you from Saba' with sure news" (27:22). It had found a woman ruling there, and her people prostrating to the sun instead of Allah (27:23-24). Sulayman sent it back with a letter to test its words (27:27-28). A Muslim learns that a report is checked before it is acted on.

question: Which prophet is the model of patience in trial?
explanation: Ayyub called upon his Lord and was found steadfast.
detail: The verse reads: "And remember Our servant Ayyub, when he called to his Lord: Satan has touched me with hardship and pain" (38:41). Allah answered at once: "Strike the ground with your foot; here is a cool spring to wash in and to drink" (38:42), and gave him back his family and as many again (38:43). Then the Qur'an says: "Indeed, We found him patient. An excellent servant" (38:44). A Muslim learns that patience does not mean silence before Allah: Ayyub endured, and he also asked.

question: What did Allah create Adam from?
explanation: 'He created him from dust, then said to him: Be!' (3:59).
detail: The verse compares two prophets: "Indeed, the likeness of 'Isa before Allah is as the likeness of Adam. He created him from dust, then said to him, Be, and he was" (3:59). The next verse adds: "The truth is from your Lord, so do not be among the doubters" (3:60). Elsewhere the Qur'an says of all people: "He created you from dust" (30:20). A Muslim learns that dust came alive by one word of Allah, so no one has reason for pride.

question: Which prophet did Allah speak to directly?
explanation: "And Allah spoke to Musa with direct speech."
detail: The verse reads: "And Allah spoke to Musa with direct speech" (4:164), at the end of a list of messengers, named and unnamed. Surah Ta-Ha records that speech in the sacred valley: "Indeed, I am your Lord, so take off your sandals; you are in the sacred valley of Tuwa; and I have chosen you, so listen to what is revealed" (20:12-13). Later Allah told him He had chosen him above the people with His words (7:144). A Muslim learns that Musa received a special honour among the messengers.

question: How many prophets come after Muhammad ﷺ?
answers: None: he is the last of the prophets
explanation: Muhammad ﷺ is the seal of the prophets: no prophet comes after him.
detail: The Qur'an states this article of faith in one verse: "Muhammad is not the father of any of your men, but the Messenger of Allah and the seal of the prophets" (33:40). A seal closes a letter. He was also sent to everyone: "Say: O mankind, indeed I am the Messenger of Allah to you all" (7:158). Every standard biography and every Muslim creed teaches this closing. A Muslim learns that the guidance he needs was completed with this last prophet, and that none will come after him.

question: Which prophet is called the intimate friend (khalil) of Allah?
explanation: Ibrahim is the father of the prophets and the intimate friend of the Most Merciful.
detail: The title is given in Surah An-Nisa': "And who is better in religion than one who submits his face to Allah, does good, and follows the way of Ibrahim? And Allah took Ibrahim as an intimate friend" (4:125). Surah Al-Baqarah then shows what Muslims say of him: "We believe in what was revealed to Ibrahim, Isma'il, Ishaq, Ya'qub and the Descendants" (2:136). Ibrahim heads that line of prophets. A Muslim learns that closeness to Allah comes from submitting to Him and doing good, as Ibrahim did.

question: Which prophet healed the blind from birth by Allah's leave?
explanation: "And you healed the blind from birth and the leper by My permission."
detail: The verse belongs to a speech Allah will make on the Day of Judgement: "O 'Isa, son of Maryam, remember My favour upon you and your mother, when I supported you with the Pure Spirit, and you spoke to people in the cradle and in maturity" (5:110). It goes on: he healed the blind from birth and the leper by Allah's permission, and brought forth the dead by His permission (5:110). A Muslim learns that 'Isa's miracles were real and were Allah's.

question: For which prophet did the mountains echo Allah's praise?
explanation: "O mountains, repeat Allah's praises with him."
detail: The verse reads: "And We certainly gave Dawud bounty from Us: O mountains, repeat praises with him, and the birds too. And We made iron soft for him" (34:10). The next verse tells him to make coats of mail from that iron and do good, for Allah sees what he does (34:11). Surah Sad adds that the mountains glorified with him in the evening and after sunrise (38:18). A Muslim learns that praising Allah joins a person to the whole creation, which praises Him too.

question: Which prophet explained the king of Egypt's dream?
explanation: Yusuf explained the seven fat cows and the seven lean ones (12:46-49).
detail: The king had seen seven fat cows eaten by seven lean ones, and seven green ears of grain with others dry (12:43). The man freed from prison remembered Yusuf and went to him: "Yusuf, O man of truth, explain to us" (12:46). Yusuf answered: seven years of steady planting, leaving the grain in its ears; then seven hard years; then a year of rain and plenty (12:47-49). A Muslim learns that knowledge from Allah is used to help people, even those who forgot him in prison.

question: Who is the father of the prophet Yusuf?
explanation: Yusuf is the son of Ya'qub, himself the son of Ishaq.
detail: The brothers' words open the trouble: "Yusuf and his brother are dearer to our father than we are, though we are a group" (12:8). Surah Yusuf names this father earlier, when he tells the boy that Allah will complete His favour "upon the family of Ya'qub, as He completed it upon your two forefathers before, Ibrahim and Ishaq" (12:6). When his sons brought Yusuf's shirt with false blood, he answered: "So beautiful patience" (12:18). A Muslim learns from this father that patience, not anger, answers a great loss.

question: What parted before Musa and his people?
answers: The sea, parted to save them from Pharaoh
explanation: "And when We parted the sea for you and saved you."
detail: Allah reminds the Children of Israel: "And when We parted the sea for you and saved you and drowned the people of Pharaoh while you were looking on" (2:50). Surah Ash-Shu'ara tells the moment itself: with Pharaoh's army behind them, Musa's companions cried that they were caught, and he answered, "No! Indeed, with me is my Lord; He will guide me" (26:61-62). Then he struck the sea with his staff, and it split (26:63). A Muslim learns that when every way seems closed, Allah can open one.

question: What is said after mentioning the Prophet's ﷺ name?
answers: "May Allah's blessings and peace be upon him"
explanation: One invokes blessings and peace upon him: salla-Llahu 'alayhi wa sallam.
detail: The practice comes from a verse of Surah Al-Ahzab: "Indeed, Allah and His angels send blessings upon the Prophet. O you who believe, send blessings upon him and greet him with peace" (33:56). So when a Muslim says salla-Llahu 'alayhi wa sallam, he is doing what this verse asks: joining Allah and His angels in honouring the Prophet ﷺ. Muslims also send blessings on him at the end of every prayer. A Muslim learns to answer the Prophet's ﷺ name with a prayer for him.

question: Which prophet called his people for a very long time before the flood?
explanation: "We sent Nuh to his people: warn your people."
detail: The surah named after him begins: "Indeed, We sent Nuh to his people: warn your people before a painful punishment comes to them" (71:1). Then he complained to his Lord: "My Lord, I called my people night and day, but my calling only made them run further away" (71:5-6); they put their fingers in their ears (71:7). Surah Al-'Ankabut gives the length: a thousand years less fifty (29:14). A Muslim learns that a caller to Allah keeps going, and leaves the result to Allah.

question: Sulayman is the son of which prophet?
explanation: 'And to Dawud We gave Sulayman — an excellent servant!' (38:30).
detail: Surah Sad names the father and the son in one line: "And to Dawud We gave Sulayman. What an excellent servant; indeed, he was ever turning back to Allah" (38:30). What is praised is not his throne but his character as a servant who kept returning to his Lord. Surah An-Naml says he inherited from Dawud and told the people: "We have been taught the speech of birds" (27:16). A Muslim learns that the best praise of a king is that he was a good servant of Allah.

question: Which prophet defeated Jalut (Goliath)?
explanation: 'And Dawud killed Jalut' (2:251).
detail: The verse closes the story of Talut's army: "So they defeated them by Allah's permission, and Dawud killed Jalut, and Allah gave him kingship and wisdom and taught him what He willed" (2:251). Just before, the few who stayed firm had said: "How many a small company has overcome a large company by Allah's permission; and Allah is with the patient" (2:249), and prayed for patience and victory (2:250). Dawud was one of that small company. A Muslim learns that victory comes from Allah to the patient, not from numbers.

question: How many prophets must a Muslim believe in?
answers: All of them, making no distinction
Only those named in the Qur'an
explanation: A Muslim believes in all of Allah's prophets, making no distinction between them.
detail: The Qur'an gives every believer these words: "The Messenger has believed in what was sent down to him from his Lord, and so have the believers. All of them believe in Allah, His angels, His books and His messengers: We make no distinction between any of His messengers" (2:285). It also says that not all of them are named: "messengers We have not told you about" (40:78). A Muslim learns to honour the prophets he knows by name and those he does not, as one family sent by one Lord.

question: Whom did Allah choose, according to the Qur'an?
answers: Adam, Nuh, the family of Ibrahim and the family of 'Imran
explanation: "Allah chose Adam and Nuh and the family of Ibrahim and the family of 'Imran."
detail: The verse reads: "Indeed, Allah chose Adam and Nuh and the family of Ibrahim and the family of 'Imran over the worlds, descendants one of another" (3:33-34). The next verse shows why the family of 'Imran is named: the wife of 'Imran prayed, "My Lord, I have dedicated to You what is in my womb" (3:35), and the child was Maryam, mother of 'Isa (3:36). A Muslim learns that the prophets come from one chosen line.

question: In which land did the prophet Yusuf become trusted by the king?
explanation: Yusuf was established in Egypt after interpreting the king's dream.
detail: The name of the land is spoken by Yusuf himself when his family arrives: "Enter Egypt, if Allah wills, safe and secure" (12:99). He had asked the king, "Appoint me over the storehouses of the land; I am a knowing guardian" (12:55), and the Qur'an says: "Thus We established Yusuf in the land" (12:56). At the reunion he raised his parents on the throne and thanked Allah for taking him out of prison (12:100). A Muslim learns that the boy thrown into a well was raised by Allah to honour.

question: Which prophet was taken by night to the Al-Aqsa Mosque?
explanation: "Exalted is He who took His servant by night."
detail: Surah Al-Isra opens with this journey: "Exalted is He who took His servant by night from the Sacred Mosque to the Farthest Mosque, whose surroundings We have blessed, to show him of Our signs" (17:1). The Farthest Mosque is Al-Aqsa. At the moment of his greatest honour the Qur'an calls him simply "His servant". The next verse turns to Musa and his Book (17:2). A Muslim learns that Al-Aqsa is a blessed place tied to his Prophet ﷺ, and that the highest title is servant of Allah.

question: Which book was given to the prophet Musa?
explanation: Allah gave Musa the Book and followed him with messengers.
detail: The verse reads: "And We gave Musa the Book, and We sent messengers after him, following one another" (2:87). The Book is named elsewhere: "Indeed, We sent down the Torah, in which was guidance and light" (5:44), and Surah Al 'Imran says Allah "sent down the Torah and the Gospel before, as guidance for the people" (3:3-4). A Muslim learns that the Torah was a true revelation to Musa, and that believing in the earlier books is part of his faith.

question: Which book was given to the prophet 'Isa?
explanation: "And We gave him the Gospel, in which was guidance and light."
detail: The verse reads: "And We sent, following in their footsteps, 'Isa son of Maryam, confirming the Torah that came before him; and We gave him the Gospel, in which was guidance and light" (5:46). Two verses earlier the Torah is described with the same words (5:44), and two verses later the Qur'an is sent "confirming the Scripture that came before it" (5:48). Torah, Gospel and Qur'an are thus one chain from one Sender. A Muslim learns that 'Isa came with a true book from Allah.

question: Which book was given to the prophet Dawud?
explanation: "And We gave to Dawud the Zabur."
detail: The verse lists those Allah sent revelation to: "We revealed to Ibrahim, Isma'il, Ishaq, Ya'qub and the Descendants, and 'Isa, Ayyub, Yunus, Harun and Sulayman; and to Dawud We gave the Zabur" (4:163). Surah Al-Isra repeats the gift (17:55), and Surah Al-Anbiya quotes a line from it: "the earth will be inherited by My righteous servants" (21:105). A Muslim learns that Dawud was both a king and a prophet with a book named in the Qur'an.

question: Which prophet's son accepted to be sacrificed in obedience to Allah?
explanation: "O my father, do as you are commanded: you will find me patient."
detail: Ibrahim had prayed for a righteous child (37:100). Then: "When the boy was old enough to work with him, he said: O my son, I have seen in a dream that I sacrifice you. He said: O my father, do as you are commanded; you will find me, if Allah wills, among the patient" (37:102). When both had submitted, Allah called: "O Ibrahim, you have fulfilled the vision" (37:104-105), and ransomed the boy with a great sacrifice (37:107). A Muslim learns from the son to say "if Allah wills".

question: Where did Musa's mother place her baby to save him?
explanation: "Cast him into the river: We will return him to you."
detail: The verse reads: "And We inspired the mother of Musa: nurse him, and when you fear for him, cast him into the river, and do not fear and do not grieve. Indeed, We will return him to you and make him one of the messengers" (28:7). Pharaoh's own family picked the baby up, and he refused every wet nurse until his sister led them to his mother, "so We returned him to his mother" (28:8-13). A Muslim learns that Allah keeps His promise, even through the house of an enemy.

question: What did Yunus say in the darkness, which every Muslim repeats?
answers: "There is no god but You, glory be to You, I was a wrongdoer"
explanation: The supplication of Yunus inside the fish.
detail: The Qur'an quotes the call itself: "And he called out in the darkness: There is no god but You; glory be to You; indeed, I have been of the wrongdoers" (21:87). The same verse says he had gone off in anger. The answer follows: "So We responded to him and saved him from the distress; and thus do We save the believers" (21:88). Surah As-Saffat tells that the fish swallowed Yunus (37:142). A Muslim learns that this same prayer is a door of rescue for every believer in distress.

question: Who is the father of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ?
explanation: He is Muhammad ﷺ, son of 'Abdullah, son of 'Abd al-Muttalib.
detail: His full name is Muhammad ibn 'Abdullah ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib ibn Hashim, of the tribe of Quraysh in Makkah; every standard biography opens with this line. All of them agree that 'Abdullah died before his son was born, so the Prophet ﷺ never knew his father. The Qur'an speaks to him of that childhood: "Did He not find you an orphan and give you shelter?" (93:6). His grandfather 'Abd al-Muttalib cared for him, then his uncle Abu Talib. A Muslim learns that Allah's last messenger began life as an orphan.

question: Who is the mother of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ?
explanation: Amina bint Wahb is the mother of the Prophet ﷺ.
detail: Amina bint Wahb was from Quraysh, the tribe of Makkah, and every standard biography records her as the mother of the Prophet ﷺ. All of them agree that she died while he was still a small boy, so he grew up with his grandfather 'Abd al-Muttalib and then his uncle Abu Talib. The Qur'an reminds him: "Did He not find you an orphan and give you shelter?" (93:6). A Muslim learns that Allah watched over His Prophet ﷺ from the cradle, and honours the mother who bore him.

question: What did 'Isa say while still in the cradle?
explanation: "Indeed, I am the servant of Allah: He has given me the Scripture."
detail: Maryam brought her baby to her people; she pointed to him, and they asked how they could speak to a baby in the cradle (19:27-29). Then he spoke: "Indeed, I am the servant of Allah. He has given me the Book and made me a prophet, and made me blessed wherever I am, and enjoined on me prayer and zakat, and to be good to my mother" (19:30-32). The Qur'an then says: "That is 'Isa, son of Maryam" (19:34). A Muslim learns that 'Isa's first words called him Allah's servant.

question: Which prophet was sent to the people of 'Ad?
explanation: "And to 'Ad, their brother Hud."
detail: The verse reads: "And to 'Ad We sent their brother Hud. He said: O my people, worship Allah; you have no god other than Him. Will you not then fear Him?" (7:65). The chiefs of his people called him a fool and a liar, and he answered that he was a messenger from the Lord of the worlds (7:66-67). They refused, so Allah saved Hud and those with him and destroyed the deniers (7:72). A Muslim learns that Hud brought the same call as every prophet: worship Allah alone.

question: Which prophet was sent to Thamud, with the she-camel?
explanation: "And to Thamud, their brother Salih: this is the she-camel of Allah."
detail: The verse reads: "And to Thamud We sent their brother Salih. He said: O my people, worship Allah; you have no god other than Him. A clear proof has come to you from your Lord: this is the she-camel of Allah, a sign for you. So leave her to eat in Allah's land and do not touch her with harm" (7:73). Yet they hamstrung the she-camel and defied their Lord's command, and an earthquake took them (7:77-78). A Muslim learns that harming what Allah protects brings ruin.

question: Which prophet is the brother of Musa, sent with him?
explanation: "And appoint for me a helper from my family: Harun, my brother."
detail: Musa had just been sent to Pharaoh and prayed: "My Lord, expand my breast for me, ease my task, and loosen the knot from my tongue" (20:25-27). Then he asked for a helper: "And appoint for me a helper from my family, Harun, my brother; strengthen me through him and let him share my task" (20:29-32). Allah answered: "You have been granted your request, O Musa" (20:36). A Muslim learns that asking Allah for help, and for a good companion in a hard task, is part of a prophet's way.

question: What title does the Qur'an give Muhammad ﷺ regarding the prophets?
explanation: "Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah and the seal of the prophets."
detail: The verse reads: "Muhammad is not the father of any of your men, but the Messenger of Allah and the seal of the prophets; and Allah has knowledge of all things" (33:40). It comes in a surah that had already said adopted sons are called by their real fathers' names (33:5). A seal closes a letter so that nothing more is added. A few verses later Allah calls him "an illuminating lamp" (33:46). A Muslim learns that prophethood was closed with Muhammad ﷺ, and that his message is the last.

question: What do the angels say to Maryam in the Qur'an?
answers: That Allah has chosen and purified her
That she will be a queen
explanation: "O Maryam, Allah has chosen you and purified you."
detail: The angels' words are: "O Maryam, indeed Allah has chosen you and purified you and chosen you above the women of the worlds. O Maryam, be devout to your Lord, prostrate, and bow with those who bow" (3:42-43). Earlier, whenever Zakariyya entered her prayer chamber he found provision with her, and she said, "It is from Allah" (3:37). Soon after, the angels bring her news of a son, the Messiah, 'Isa (3:45). A Muslim learns that Maryam was chosen for her devotion, and answered it with more worship.

question: How did Ayyub call upon his Lord in his trial?
answers: "Adversity has touched me, and You are the Most Merciful"
explanation: "Adversity has touched me, and You are the most merciful of the merciful."
detail: The verse reads: "And Ayyub, when he called to his Lord: Indeed, adversity has touched me, and You are the most merciful of the merciful" (21:83). He named his pain and Allah's mercy, nothing more. The reply came at once: "So We responded to him and removed what afflicted him, and We gave him his family and the like of them with them" (21:84). The next verse counts Isma'il, Idris and Dhul-Kifl with him among the patient (21:85). A Muslim learns to bring his hurt to Allah in humble words.

question: What did Allah teach Adam?
explanation: "And He taught Adam all the names."
detail: The verse reads: "And He taught Adam the names, all of them; then He showed them to the angels and said: Tell Me the names of these, if you are truthful" (2:31). The angels replied: "Glory be to You! We have no knowledge except what You have taught us" (2:32). Then Adam told them the names (2:33), and Allah commanded the angels to prostrate to Adam (2:34). A Muslim learns that knowledge is a gift from Allah, and that it raised the first man in honour.

question: Which prophet ruled a kingdom no one after him would have?
explanation: "Grant me a kingdom such as will not belong to anyone after me."
detail: The prayer reads: "My Lord, forgive me, and grant me a kingdom such as no one after me will have. Indeed, You are the Giver" (38:35). Notice that he asks for forgiveness first. Allah answered: "So We subjected to him the wind, blowing gently by his command wherever he wished" (38:36), and the devils, every builder and diver (38:37). Then He said: "This is Our gift, so give or withhold without account" (38:39). A Muslim learns that Sulayman's unmatched power came as a gift after a prayer for forgiveness.

question: Which prophet was saved with his family, except his wife?
explanation: "Set out with your family in a portion of the night… except your wife."
detail: The angels who came to Lut said: "O Lut, we are messengers of your Lord; they will never reach you. So leave with your family in a part of the night, and let none of you look back, except your wife; what strikes them will strike her" (11:81). At dawn Allah turned the town upside down and rained stones on it (11:82). Surah At-Tahrim explains her fate: she was under a righteous servant but betrayed him (66:10). A Muslim learns that each person answers for his own faith.

question: What did Ibrahim warn his people against?
explanation: "Do you take idols as deities?"
detail: The verse reads: "And when Ibrahim said to his father: Do you take idols as gods? Indeed, I see you and your people in clear error" (6:74). Afterwards he saw a star, then the moon, then the sun, and each time they set he said, "I do not love things that set" (6:76-78). Then he declared: "I have turned my face to Him who created the heavens and the earth" (6:79). A Muslim learns that only the Creator, who never sets, deserves worship.

question: Which word means one sent by Allah to mankind?
explanation: A rasul is one sent by Allah, entrusted with a message for mankind.
detail: The word rasul runs through the Qur'an. It is the title in the testimony of faith: "Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah" (48:29). The Qur'an says that no people was left without one: "And for every nation there is a messenger" (10:47). It also states the task: "Upon the Messenger is only clear delivery" (24:54); he carries the message faithfully from Allah. A Muslim learns to see every messenger, from Nuh to Muhammad ﷺ, as a trusted carrier of one message: worship Allah alone.

question: As what did Allah send the Prophet ﷺ, according to Surah Al-Ahzab?
answers: A witness, a bringer of good news and a warner
explanation: 'O Prophet, We have sent you as a witness, a bringer of good tidings and a warner' (33:45).
detail: The two verses read: "O Prophet, indeed We have sent you as a witness, a bringer of good news and a warner, and as one who calls to Allah by His permission, and an illuminating lamp" (33:45-46). The next verse gives the good news: "they will have from Allah great bounty" (33:47). Surah Al-Baqarah explains the witness: "so that the Messenger may be a witness over you" (2:143). A Muslim learns that his Prophet ﷺ brings hope, warns of danger and lights the way.

question: Why was Muhammad ﷺ sent, according to the Qur'an?
answers: As a mercy to the worlds
explanation: "And We have not sent you except as a mercy to the worlds."
detail: The verse comes near the end of Surah Al-Anbiya: "And We have not sent you except as a mercy to the worlds" (21:107). The next verse gives the heart of that mercy: "it is only revealed to me that your God is one God" (21:108). Surah At-Tawbah shows that mercy in him: "what you suffer is hard on him; to the believers he is kind and merciful" (9:128). A Muslim learns that the Prophet ﷺ was sent for all the worlds, and tries to carry his mercy to others.

question: Which prophet does the Qur'an call 'a most grateful servant'?
explanation: 'Indeed, he was a grateful servant' (17:3), said of Nuh.
detail: The verse reads: "O descendants of those We carried with Nuh; indeed, he was a grateful servant" (17:3). It addresses the Children of Israel, whose ancestors were saved on the Ark. Nuh's gratitude is shown in Surah Al-Mu'minun, where Allah tells him what to say once aboard: "Praise be to Allah, who saved us from the wrongdoing people" (23:28). After a lifetime of calling his people, he answered rescue with praise. A Muslim learns that thanks to Allah is the right answer to rescue.

question: What sign was Zakariyya given after the news of his son?
answers: Not to speak to people for three days
explanation: 'Your sign is that you will not speak to people for three days' (3:41).
detail: Zakariyya had prayed, "My Lord, grant me from Yourself a good offspring" (3:38), and the angels called to him with the news of Yahya (3:39). He asked how, and was told that Allah does what He wills (3:40). Then he asked for a sign: "Your sign is that you will not speak to people for three days except by gesture. And remember your Lord much, and exalt Him in the evening and the morning" (3:41). A Muslim learns that the first answer to an answered prayer is remembrance.

question: In which language was each messenger sent?
answers: In the language of his own people
explanation: "We did not send any messenger except in the language of his people."
detail: The verse reads: "And We did not send any messenger except in the language of his people, to make things clear for them. Then Allah sends astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills" (14:4). Surah Ibrahim opens with the Book sent down to bring people out of darkness into light (14:1), and the next verse sends Musa to his people with the same task (14:5). A Muslim learns that the Qur'an came in Arabic for the same reason: faith is meant to be understood.

question: Which surah tells one prophet's story from beginning to end?
explanation: "We relate to you the best of stories" — the story of Yusuf.
detail: The surah opens: "Indeed, We have sent it down as an Arabic Qur'an that you might understand. We relate to you the best of stories in what We have revealed to you of this Qur'an" (12:1-3). The story begins at once with Yusuf telling his father of eleven stars, the sun and the moon bowing to him (12:4), and runs to his reunion with his parents in Egypt (12:99-100). A Muslim reads the story of Yusuf as one long lesson in patience and trust in Allah.

question: How does the Qur'an describe Ibrahim in Surah Maryam?
answers: A man of truth, a prophet
explanation: "He was a man of truth, a prophet."
detail: Surah Maryam turns to Ibrahim with these words: "And mention in the Book Ibrahim. Indeed, he was a man of truth and a prophet" (19:41). The verses that follow show both qualities at once: he asks his father gently why he worships what cannot hear, see or help him (19:42), and when his father threatens to stone him, he answers, "Peace be upon you; I will ask forgiveness for you from my Lord" (19:47). A Muslim learns that truthfulness and gentleness belong together, even toward those who reject the truth.

question: Which queen came to see the prophet Sulaiman?
explanation: She submitted with Sulaiman to Allah, Lord of the worlds.
detail: The Qur'an does not name her; the hoopoe describes a woman ruling over Saba with a great throne, whose people bowed to the sun (27:23-24). Sulaiman sent her a letter that began in the name of Allah and asked her to come in submission (27:30-31); she came, and found her own throne brought before her (27:42). Then: "She said, 'My Lord, I have wronged myself, and I submit with Sulaiman to Allah, Lord of the worlds'" (27:44). A Muslim learns that turning to Allah begins with admitting one's own wrong.

question: Which prophet asked to see how Allah gives life back?
explanation: "My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead."
detail: The verse gives the exchange: "And when Ibrahim said, 'My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead.' He said, 'Have you not believed?' He said, 'Yes, but so that my heart may be at rest'" (2:260). Allah told him to take four birds, place a part of them on each hill, then call them, and they would come to him in haste. A Muslim learns that asking Allah to strengthen the heart is a prayer of faith, not of doubt.

question: Which prophet travelled to learn from a knowledgeable servant?
explanation: Musa journeyed until he met a servant of Allah to whom He had given knowledge.
detail: Musa set out with a promise: "I will not cease until I reach the junction of the two seas" (18:60). They forgot their fish at a rock, and turned back to find it (18:61-64). There they found "a servant from among Our servants to whom We had given mercy from Us and taught knowledge from Us" (18:65), and Musa asked to follow him and be taught (18:66). A Muslim learns that a prophet who spoke with Allah still travelled far and asked humbly to learn.

question: What does Surah Al-Ikhlas teach about Allah?
answers: That He is One, and none is equal to Him
explanation: "Say: He is Allah, One… and there is none comparable to Him."
detail: The four verses read: "Say: He is Allah, One. Allah, the Eternal Refuge. He neither begets nor is born, nor is there to Him any equivalent" (112:1-4). The surah opens with "Say", a command to the Prophet ﷺ to declare who Allah is. Each verse closes a door: no partner, no need, no parent, no child, no likeness, as the Qur'an says elsewhere, "There is nothing like unto Him" (42:11). A Muslim recites these verses in prayer and learns the plainest statement of who he worships.

question: What did the Meccans call the Prophet ﷺ before the revelation?
explanation: His uprightness was so well known that he was called al-Amin.
detail: Every standard biography records that, long before revelation, the people of Makkah called him al-Amin, the trustworthy. When Quraysh rebuilt the Ka'bah and quarrelled over who would set the Black Stone in place, they agreed that the next man to enter would decide; it was he, and they said, "This is al-Amin." He laid the stone on a cloak, had a chief of each clan lift a corner, and set it in place himself. A Muslim learns that his honesty was known to his people before his message was.

question: Whom does the Qur'an present as the best example to follow?
explanation: "There has certainly been for you in the Messenger of Allah an excellent pattern."
detail: The verse reads: "There has certainly been for you in the Messenger of Allah an excellent pattern for anyone whose hope is in Allah and the Last Day and who remembers Allah often" (33:21). It stands in the account of the Battle of the Confederates, when armies besieged Madinah and hearts reached the throats (33:10). The believers in the trench said, "This is what Allah and His Messenger promised us" (33:22). A Muslim learns to follow him in patience under hardship as well as in ease.

question: In which city was the Prophet ﷺ born?
explanation: The Prophet ﷺ was born in Makkah, in the tribe of Quraysh.
detail: Every standard biography records that he was born in Makkah, in the clan of Banu Hashim of Quraysh. His father 'Abdullah had died before his birth, and the Qur'an recalls it: "Did He not find you an orphan and give you shelter?" (93:6). The Qur'an calls Makkah the Mother of Cities (6:92), swears by "this secure city" (95:3), and names it the place of the first House built for mankind (3:96). A Muslim learns that the last Prophet ﷺ was born beside the House that Ibrahim raised.

question: To which city did the Prophet ﷺ emigrate?
explanation: The Hijra went from Makkah to Madinah, then called Yathrib.
detail: Every standard biography records that the Prophet ﷺ left Makkah with Abu Bakr for Yathrib, where the tribes of Aws and Khazraj had pledged to protect him. The Qur'an recalls the journey: "If you do not aid him, Allah has already aided him, when those who disbelieved drove him out, the second of two, when they were in the cave" (9:40). A Muslim learns that Madinah became the home of Islam because a people opened their doors to a persecuted messenger.

question: What is the move from Makkah to Madinah called?
explanation: The Hijra marks the start of the Muslim calendar.
detail: The word hijra means leaving home; every standard biography uses it for the departure of the Prophet ﷺ from Makkah to Madinah, and in the caliphate of 'Umar the years of the Muslim calendar were counted from that event. The Qur'an speaks of it as done for Allah: "And whoever emigrates for the cause of Allah will find on the earth many locations and abundance" (4:100). A Muslim learns that the calendar begins not with a birth or a victory but with a sacrifice made for faith.

question: Who is the first wife of the Prophet ﷺ?
explanation: Khadija bint Khuwaylid, the first to believe in him.
detail: Every standard biography records that Khadija bint Khuwaylid, a merchant of Quraysh, proposed marriage to him after seeing his honesty in trade. When he came down from the cave of Hira shaken by the first revelation, she wrapped him in a cloak and told him that Allah would never disgrace him, because he kept ties with his family and helped the poor. She stood by him until her death in Makkah. A Muslim learns that the first to accept Islam was a wife who knew her husband's character.

question: In which cave did the Prophet ﷺ hide during the Hijra?
explanation: He hid there three days with Abu Bakr before travelling on to Medina.
detail: Every standard biography records that Thawr is a mountain south of Makkah, in the opposite direction from Madinah, chosen so that the searchers would look the wrong way. The Qur'an tells what was said inside: "when he said to his companion, 'Do not grieve; indeed, Allah is with us.' And Allah sent down His tranquillity upon him and supported him with soldiers you did not see" (9:40). A Muslim learns that careful planning and complete trust in Allah went together in the Prophet's ﷺ own journey.

question: What is the first word revealed to the Prophet ﷺ?
explanation: "Read, in the name of your Lord who created."
detail: The first verses read: "Read in the name of your Lord who created, created man from a clinging clot. Read, and your Lord is the Most Generous, who taught by the pen, taught man what he did not know" (96:1-5). The sira records that they came in the cave of Hira outside Makkah, when the angel Jibril appeared and told him to read; he answered that he was not a reader, and the angel repeated the command. A Muslim learns that Islam began with a call to knowledge.

question: Which angel brought the revelation to the Prophet ﷺ?
explanation: Jibril is the angel charged with bringing down the revelation.
detail: The Qur'an names him: "Say, whoever is an enemy to Jibril, it is he who has brought it down upon your heart by permission of Allah" (2:97), and calls him "the Trustworthy Spirit" who brought the Qur'an down upon the heart of the Prophet ﷺ (26:193-194). Every standard biography records that he first came to the Prophet ﷺ in the cave of Hira. A Muslim learns that the Qur'an reached the Prophet ﷺ through an angel Allah Himself calls trustworthy.

question: In which city is the grave of the Prophet ﷺ?
explanation: His grave is in Madinah, beside his mosque.
detail: Every standard biography records that the Prophet ﷺ died in Madinah, in the room of his wife 'Aisha beside his mosque, and was buried there. Abu Bakr and 'Umar were later buried next to him, and the mosque was extended until it enclosed the room. On the day he died, Abu Bakr recited: "Muhammad is not but a messenger; messengers have passed on before him" (3:144). A Muslim who visits Madinah greets him at his grave with peace, and learns that even the best of creation returned to Allah.

question: Which tribe did the Prophet ﷺ come from?
explanation: The Prophet ﷺ was of Quraysh, the tribe of Makkah.
detail: The Qur'an has a surah named after the tribe: "For the accustomed security of Quraysh, their security in the journey of winter and summer, let them worship the Lord of this House, who has fed them against hunger and made them safe from fear" (106:1-4). Quraysh lived around the Ka'bah, kept the House and traded by two yearly caravans. Every standard biography records that the Prophet ﷺ belonged to its clan of Banu Hashim. A Muslim learns that the message was addressed first to the Prophet's ﷺ own people.

question: What are the Prophet's ﷺ companions called?
explanation: The Sahaba are those who saw the Prophet ﷺ while believing in him.
detail: The word sahabi comes from sahib, companion, the very word the Qur'an uses for Abu Bakr in the cave: "when he said to his companion, 'Do not grieve'" (9:40). The Qur'an describes them together: "Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, and those with him are firm against the disbelievers, merciful among themselves; you see them bowing and prostrating" (48:29). A Muslim says "may Allah be pleased with him" after a companion's name, and learns the religion through what they passed on.

question: Who accompanied the Prophet ﷺ on the Hijra?
explanation: Abu Bakr was his companion in the cave during the Hijra.
detail: Every standard biography records that Abu Bakr had kept two camels ready, and that the Prophet ﷺ came to his house to tell him the time had come. His daughter Asma brought food to the cave, and his son 'Abdullah brought news from Makkah. The Qur'an calls him his companion: "when they were in the cave, when he said to his companion, 'Do not grieve; indeed, Allah is with us'" (9:40). A Muslim learns that Abu Bakr's place at the Prophet's ﷺ side is written in the Qur'an itself.

question: Who was the Prophet's ﷺ caller to prayer?
explanation: Bilal ibn Rabah called the prayer in Madinah.
detail: Every standard biography records that Bilal ibn Rabah was an enslaved man in Makkah, tortured by his master for believing, and that he kept repeating "Ahad, Ahad", until Abu Bakr bought him and set him free. In Madinah the Prophet ﷺ chose Bilal to call the adhan, and on the day Makkah was opened Bilal called the adhan from the roof of the Ka'bah. A Muslim learns that the voice that called the first believers to prayer belonged to a man once bought and sold.

question: What is the first battle of Islam called?
explanation: Badr is the first great battle, in the second year of the Hijra.
detail: The Qur'an names the place: "And already had Allah given you victory at Badr while you were few in number" (3:123). Surah Al-Anfal tells how the believers called on their Lord and He answered, "I will reinforce you with a thousand of the angels, following one another" (8:9). Every standard biography records that the Muslims went out to meet a caravan and found an army from Makkah instead. A Muslim learns that victory at Badr came from Allah, not from numbers.

question: What are those who emigrated from Makkah to Madinah called?
explanation: The Muhajirun are the emigrants; the Ansar are those who received them.
detail: The Qur'an uses the name itself: "The first forerunners among the Muhajirun and the Ansar: Allah is pleased with them and they are pleased with Him" (9:100). Surah Al-Hashr describes what they gave up: "the poor emigrants who were expelled from their homes and their properties, seeking bounty from Allah and His approval" (59:8). They left houses, trade and family with nothing but their faith. A Muslim learns that leaving what is dear for the sake of Allah earned them a name the Qur'an records with praise.

question: What are the people of Madinah who received the emigrants called?
explanation: The Ansar, "the helpers", are the Aws and the Khazraj of Madinah.
detail: The name means "the helpers", and the Qur'an describes them next: "And those who were settled in the home and in faith before them love those who emigrated to them, and give preference over themselves even though they are in want" (59:9). Every standard biography records that the Prophet ﷺ paired each emigrant with a brother from the Ansar, who shared his house and his livelihood. A Muslim learns that receiving a stranger as a brother is one of the acts the Qur'an praises most warmly.

question: What did the Prophet ﷺ build first in Madinah?
explanation: He built his mosque as soon as he arrived in Madinah.
detail: Every standard biography records that when the Prophet ﷺ entered Madinah, his camel knelt on an open plot, and he bought the land. He built the mosque there with walls of mud brick, pillars of palm trunks and a roof of palm branches, carrying the bricks with his own hands. The Qur'an says of such houses that Allah has ordered them to be raised and His name remembered in them (24:36). A Muslim learns that the first foundation of the new community was a place to pray together.

question: Which daughter of the Prophet ﷺ married 'Ali?
explanation: Fatima, the Prophet's ﷺ daughter, married 'Ali ibn Abi Talib.
detail: Every standard biography records that Fatima was the daughter of the Prophet ﷺ and Khadija, that she married 'Ali ibn Abi Talib in Madinah, and that their sons al-Hasan and al-Husayn were his grandsons. The Prophet ﷺ said that Fatima was a part of him, and that whoever angered her angered him. She outlived her father by only a few months. A Muslim learns that the household of the Prophet ﷺ is honoured, and that Fatima and 'Ali are the parents of his line.

question: Who was the first caliph after the Prophet ﷺ?
explanation: Abu Bakr as-Siddiq was the first caliph.
detail: Every standard biography records that during his last illness the Prophet ﷺ told Abu Bakr to lead the Muslims in prayer, and that on the day of his death Abu Bakr steadied the companions by reciting: "Muhammad is not but a messenger; messengers have passed on before him" (3:144). The Muslims then gave him their pledge as khalifa, a word meaning the one who comes after. A Muslim learns that the first leader after the Prophet ﷺ was the companion who had stood beside him in the cave (9:40).

question: What was Madinah called before?
explanation: Yathrib took the name Madinat an-Nabi, the city of the Prophet ﷺ.
detail: The Qur'an uses both names. During the siege of the Trench, the hypocrites cried, "O people of Yathrib, there is no place for you here, so go back" (33:13); elsewhere it speaks of "the people of Madinah and the bedouins around them" (9:120). Every standard biography records that once the Prophet ﷺ settled in Yathrib, the town took the name Madinat an-Nabi, the City of the Prophet, and then simply al-Madinah, the City. A Muslim learns that a town was renamed for the man it sheltered.

question: How old was the Prophet ﷺ at the first revelation?
explanation: Revelation came to him when he was forty years old.
detail: Every standard biography records that the Prophet ﷺ was forty years old when the angel Jibril came to him in the cave of Hira. Before that he had spent years in Makkah trading honestly and going out to the cave alone to worship. The Qur'an names forty as the age of full strength, when a person says, "My Lord, enable me to be grateful for Your favour" (46:15). A Muslim learns that a whole life of good character came before the first word of revelation.

question: In which city is the Ka'bah?
explanation: The Ka'bah stands at the centre of the Sacred Mosque, in Makkah.
detail: The Qur'an says: "Indeed, the first House established for mankind was that at Bakkah, blessed and a guidance for the worlds" (3:96), Bakkah being another name of Makkah. It tells how Ibrahim and Isma'il raised its foundations, praying, "Our Lord, accept this from us" (2:127), and it calls the Ka'bah "the Sacred House, a standing for the people" (5:97). A Muslim learns that the building at the heart of Makkah is the oldest house of worship, raised by a prophet and his son.

question: In which city is the Al-Aqsa Mosque?
explanation: The Al-Aqsa Mosque is in Jerusalem (al-Quds).
detail: The Qur'an names it in the first verse of Surah Al-Isra: "Exalted is He who took His Servant by night from the Sacred Mosque to the Farthest Mosque, whose surroundings We have blessed" (17:1). The Farthest Mosque is al-Masjid al-Aqsa in Jerusalem, reached by the Prophet ﷺ on the Night Journey. Every standard biography records that in Madinah the Muslims prayed toward Jerusalem until the Qur'an turned them toward the Ka'bah (2:144). A Muslim learns that a distant city is bound to his prayer and to his Prophet's ﷺ story.

question: Which uncle of the Prophet ﷺ protected him in Makkah?
explanation: Abu Talib, the father of 'Ali, protected his nephew against Quraysh.
detail: Every standard biography records that Abu Talib, brother of the Prophet's ﷺ father 'Abdullah, took the orphan boy into his home after the death of their father 'Abd al-Muttalib. When the message came, Abu Talib refused the demand of Quraysh to hand over his nephew, and when Quraysh boycotted Banu Hashim, he went with his clan into the mountain pass and shared their hunger. He died in the same year as Khadija. A Muslim learns that Allah placed protection for His Messenger in the loyalty of an uncle.

question: What was the trade of Khadija, the Prophet's ﷺ first wife?
explanation: Khadija was a respected merchant of Makkah.
detail: Every standard biography records that Khadija bint Khuwaylid owned goods that she sent out for trade with the caravans of Quraysh. Hearing of the young man's honesty, she employed Muhammad ﷺ to take her goods to Syria with her servant Maysara, who returned with a good profit and with praise for the way he had dealt. That honesty in business led her to propose marriage, and her wealth later supported him through the first years of the message. A Muslim learns that fair trade is part of good character.

question: What is the Prophet's ﷺ last pilgrimage called?
explanation: The Farewell Pilgrimage took place in the year 10 of the Hijra.
detail: Every standard biography records that in the tenth year after the Hijra the Prophet ﷺ led the pilgrimage himself and preached to the pilgrims at 'Arafah. He told them he did not know whether he would meet them there after that year, and asked whether he had conveyed the message, and they said yes. On that pilgrimage came the verse: "This day I have perfected for you your religion" (5:3). A Muslim learns that the last sermon of the Prophet ﷺ was his farewell, and that his message was complete.

question: What is the account of the Prophet's ﷺ life called?
explanation: The Sira is the account of his life; the Sunnah is what he said and did.
detail: The word sira means a way of going, and so a person's course through life; every standard biography of the Prophet ﷺ is called by this name. The Qur'an holds parts of the story: his orphanhood, "Did He not find you an orphan and give you shelter?" (93:6); the cave of the Hijra (9:40); the opening of Makkah (110:1-2). The Sira arranges these into one life from birth to death. A Muslim reads it to know the man he is told to take as his pattern (33:21).

question: What is a saying reported from the Prophet ﷺ called?
explanation: A hadith is a saying, act or approval of the Prophet ﷺ.
detail: The word hadith means a report; each hadith gives first the chain of those who passed it on, then the text itself. In Sahih al-Bukhari 8, for example, Ibn 'Umar reports that the Prophet ﷺ said Islam is built on five. The hadith matters because the Qur'an commands: "Whatever the Messenger gives you, take it; and whatever he forbids you, refrain from it" (59:7). A Muslim learns that the Qur'an and the hadith are read together, one as the Book and the other as its living example.

question: Which two hadith collections are held the most rigorous?
explanation: Together they are called "the two Sahihs".
detail: Every standard account records that Imam al-Bukhari and his younger contemporary Imam Muslim, both in the third century after the Hijra, each gathered only reports whose chain of narrators was unbroken and whose every narrator was known to be trustworthy. The word sahih means sound. A hadith found in both books is called "agreed upon"; the hadith that Islam is built on five, Sahih al-Bukhari 8, is one of them. A Muslim learns that careful checking of who said what is a duty the community took seriously.

question: Which caliph had the Qur'an copied and sent to the provinces?
explanation: 'Uthman had official copies made and sent to the main cities.
detail: Every standard account records that the Qur'an was first gathered onto sheets in the caliphate of Abu Bakr, by Zayd ibn Thabit, and that those sheets were kept by Hafsa. In the caliphate of 'Uthman, Hudhayfa warned that Muslims in the provinces were disputing over how to recite. 'Uthman borrowed Hafsa's sheets, had Zayd copy them, and sent a copy to each main city. A Muslim learns that the text he reads today is the one 'Uthman sent out, and that Allah promised to guard it (15:9).

question: How many caliphs are "the rightly guided caliphs"?
explanation: Abu Bakr, 'Umar, 'Uthman and 'Ali.
detail: Every standard account names them in the order they ruled: Abu Bakr, then 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, then 'Uthman ibn 'Affan, then 'Ali ibn Abi Talib. All four were among the earliest Muslims, and all four were tied to him by marriage: Abu Bakr and 'Umar were the fathers of his wives 'Aisha and Hafsa, while 'Uthman and 'Ali married his daughters. They are called rashidun, rightly guided, because they governed by his example. A Muslim learns their four names as the leaders who kept the community together after him.

question: Which direction do Muslims pray toward?
explanation: The qibla is the direction of the Ka'bah.
detail: The Qur'an records the moment the direction was fixed: "We have certainly seen the turning of your face toward the heaven, and We will surely turn you to a qibla with which you will be pleased. And wherever you are, turn your faces toward it" (2:144). Every standard biography records that in Madinah the Muslims had prayed toward Jerusalem until this verse came. A Muslim learns that turning toward the Ka'bah is obedience to this verse and a sign of one community.

question: What is that direction of prayer called?
explanation: The qibla is the direction; the mihrab is the niche that marks it.
detail: The Qur'an uses the word itself in the verses about the change of direction: "The foolish among the people will say, 'What has turned them away from their qibla, which they used to face?'" (2:142). The next verse explains that the first qibla was a test to show who would follow the Messenger ﷺ (2:143). The word comes from a root meaning to face or turn toward. A Muslim learns that the qibla is not a holy direction in itself but the direction Allah chose.

question: What is the place where Muslims pray together called?
explanation: The masjid is the place of prostration, the mosque.
detail: The word masjid comes from sajada, to prostrate, so a mosque is a place of prostration. The Qur'an says: "The mosques are for Allah, so do not invoke with Allah anyone" (72:18), and that they are maintained by those who believe in Allah and the Last Day, establish prayer and give zakat (9:18). Every standard biography records that the first thing the Prophet ﷺ built in Madinah was his mosque. A Muslim learns that a mosque is defined by what happens in it: prostration to Allah alone.

question: What is the call to prayer called?
explanation: The adhan is the call; the one who gives it is the muezzin.
detail: Every standard biography records that in Madinah the Prophet ﷺ established the adhan, and Bilal became the first to call it. Its words are heard five times a day: Allah is greatest; I bear witness that there is no god but Allah; I bear witness that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah; come to prayer; come to success; Allah is greatest; there is no god but Allah. A Muslim learns to answer the adhan by repeating its words and then going to pray.

question: On which day do Muslims gather for the great prayer?
explanation: The Friday prayer (al-jumu'ah) gathers the community every week.
detail: The Qur'an commands it: "O you who have believed, when the call is made for prayer on the day of Jumu'ah, then proceed to the remembrance of Allah and leave trade" (62:9). The name jumu'ah means gathering, and the surah is named after it. In every Muslim town the Friday prayer replaces the midday prayer, with a sermon before it. A Muslim learns that once a week the shops close, the community stands in rows together, and then goes back to work.

question: What is the person who leads the prayer called?
explanation: The imam is the one the congregation lines up behind to pray.
detail: The word imam means the one in front, whom others follow; the Qur'an gives it to Ibrahim, "Indeed, I will make you a leader for the people" (2:124). In the prayer the imam stands ahead of the rows, and the congregation bows and prostrates when he does. Every standard biography records that the Prophet ﷺ led the prayers, and that in his final illness he ordered Abu Bakr to lead in his place. A Muslim learns that praying behind an imam is following one voice together.

question: What is someone who has memorised the whole Qur'an called?
explanation: A hafiz is one who keeps the whole Qur'an in memory.
detail: The word hafiz means one who keeps and guards; the Qur'an uses the same root when Allah says of the Book: "Indeed, it is We who sent down the Qur'an, and indeed, We will be its guardian" (15:9). Every standard biography records that the companions learned the verses by heart as they came down, and that the Prophet ﷺ reviewed the whole Qur'an with Jibril every Ramadan. A Muslim learns that memorising the Qur'an is one of the ways Allah keeps His promise to guard it.

question: Which companion is known as the greatest narrator of hadith?
explanation: Abu Hurayra spent the Prophet's ﷺ last years at his side.
detail: Every standard account records that Abu Hurayra came to Madinah, embraced Islam and attached himself to the Prophet ﷺ, following him constantly to hear what he said. He himself explained that while the Muhajirun were busy in the markets and the Ansar with their land, he stayed close and remembered. He was called father of the kitten after a small cat he kept. A Muslim learns that a great part of what the community knows of the Prophet's ﷺ words came through one attentive listener.

question: Which caliph is called as-Siddiq, "the truthful"?
explanation: Abu Bakr as-Siddiq, the first free man to believe.
detail: Every standard biography records that Abu Bakr believed the moment the Prophet ﷺ told him of the message, and that when Quraysh mocked the Night Journey to Jerusalem, he answered that if the Prophet ﷺ had said it, it was true; from then he was called as-Siddiq. The word means one who affirms the truth without hesitation, and the Qur'an gives it to Ibrahim (19:41) and to Maryam (5:75). A Muslim learns that Abu Bakr's title was earned by believing at once what others took years to accept.

question: Which caliph is called al-Faruq?
explanation: 'Umar, who distinguished truth from falsehood, was given that title.
detail: Every standard biography records that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab had been a fierce opponent of Islam, and that his acceptance of the faith changed the position of the Muslims: after it they prayed openly at the Ka'bah. Al-Faruq means the one who separates, and 'Umar was known for a justice that drew a sharp line between right and wrong. He was chosen by Abu Bakr to succeed him and ruled as the second caliph. A Muslim learns that strength placed in the service of truth becomes justice.

question: Which caliph had the Qur'an gathered into a single volume?
explanation: Abu Bakr ordered what had been written down to be gathered together.
detail: Every standard account of the Qur'an's history, and the words of Zayd ibn Thabit recorded in Sahih al-Bukhari, tell that after many reciters were killed at Yamama, 'Umar urged Abu Bakr to gather the Qur'an, and Abu Bakr gave the task to Zayd, who collected it from what was written down and from the memories of the reciters. The pages were kept with Abu Bakr, then with 'Umar. Allah had promised: "Indeed, it is We who sent down the Reminder, and We are its guardian" (15:9). A Muslim sees in this care one way that promise was kept.

question: Which grandfather raised the Prophet ﷺ as a child?
explanation: His grandfather 'Abd al-Muttalib took charge of him after his birth.
detail: Every standard biography records that the Prophet's ﷺ father 'Abdullah died before he was born and his mother Amina while he was still a small boy, so his grandfather 'Abd al-Muttalib, a respected elder of Quraysh, took him into his care and kept him close. When the grandfather died, the boy passed to his uncle Abu Talib, who protected him all his life. The Qur'an recalls those years: "Did He not find you an orphan and give you shelter?" (93:6). A Muslim learns that Allah cared for His Prophet ﷺ through his own family.

question: How does the Qur'an recall the Prophet's ﷺ childhood?
answers: Allah found him an orphan and sheltered him
He lived alone in the desert
explanation: 'Did He not find you an orphan and give you shelter?' (93:6).
detail: The verse comes in Surah Ad-Duha, where Allah swears by the morning brightness and the still night and tells His Prophet ﷺ: "Your Lord has not forsaken you, nor does He hate you" (93:3). Then He counts three favours: "Did He not find you an orphan and give you shelter? And find you unaware and guide you? And find you poor and make you self-sufficient?" (93:6-8). The surah ends by asking him to pass the kindness on: do not oppress the orphan, do not turn away the one who asks (93:9-10). A Muslim learns that remembering Allah's help makes us gentle with others.

question: Which battle came after Badr?
explanation: The following year came the battle of Uhud, near Medina.
detail: The Qur'an speaks of Uhud in Surah Al 'Imran, right after naming Badr: "Allah had already given you victory at Badr when you were few" (3:123). It then turns to the morning the Prophet ﷺ went out to set the believers in their positions for battle (3:121), at the mountain of Uhud outside Medina. Every standard biography tells that the archers left the hill they were told to hold, the Prophet ﷺ was wounded, and his uncle Hamza was killed; the Qur'an adds that Allah forgave them (3:152). A Muslim learns that hardship after victory is also a test.

question: What did the Muslims dig around Medina to defend it?
explanation: They dug a trench, which gave the Battle of the Trench its name.
detail: Surah Al-Ahzab, the Confederates, keeps the memory of this battle: "Remember the favour of Allah upon you when armies came to you and We sent upon them a wind and armies you did not see" (33:9). The enemy tribes had joined together against Medina, and every standard biography records that the Muslims, with the Prophet ﷺ carrying earth beside them, dug a wide trench across the open side of the city so that horsemen could not cross. The Qur'an recalls the fear of those days, when "hearts reached the throats" (33:10). A Muslim learns that hard work goes together with trust in Allah's help.

question: Whose daughter was 'A'isha, the Prophet's ﷺ wife?
explanation: 'A'isha was the daughter of Abu Bakr as-Siddiq.
detail: 'A'isha was the daughter of Abu Bakr as-Siddiq, the Prophet's ﷺ closest friend and the first caliph after him. The Qur'an speaks of her father as the companion in the cave during the emigration: "the second of the two, when they were in the cave, when he said to his companion: do not grieve, indeed Allah is with us" (9:40). Every standard biography records that the Prophet ﷺ died in 'A'isha's room and was buried there, and that she taught the companions and passed on a great number of his words. A Muslim learns her name as a mother of the believers and a teacher.

question: What does the Qur'an call the Prophet's ﷺ wives?
explanation: 'And his wives are their mothers' (33:6).
detail: The full verse reads: "The Prophet is closer to the believers than their own selves, and his wives are their mothers" (33:6). It stands near the beginning of Surah Al-Ahzab, after Allah has said that calling an adopted boy someone's son does not make him a true son (33:4-5); here, by contrast, Allah Himself gives the Prophet's ﷺ wives the title of mothers. Later in the surah He says that no one may marry them after him (33:53). A Muslim honours Khadija, 'A'isha and the other wives of the Prophet ﷺ with the respect owed to a mother.

question: Which companion was both a cousin and a son-in-law of the Prophet ﷺ?
explanation: 'Ali, the Prophet's ﷺ cousin, married his daughter Fatima.
detail: Every standard biography records that 'Ali was the son of Abu Talib, the uncle who raised the Prophet ﷺ, that he grew up in the Prophet's ﷺ own household, and that he accepted Islam as a boy, among the very first. On the night of the emigration he slept in the Prophet's ﷺ bed so the watchers outside would think he was still there. In Medina he married Fatima, the Prophet's ﷺ daughter; their sons were al-Hasan and al-Husayn, and years later 'Ali became the fourth caliph. A Muslim remembers him as bound to the Prophet ﷺ by blood, by marriage and by faith.

question: What is the Prophet's ﷺ mosque in Medina called?
explanation: The Prophet's Mosque, an-Nabawi, stands in Medina.
detail: Every standard biography records that when the Prophet ﷺ arrived in Medina after the emigration, one of the first things he did was to build a mosque, working beside his companions. From it he led the five prayers, taught the Qur'an and received delegations, and when he died he was buried in the room of 'A'isha that opened onto it. Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim record his words that a prayer in his mosque is better than a thousand prayers anywhere else, except al-Masjid al-Haram. A Muslim who visits Medina prays there and sends his greeting of peace to the Prophet ﷺ.

question: What is the mount of the Prophet's ﷺ night journey called?
explanation: The mount of the night journey is called al-Buraq.
detail: The Qur'an tells of the journey: "Exalted is He who took His servant by night from al-Masjid al-Haram to al-Masjid al-Aqsa, whose surroundings We have blessed" (17:1). The account of the night journey in Sahih Muslim, in the words of Anas ibn Malik, gives the mount its name: the Prophet ﷺ said that al-Buraq was brought to him, a white animal larger than a donkey and smaller than a mule, which set its hoof down as far as its eye could see. The name comes from the Arabic word for lightning. A Muslim learns that the night journey was a real journey, with a real mount, granted by Allah.

question: How many pillars of Islam are there?
explanation: Five: the testimony of faith, prayer, zakat, fasting and pilgrimage.
detail: Ibn 'Umar reports in Sahih al-Bukhari 8 that the Prophet ﷺ named the five: the testimony that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, establishing the prayer, giving the zakat, the pilgrimage, and fasting Ramadan. The Qur'an speaks of each: "establish prayer and give zakat" (2:43), "decreed upon you is fasting" (2:183), and the pilgrimage owed to Allah by whoever can make the journey (3:97). The word pillar is used because a house cannot stand if one support is missing. A Muslim learns the five as one whole, not as a list to choose from.

question: What is the first pillar of Islam?
explanation: One enters Islam by testifying that there is no god but Allah and Muhammad ﷺ is His messenger.
detail: The shahada is spoken in Arabic: la ilaha illa Allah, Muhammadun rasul Allah. Its two halves are both in the Qur'an: "So know that there is no god but Allah" (47:19) and "Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah" (48:29). In Sahih al-Bukhari 8 the Prophet ﷺ names it first among the five pillars, and every Muslim repeats it in the sitting of every prayer, in the call to prayer, and as the words a person says to enter Islam. A Muslim learns that the whole religion begins with these two sentences: one Lord to worship, one messenger to follow.

question: How many obligatory prayers does a Muslim perform each day?
explanation: Five prayers, spread from dawn to night.
detail: Every Muslim performs the same five: Fajr before sunrise, Dhuhr after midday, 'Asr in the afternoon, Maghrib just after sunset and 'Isha at night. The Qur'an says: "Indeed, prayer has been decreed upon the believers at fixed times" (4:103), and: "Establish prayer from the decline of the sun until the darkness of the night, and the recitation of dawn" (17:78). Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim record, in the hadith of the night journey, that the prayers were first fifty and were reduced to five, with the reward of fifty kept. A Muslim learns that his day is shaped around five meetings with his Lord.
