sourceDisplay: Well-established practice — the five daily prayers

question: Which month do Muslims fast?
explanation: 'The month of Ramadan, in which the Qur'an was sent down' (2:185).
detail: The verse continues: "The month of Ramadan, in which the Qur'an was sent down as guidance for the people and clear proofs of guidance and the criterion. So whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it; and whoever is ill or on a journey, then an equal number of other days. Allah wants ease for you and does not want hardship for you" (2:185). Two verses earlier fasting is made a duty, as it was for the nations before (2:183). A Muslim learns that Ramadan is the month of the Book as much as the month of fasting, and that Allah's rule makes room for the sick and the traveller.

question: What is the obligatory almsgiving of Islam called?
explanation: Zakat is the share of one's wealth given each year.
detail: The word zakat means purification and growth, and the Qur'an joins it to prayer again and again: "Establish prayer and give zakat" (2:43). It also says who receives it: "Charity is only for the poor and the needy" and the other groups the verse names (9:60), and the Prophet ﷺ was told: "Take from their wealth a charity by which you purify them" (9:103). In Sahih al-Bukhari 8 it is counted among the five pillars of Islam. A Muslim learns that giving a share of what he owns makes the rest clean, and that the poor have a right in his wealth.

question: What is the major pilgrimage to Mecca called?
explanation: The hajj is the pilgrimage made once in a lifetime by those able to.
detail: The Qur'an makes the duty plain: "And due to Allah from the people is a pilgrimage to the House, for whoever is able to find a way to it" (3:97). It also tells how the call began, when Ibrahim was commanded: "Proclaim to the people the pilgrimage; they will come to you on foot and on every lean camel, from every distant pass" (22:27). Pilgrims wear simple white clothing, circle the Ka'ba, walk between Safa and Marwa, which the Qur'an counts among the symbols of Allah (2:158), and stand at 'Arafat (2:198). A Muslim who can travel makes the journey once, answering Ibrahim's call.

question: How many articles of faith (arkan al-iman) are there?
explanation: Belief in Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers, the Last Day and destiny.
detail: The six are named by the Prophet ﷺ himself in the hadith of Jibril, reported by 'Umar in Sahih Muslim 8: when Jibril came in the form of a man and asked him about iman, he answered that it is to believe in Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers, the Last Day, and in destiny, its good and its bad. The Qur'an lists most of them in one verse: "all of them believe in Allah, His angels, His books and His messengers" (2:285). A Muslim learns the six as the beliefs that stand behind the five pillars.

question: How many gods does a Muslim believe in?
explanation: 'Say: He is Allah, the One' (112:1).
detail: The surah has only four verses: "Say: He is Allah, the One. Allah, the Eternal Refuge. He neither begets nor is born, and there is none equal to Him" (112:1-4). It is called Al-Ikhlas, sincerity, because it speaks of nothing but Allah alone, and Sahih al-Bukhari records the Prophet ﷺ saying that it equals a third of the Qur'an. Every other verse that speaks of Allah agrees with it: "Your God is one God; there is no god but Him" (2:163). A Muslim learns the surah by heart as a small child, and with it the whole of his belief about Allah.

question: What do Muslims call God in Arabic?
explanation: Allah is the name of the Creator in Arabic.
detail: The name appears in the very first line of the Qur'an, "In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful" (1:1), and Allah uses it of Himself when He speaks to Musa: "Indeed, I am Allah; there is no god but Me, so worship Me" (20:14). The Qur'an also asks: "Do you know of anyone who shares His name?" (19:65), for no one else has ever been called Allah. His other names belong to Him too: "To Allah belong the most beautiful names" (7:180). A Muslim learns that Allah is not a title but His own name, in every language Muslims speak.

question: What is the Muslims' holy book called?
explanation: The Qur'an is the book revealed to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ.
detail: The Qur'an speaks of itself: "This is the Book about which there is no doubt, a guidance for those mindful of Allah" (2:2), and tells how it came: "The Trustworthy Spirit brought it down upon your heart, in a clear Arabic tongue" (26:193-195). Its name means the recitation, and its first revealed word was a command to read (96:1). It came down over the years of the Prophet's ﷺ mission, and Allah promised to guard it: "Indeed, it is We who sent down the Reminder, and We are its guardian" (15:9). A Muslim learns the Qur'an as the words of Allah, kept unchanged since they were revealed.

question: What is the House of Allah built in Mecca called?
explanation: 'The first House established for mankind is the one at Bakka' (3:96).
detail: The verse continues: "the first House established for mankind is the one at Bakka, blessed and a guidance for the worlds; in it are clear signs, the standing place of Ibrahim" (3:96-97). Bakka is Makka, and the Qur'an tells who raised the walls: "When Ibrahim was raising the foundations of the House, with Isma'il: our Lord, accept it from us" (2:127). Muslims everywhere turn towards it in prayer, as they were told: "Turn your face towards al-Masjid al-Haram" (2:144). A Muslim learns that the Ka'ba is not worshipped; it is the direction of worship and the House Ibrahim built for Allah alone.

question: What does a Muslim say before starting to eat?
explanation: The Prophet ﷺ taught a boy: 'Say Bismillah, and eat with your right hand.'
detail: 'Umar ibn Abi Salama tells the story himself in Sahih al-Bukhari 5376: he was a boy living in the Prophet's ﷺ house, and at meals his hand wandered all over the dish, so the Prophet ﷺ said to him, "Boy, say the name of Allah, eat with your right hand, and eat from what is nearest to you." He adds that this remained his way of eating ever after. The Qur'an tells the believers to "eat of the good things We have provided you and be grateful to Allah" (2:172). A Muslim learns table manners from the Prophet's ﷺ own words: Allah's name first, the right hand, the food in front of you.

question: How do Muslims greet one another?
explanation: 'As-salamu 'alaykum' means: peace be upon you.
detail: The greeting is in Arabic, as-salamu 'alaykum, and it is what the angels say to the people of Paradise: "Peace be upon you for what you patiently endured" (13:24). The Qur'an tells the believers: "When you enter houses, greet one another with a greeting from Allah, blessed and good" (24:61). Sahih Muslim records the Prophet ﷺ saying that the believers will not enter Paradise until they believe, nor believe until they love one another, and that spreading the salam among themselves brings that love. A Muslim learns that his greeting is a prayer for the other person's safety.

question: What is the reply to 'as-salamu 'alaykum'?
explanation: The greeting is returned: 'and upon you be peace'.
detail: The Qur'an sets the rule for every greeting: "When you are greeted with a greeting, greet with one better than it, or return it" (4:86). So the reply to as-salamu 'alaykum is wa 'alaykum as-salam, and the better reply adds wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh, and the mercy of Allah and His blessings. The verse ends: "Indeed, Allah keeps account of everything" (4:86), so even a greeting is counted. A Muslim learns to answer every salam he hears, and to add to it when he can.

question: What is the festival right after the month of Ramadan called?
explanation: 'Id al-Fitr, the festival of breaking the fast.
detail: The festival's name means the breaking of the fast, and it comes on the first day of Shawwal, the month after Ramadan. The Qur'an, after commanding the fast, says why the month ends in thanks: "so that you complete the number and glorify Allah for having guided you, and that you may be grateful" (2:185). On the morning of 'Id Muslims give a charity of food to the poor before the prayer, then gather for the 'Id prayer and visit one another. Sahih al-Bukhari records the Prophet ﷺ saying that every people has its festival and this is ours. A Muslim learns that a hard month ends in gratitude and sharing.

question: What is the festival of sacrifice called?
explanation: 'Id al-Adha falls during the days of the pilgrimage.
detail: The festival's name means the sacrifice, and it falls on the tenth day of Dhu al-Hijja, when the pilgrims at Mina offer their animals and Muslims everywhere do the same. It recalls Ibrahim, ready to sacrifice his son when Allah commanded it in a dream, until Allah called: "O Ibrahim, you have fulfilled the vision," and "We ransomed him with a great sacrifice" (37:104-107). The Qur'an says what the offering is for: "Their meat will not reach Allah, nor their blood, but what reaches Him is your piety" (22:37). A Muslim learns that the meat is shared with family and the poor, and that the real gift is obedience.

question: What are Allah's creatures who always obey Him and never disobey called?
explanation: The angels carry out what Allah commands and never disobey.
detail: The Qur'an describes the angels with these words: "They do not disobey Allah in what He commands them, and they do what they are commanded" (66:6), and again: "Those who are near Him are not too proud to worship Him, nor do they tire; they glorify Him night and day and never slacken" (21:19-20). They are made by Allah and sent as His messengers, with wings, two, three and four (35:1); Jibril brought the Qur'an down to the Prophet's ﷺ heart (2:97). A Muslim learns to believe in beings he cannot see, whose whole life is obedience to Allah.

question: What is Paradise called in Arabic?
explanation: Al-Janna, literally 'the garden', is the home promised to the believers.
detail: The Qur'an calls it a garden because it is full of trees and water: "gardens beneath which rivers flow" (2:25) is its most frequent description. It is "as wide as the heavens and the earth, prepared for the God-fearing" (3:133), and those who enter hear: "Enter it in peace, safe" (15:46). Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim record the Prophet ﷺ saying that Allah has prepared for His righteous servants what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has imagined. A Muslim learns to work for a home more beautiful than anything in this world.

question: What is the washing with water done before praying called?
explanation: Wudu' is the purification that comes before prayer.
detail: The Qur'an itself gives the steps: "O you who believe, when you rise for prayer, wash your faces and your hands up to the elbows, wipe your heads, and wash your feet up to the ankles" (5:6). The same verse says that Allah does not want to make things hard for you, but wants to purify you and complete His favour upon you. Sahih al-Bukhari records the Prophet ﷺ saying that the prayer of one who has lost his purity is not accepted until he performs wudu'. A Muslim learns that he comes to speak with his Lord clean, and that wudu' is the first part of the prayer.

question: What is one unit of the prayer called?
explanation: A rak'ah contains the standing, the bowing and the prostrations.
detail: The word rak'ah comes from ruku', the bowing, and the Qur'an calls the believers "those who bow and those who prostrate" (9:112) and commands: "O you who believe, bow and prostrate and worship your Lord" (22:77). One rak'ah runs in this order: standing with the recitation of al-Fatiha, bowing, standing again, prostrating, sitting, prostrating again. Every Muslim counts the prayers by their rak'ahs: Fajr has two, Maghrib three, and Dhuhr, 'Asr and 'Isha four each. A Muslim learns the rak'ah as the building block of the whole prayer.

question: Which surah is recited in every unit of prayer?
explanation: Al-Fatiha, the opening surah, is recited in every rak'ah.
detail: 'Ubada ibn as-Samit reports in Sahih al-Bukhari that the Prophet ﷺ said there is no prayer for one who does not recite the Opening of the Book. The Prophet ﷺ also called it, in Sahih al-Bukhari, the "seven of the oft-repeated" spoken of in the Qur'an (15:87), and it is repeated at least seventeen times a day across the five prayers. Its seven verses praise Allah, Lord of the worlds, and then ask Him: "You alone we worship and You alone we ask for help; guide us to the straight path" (1:5-6). A Muslim learns al-Fatiha first of all the surahs, because without it the prayer cannot be made.

question: What is that which is permitted in Islam called?
explanation: Halal means what is lawful.
detail: The Qur'an uses the word in its commands about food: "O mankind, eat of what is on the earth, lawful and good" (2:168), and: "Eat of what Allah has provided you, lawful and good, and be grateful for the favour of Allah" (16:114). It describes the Prophet ﷺ as one who "makes lawful for them the good things and forbids them the bad" (7:157). Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim record him saying that the halal is clear and the haram is clear. A Muslim learns that what Allah has allowed is wide and good, and that eating it with thanks is itself worship.

question: What is that which is forbidden in Islam called?
explanation: Haram means what is unlawful.
detail: The same root gives al-Masjid al-Haram, the sacred mosque, for haram first means what is set apart and not to be touched. The Qur'an tells the Prophet ﷺ: "Say: my Lord has only forbidden shameful deeds, open and hidden, and sin, and wrongful oppression, and that you associate with Allah what He has sent no authority for" (7:33). It also warns: "Do not say, about what your tongues falsely describe, this is lawful and this is unlawful" (16:116). A Muslim learns that only Allah decides what is haram, and that the list is short beside all that He permits.

question: Which meat does the Qur'an forbid?
explanation: 'He has forbidden you carrion, blood and the flesh of swine' (2:173).
detail: The verse reads in full: "He has only forbidden you carrion, blood, the flesh of swine, and what has been offered to other than Allah; but whoever is forced by need, without desiring it or going too far, there is no sin on him; indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful" (2:173). The verse before it opens with the wide permission: "eat of the good things We have provided you and be grateful to Allah" (2:172). The same four things are forbidden again in 6:145 and 16:115. A Muslim learns that the rule is clear and small, and that Allah lifts it for someone who has nothing else to eat.

question: Which drink does the Qur'an command us to avoid?
explanation: 'Wine, gambling… are an abomination, so avoid them' (5:90).
detail: The verse gives a list and a reason: "O you who believe, intoxicants, gambling, sacrificing at altars and divining arrows are only filth from the work of Satan, so avoid it that you may succeed" (5:90). The next verse explains what wine does: Satan uses it "to sow enmity and hatred among you and to keep you from the remembrance of Allah and from prayer" (5:91). The Arabic word khamr covers every drink that clouds the mind, and Sahih Muslim records the Prophet ﷺ saying that every intoxicant is khamr and every intoxicant is forbidden. A Muslim learns that the mind is a trust, kept clear for remembering Allah.

question: What does the one who sneezes say, as the Prophet ﷺ taught?
explanation: 'When one of you sneezes, let him say: al-hamdu lillah.'
detail: Abu Hurayra reports in Sahih al-Bukhari 6224 the whole exchange: when one of you sneezes, let him say al-hamdu lillah; let his brother or companion answer yarhamuk Allah, may Allah have mercy on you; and let the one who sneezed reply yahdikum Allah wa yuslih balakum, may Allah guide you and set your affairs right. So a sneeze becomes three short prayers passed between two people. The words al-hamdu lillah are the same that open al-Fatiha: "Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds" (1:2). A Muslim learns to thank Allah even for a sneeze, and to answer with a prayer for the one beside him.

question: How do you say 'the prayer' in Arabic?
explanation: As-salat is the Muslim's ritual prayer.
detail: The word salat is the Qur'an's own word for the prayer; Allah says to Musa: "Establish the prayer for My remembrance" (20:14). The Qur'an tells what it does for the one who prays: "Indeed, the prayer keeps one away from shameful and wrong deeds, and the remembrance of Allah is greater" (29:45), and it names it beside patience as the believer's help: "Seek help through patience and prayer" (2:45). The call to prayer uses the word too: hayya 'ala as-salah, come to the prayer. A Muslim learns that as-salat has set words and movements, different from the free asking of du'a.

question: What is asking Allah for something in your own words called?
explanation: Du'a is supplication, calling upon Allah.
detail: The Qur'an says the invitation comes from Allah Himself: "Your Lord says: call upon Me, I will answer you" (40:60), and: "When My servants ask you about Me, indeed I am near; I answer the call of the caller when he calls on Me" (2:186). The prophets prayed this way: Ibrahim asked, "My Lord, make me one who establishes prayer, and of my descendants too" (14:40), and Zakariyya called on his Lord in a low voice for a son (19:3-4). Du'a needs no set words, time or place, only a heart turned to Allah. A Muslim learns to speak to his Lord in his own words, sure that he is heard.

question: What does 'al-hamdu lillah' mean?
explanation: It is the second verse of al-Fatiha: 'Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds' (1:2).
detail: Al-Fatiha opens: "In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful. Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds" (1:1-2). Hamd is praise given with love and thanks, and verse 1:2 gives it to Allah because He is Lord of every world there is. The same words open four other surahs, Al-An'am, Al-Kahf, Saba and Fatir, and the Qur'an says they are the last words of the people of Paradise: "the end of their call is: praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds" (10:10). A Muslim says al-hamdu lillah after eating, after sneezing and when good news comes, and hears it in every rak'ah.

question: What does the word 'islam' mean?
explanation: Islam comes from a root meaning to submit and to be at peace.
detail: The root of the word gives salam, peace, and aslama, to hand oneself over. The Qur'an shows Ibrahim doing exactly that: "When his Lord said to him: submit, he said: I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds" (2:131). Allah names the religion with this word, "Indeed, the religion with Allah is Islam" (3:19), and during the Prophet's ﷺ pilgrimage the verse came down: "This day I have perfected your religion for you and chosen Islam for you as religion" (5:3). A Muslim learns that islam is the word Allah chose, meaning to give oneself to Him and find peace in it.

question: What does the word 'muslim' mean?
explanation: A muslim is one who submits to Allah alone.
detail: The Qur'an says who gave the name: "It is He who named you Muslims, before and in this" (22:78). Ibrahim and Isma'il prayed with the word while building the Ka'ba: "Our Lord, make us both submitting to You, and of our descendants a nation submitting to You" (2:128), and Ya'qub told his sons: "do not die except as Muslims" (2:132). The Qur'an says of Ibrahim that "he was not a Jew nor a Christian, but he was upright, a Muslim" (3:67). A Muslim learns that his name links him to every prophet who gave himself to Allah, long before the Prophet ﷺ was born.

question: Who created the heavens and the earth, according to the Qur'an?
explanation: 'Praise be to Allah, who created the heavens and the earth' (6:1).
detail: The surah opens with praise and its reason: "Praise be to Allah, who created the heavens and the earth and made the darkness and the light; yet those who disbelieve set up equals to their Lord" (6:1). The next verse turns to the human being: "It is He who created you from clay, then decreed a term" (6:2). Elsewhere the Qur'an says that He created the heavens and the earth in six days and then rose over the Throne (7:54), and that He has no partner in His dominion (25:2). A Muslim learns to look at the sky and the earth and answer with the words that open Surah Al-An'am.

question: How many names of Allah does the hadith mention?
explanation: 'Allah has ninety-nine names, one hundred less one.'
detail: Abu Hurayra reports in Sahih al-Bukhari 2736 that the Prophet ﷺ said Allah has ninety-nine names, one hundred less one, and that whoever learns them all by heart will enter Paradise. The Qur'an is where the names are found: "To Allah belong the most beautiful names, so call on Him by them" (7:180), and one passage gathers many of them: the King, the Holy, the Peace, the Creator, the Maker, the Fashioner (59:23-24). A Muslim learns the names from the Qur'an and calls on Allah by the one that fits his need: the Forgiving when he has erred, the Provider when he is in want.

question: What do the angels called 'noble scribes' do?
explanation: 'Noble scribes, who know whatever you do' (82:11-12).
detail: The verse names the angels "noble and writing" (82:11), and the verses around it complete the picture: "Indeed, over you are keepers" (82:10), "they know whatever you do" (82:12). They come in Surah Al-Infitar, just after Allah asks: "O man, what has deceived you about your generous Lord?" (82:6), and just before the surah says that the righteous will be in bliss and the wicked in the Fire (82:13-14). Surah Qaf adds that the two angels sit on the right and on the left, and that no word is spoken without a watcher ready beside him (50:17-18). A Muslim learns that nothing he does is lost, and that his own record will be shown to him.

question: Which night does the Qur'an describe as better than a thousand months?
explanation: 'The Night of Decree is better than a thousand months' (97:3).
detail: The surah is only five verses: "Indeed, We sent it down on the Night of Decree. And what will make you know what the Night of Decree is? The Night of Decree is better than a thousand months" (97:1-3). The next verses say that the angels and the Spirit come down in it with every matter, and that it is peace until dawn (97:4-5). What was sent down is the Qur'an, and Surah Al-Baqara places that sending in Ramadan (2:185). Sahih al-Bukhari records the Prophet ﷺ telling the believers to seek it in the odd nights of the last ten of Ramadan. A Muslim spends those nights in prayer, hoping to meet the night named in 97:3.

question: What is believing in one single God called?
explanation: Tawhid is the oneness of Allah, the heart of every prophet's message.
detail: The word comes from wahid, one, and means making Allah one: worshipping Him alone, with no partner. The Qur'an says every messenger was sent with this: "We sent no messenger before you without revealing to him: there is no god but Me, so worship Me" (21:25), and: "We sent to every nation a messenger, saying: worship Allah and shun false gods" (16:36). Its shortest statement is Surah Al-Ikhlas, "Say: He is Allah, the One" (112:1), and its daily statement is the first half of the shahada. A Muslim learns that tawhid is the one message Nuh, Ibrahim, Musa, 'Isa and Muhammad ﷺ all shared.

question: What is associating anyone with Allah in worship called?
explanation: Shirk is association: worshipping something alongside Allah.
detail: The word means making a partner, and the Qur'an treats it as the one wrong Allah says He does not forgive: "Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, but forgives what is less than that for whom He wills" (4:48). The wise man Luqman gave his son this as his first lesson: "O my son, do not associate anything with Allah; indeed, association is a great injustice" (31:13). The command is put simply elsewhere: "Worship Allah and associate nothing with Him" (4:36). A Muslim learns to keep every act of worship for Allah alone.

question: What is the day on which everyone will be judged called?
explanation: Yawm al-Qiyama, the Day of Resurrection, when everyone will see their deeds.
detail: The Qur'an swears by that Day: "I swear by the Day of Resurrection" (75:1), and gives it other names too: the Day of Judgement, the Hour, the Day of Reckoning. It tells what happens: "That Day people will come forward in separate groups to be shown their deeds. Whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it, and whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it" (99:6-8). The scales will be set up so that no soul is wronged (21:47), and every Muslim names the Day in each rak'ah, when al-Fatiha calls Allah "Master of the Day of Judgement" (1:4). A Muslim learns to live as one who will be shown his deeds.

question: How many months are in the year according to the Qur'an?
explanation: 'The number of months with Allah is twelve' (9:36).
detail: The verse says: "Indeed, the number of months with Allah is twelve months, in the decree of Allah from the day He created the heavens and the earth; of them, four are sacred" (9:36). The Muslim months follow the moon: the Qur'an says the crescents are "measures of time for the people and for the pilgrimage" (2:189), and that Allah made the moon's stages "so that you may know the number of years and the reckoning" (10:5). Ramadan is the ninth of the twelve, and Dhu al-Hijja, the month of the pilgrimage, the last. A Muslim learns that his calendar is counted by the new moon, and that four of its months are sacred.

question: How many prostrations are there in a single rak'ah?
explanation: Every rak'ah contains two prostrations.
detail: Every Muslim prays the same way: after bowing and standing straight again, he goes down to the ground, sits up, and goes down a second time before rising or sitting for the tashahhud. Sahih al-Bukhari records the Prophet ﷺ saying that he was commanded to prostrate on seven bones: the forehead with the nose, the two hands, the two knees and the toes of the two feet. The Qur'an closes Surah Al-'Alaq with the command "Prostrate and draw near" (96:19), and Sahih Muslim records the Prophet ﷺ saying that a servant is nearest to his Lord when prostrating. A Muslim learns that the two prostrations are the closest moments of the prayer.
sourceDisplay: Well-established practice — the form of the prayer

question: How many surahs does the Qur'an contain?
explanation: The Qur'an has 114 surahs, from al-Fatiha to an-Nas.
detail: Open any mushaf at its index and the count is there: one hundred and fourteen surahs, beginning with Al-Fatiha and ending with An-Nas. The Qur'an itself uses the word surah for its chapters, calling Surah An-Nur "a surah which We have sent down and made obligatory" (24:1), and it challenges doubters to "produce a surah like it" (2:23). Some surahs run to hundreds of verses and some to three. A Muslim who learns the number 114 learns the shape of the Book he will read all his life.

question: Which is the first surah of the Qur'an?
explanation: Al-Fatiha, 'the opening', is the first surah.
detail: Al-Fatiha stands at the head of every copy of the Qur'an, and every Muslim who prays recites it in each rak'ah, so it is the surah a child learns first. It gathers praise, "All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds" (1:2), a promise, "You alone we worship and You alone we ask for help" (1:5), and a request, "Guide us to the straight path" (1:6). Its name means the opening, because the Book opens with it. A Muslim opens his prayer with the same seven verses.

question: What does the word 'Qur'an' mean?
explanation: Qur'an comes from a root meaning to read and to recite.
detail: The Qur'an names itself with the very word for reciting. In Surah Al-Qiyama Allah says of the revelation: "Indeed, upon Us is its collection and its recitation (qur'anahu). So when We have recited it, then follow its recitation" (75:17-18). The first words sent down to the Prophet ﷺ were "Read, in the name of your Lord who created" (96:1), and the dawn prayer is called "the recitation of dawn" (17:78). A Muslim learns from the name itself that the Qur'an is a Book meant to be read aloud.

question: Over roughly how many years was the Qur'an sent down?
explanation: The revelation came down over some twenty-three years.
detail: The first verses came to the Prophet ﷺ in the cave of Hira when he was forty, and the last came shortly before he died at sixty-three; every standard biography counts those twenty-three years. The Qur'an explains why it did not come all at once: "a Qur'an which We have separated, that you may recite it to the people over a prolonged period" (17:106), and "that We may strengthen your heart thereby" (25:32). A Muslim learns that the Book came verse by verse, as the community needed it.

question: What is a verse of the Qur'an called?
explanation: Each numbered sentence of the Qur'an is an aya, a 'sign'.
detail: The word aya means a sign, and the Qur'an uses it for two things at once: the signs Allah places in creation, "And of His signs is the creation of the heavens and the earth" (30:22), and the sentences of the Book, "a Book whose verses (ayat) are perfected" (11:1). Each aya carries a number in the mushaf, so a verse can be found as 2:255 or 112:1. A Muslim learns that every verse he reads is called a sign because it points him to Allah.

question: What is a chapter of the Qur'an called?
explanation: The Qur'an is divided into surahs, each with its own name.
detail: The Qur'an uses the word surah for its own chapters. It says of Surah An-Nur: "A surah which We have sent down and made obligatory" (24:1), and to those who doubted the Book: "Then bring ten surahs like it" (11:13). Each surah takes its name from something inside it: Al-Baqara from the cow Musa's people were told to sacrifice (2:67), Al-Kahf from the cave of the young men (18:9). A Muslim finds his way around the Qur'an by these one hundred and fourteen names.

question: Which is the longest surah in the Qur'an?
explanation: Al-Baqara is the longest surah in the Qur'an.
detail: Al-Baqara, the second surah, has 286 verses, more than any other. Its name comes from the cow that Musa's people were commanded to sacrifice (2:67). It holds the Verse of the Throne (2:255) and the longest single verse of the Qur'an, the verse on writing down a debt (2:282). It closes with the prayer: "Our Lord, do not burden us with more than we can bear" (2:286). A Muslim who reads it meets law, stories and prayer in one surah.

question: Which is the shortest surah in the Qur'an?
explanation: Al-Kawthar has only three verses.
detail: Al-Kawthar is surah 108, and the whole of it can be recited in one breath: "Indeed, We have granted you al-Kawthar. So pray to your Lord and sacrifice. Indeed, your enemy is the one cut off" (108:1-3). It is addressed to the Prophet ﷺ, and it turns a gift into a duty: because Allah has given, the Prophet ﷺ is to pray and sacrifice for Him alone. A Muslim learns from its three verses that the answer to a gift from Allah is worship.

question: Which sentence opens almost every surah?
answers: In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate
There is no god but Allah
explanation: The basmala opens 113 of the 114 surahs.
detail: The basmala, "In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate", stands at the head of every surah except At-Tawba, so a reader meets it 113 times. It also appears inside a surah, opening the letter Sulayman sent to the queen of Saba': "Indeed, it is from Sulayman, and indeed, it is: In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate" (27:30). The first revelation began with Allah's name too (96:1). A Muslim says the basmala before reading, eating and beginning any task.

question: Whose speech is the Qur'an?
explanation: The Qur'an calls itself 'the speech of Allah' (kalam Allah) in 9:6.
detail: The verse belongs to the opening of Surah At-Tawba, where Allah sets out how the believers are to deal with the polytheists of Makkah: "And if any one of the polytheists seeks your protection, then grant him protection so that he may hear the words of Allah; then deliver him to his place of safety" (9:6). Even an enemy is kept safe so that he can listen, because what he hears is the speech of Allah Himself. A Muslim handles the Qur'an with care because he holds Allah's own words.

question: Into how many parts (juz') is the Qur'an divided?
explanation: The Qur'an is divided into thirty juz', one for each night of Ramadan.
detail: Every printed mushaf marks the thirty ajza' in its margins, so a reader can measure his progress. The division follows the Qur'an's own instruction: "So recite what is easy of the Qur'an" (73:20). Ramadan is "the month in which the Qur'an was sent down" (2:185), and one juz' a night finishes the Book by its end. A Muslim keeps the whole Qur'an in his life a portion at a time.

question: Which surah bears a woman's name?
explanation: Surah 19 carries the name of Maryam.
detail: Surah 19 tells Maryam's story from inside her own life: "And mention in the Book Maryam, when she withdrew from her family to a place toward the east" (19:16), the angel's news of a pure boy, and her return carrying 'Isa, who spoke from the cradle (19:29-30). Elsewhere the angels say to her: "O Maryam, indeed Allah has chosen you and purified you and chosen you above the women of the worlds" (3:42). A Muslim learns her name as a surah he can read.

question: What are the last two surahs, used to seek refuge, called?
explanation: Al-Falaq and An-Nas are called al-Mu'awwidhatan, 'the two of refuge'.
detail: The two surahs are twins in their opening words. Al-Falaq begins: "Say, I seek refuge in the Lord of daybreak" (113:1), and An-Nas begins: "Say, I seek refuge in the Lord of mankind" (114:1). The Arabic verb for seeking refuge, a'udhu, gives them their shared name, al-Mu'awwidhatan. Al-Falaq asks protection from darkness, from those who blow on knots and from the envier; An-Nas asks protection from the whisperer who retreats. A Muslim recites the two of them for safety, and they close the whole Qur'an.

question: Which word opens Surah al-Fatiha, after the basmala?
explanation: 'Al-hamdu lillahi rabbi l-'alamin' opens al-Fatiha.
detail: After the basmala, the first verse of Al-Fatiha reads: "All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds" (1:2). Al-hamdu means praise and thanks together, and the Qur'an opens with it before any request is made. Four other surahs begin with the same words, Al-An'am (6:1), Al-Kahf (18:1), Saba' (34:1) and Fatir (35:1), and the people of Paradise end their prayer with them: "praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds" (10:10). A Muslim learns to put praise before asking, exactly in the order of the Fatiha.

question: What is the explanation of the Qur'an's meaning called?
explanation: Tafsir is the science that explains the meaning of the verses.
detail: Tafsir is the work of explaining what a verse means: its words, the story behind it, and how its parts fit together. The Qur'an itself uses the word when it says that Allah answers every objection with "the truth and the best explanation (tafsir)" (25:33). The Prophet ﷺ was the first to explain the Book, as Allah told him: "that you may make clear to the people what was sent down to them" (16:44). A Muslim reads tafsir so that the verses he recites become verses he understands.

question: Which surah does not begin with the basmala?
explanation: At-Tawba is the only surah that does not open with the basmala.
detail: Surah At-Tawba, the ninth surah, begins straight away with its first verse, without the basmala: "A declaration of disassociation from Allah and His Messenger to those with whom you had made a treaty among the polytheists" (9:1). A reader who finishes Al-Anfal moves directly into At-Tawba with no line of separation. The surah is also known as Bara'a, from that first word; its name At-Tawba comes from the verses in which Allah turns in mercy to the believers (9:117-118). A Muslim recognises the surah by its missing basmala.

question: What is someone who recites the Qur'an aloud called?
explanation: The qari' is the reciter of the Qur'an.
detail: The word qari' comes from the same root as Qur'an, qara'a, to read or recite, so the reciter's name and the Book's name are cousins. The first command given to the Prophet ﷺ was exactly this: "Read" (96:1). The Qur'an also tells how the reading should be done: "And recite the Qur'an with measured recitation" (73:4), and how it should be received: "So when the Qur'an is recited, then listen to it and pay attention" (7:204). A Muslim who learns to recite well becomes a qari' in his own home.

question: In which surah is the Verse of the Throne found?
explanation: The Verse of the Throne is verse 255 of Surah al-Baqara.
detail: The verse reads: "Allah, there is no deity except Him, the Ever-Living, the Sustainer of all existence. Neither drowsiness overtakes Him nor sleep. To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. His Throne extends over the heavens and the earth, and their preservation tires Him not. And He is the Most High, the Most Great" (2:255). A Muslim learns Ayat al-Kursi by heart as one verse that describes Allah completely.

question: What does 'An-Nur', the title of surah 24, mean?
explanation: An-Nur means 'the light'.
detail: Surah 24 takes its name from a verse in its middle: "Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth. The example of His light is like a niche within which is a lamp, the lamp within a glass, the glass as if it were a brilliant star" (24:35). The same verse ends: "Allah guides to His light whom He wills" (24:35), and the next describes houses in which His name is remembered morning and evening (24:36). A Muslim thinks of guidance as a light that Allah gives.

question: Which surah is named 'The Most Merciful'?
explanation: Surah 55 is called Ar-Rahman.
detail: Surah 55 opens with the name itself and lists what the Most Merciful has done: "The Most Merciful. Taught the Qur'an. Created man. Taught him speech" (55:1-4). It then goes through the sun and moon, the sea, the fruits and Paradise, and after each gift asks the same question thirty-one times: "So which of the favours of your Lord would you deny?" (55:13). Ar-Rahman is one of the two names of mercy in the basmala. A Muslim learns to look at the world as a list of favours.

question: Which surah is named after the cave?
explanation: Al-Kahf means 'the cave'.
detail: Surah 18 is named after the cave in which a group of young believers took shelter from a king who opposed their faith: "When the youths retreated to the cave and said, 'Our Lord, grant us from Yourself mercy'" (18:10). Allah made them sleep, and the Qur'an gives their stay as three hundred years and nine (18:25). The same surah tells of Musa's journey with a servant of Allah given knowledge (18:65), and of Dhul-Qarnayn (18:83). A Muslim reads Al-Kahf and finds stories of faith kept safe through hardship.

question: What does 'An-Nisa'', the title of surah 4, mean?
explanation: An-Nisa' means 'the women'.
detail: Surah 4 is named An-Nisa', the women, because so many of its verses deal with the rights of women, orphans and families. It opens with the origin of every human being: "O mankind, fear your Lord, who created you from one soul and created from it its mate, and dispersed from both of them many men and women" (4:1). It gives women a fixed share of inheritance (4:7). A Muslim learns that a whole surah stands guard over the rights of women.

question: What does 'Al-Ma'ida', the title of surah 5, mean?
explanation: Al-Ma'ida means 'the table spread'.
detail: The name comes from the last story in surah 5, when the disciples of 'Isa asked: "O 'Isa, son of Maryam, can your Lord send down to us a table from the heaven?" (5:112). 'Isa prayed: "O Allah, our Lord, send down to us a table from the heaven to be for us a festival and a sign from You" (5:114), and Allah answered that He would send it. A Muslim learns that a table of food can be a sign from Allah.

question: Which prophet gives his name to surah 71?
explanation: Surah 71 is called Nuh.
detail: Surah 71 is given wholly to Nuh and his people. It begins: "Indeed, We sent Nuh to his people, saying, 'Warn your people before there comes to them a painful punishment'" (71:1), and lets Nuh tell of his long effort: "My Lord, indeed I invited my people night and day, but my invitation increased them only in flight" (71:5-6). The surah ends with his prayer for his parents and every believer who entered his house (71:28). A Muslim learns from Surah Nuh what patience in calling to Allah looks like.

question: How many verses does Surah al-Fatiha have?
explanation: Al-Fatiha has seven verses.
detail: The seven verses of Al-Fatiha are short enough to count on one hand, and every Muslim recites them in each rak'ah of every prayer. They move from praise of Allah, "Lord of the worlds" (1:2), "the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate" (1:3), "Master of the Day of Judgement" (1:4), to a promise, "You alone we worship and You alone we ask for help" (1:5), to a request, "Guide us to the straight path" (1:6). A Muslim who prays five times a day says these seven verses at least seventeen times.

question: Where does the Qur'an say it is preserved?
explanation: 'It is a glorious Qur'an, on a Guarded Tablet' (85:21-22).
detail: The words close Surah Al-Buruj: "But this is a glorious Qur'an" (85:21), "in a Preserved Tablet" (85:22). The surah has just told of the people of the ditch, believers burned for their faith, and warned those who deny the truth (85:19-20); then it declares that the Book they reject is kept safe with Allah. Another surah says: "Indeed, it is We who sent down the message, and indeed, We will be its guardian" (15:9). A Muslim learns that the Qur'an in his hands is protected by its Sender.

question: Which surah is named after the moon?
explanation: Al-Qamar means 'the moon'.
detail: Surah 54 opens with the moon itself: "The Hour has come near, and the moon has split" (54:1). It then recalls the peoples who denied their messengers, and after each story repeats the same invitation: "And We have certainly made the Qur'an easy for remembrance, so is there any who will remember?" (54:17), four times in all. A Muslim learns from Al-Qamar that the Qur'an is made easy to learn, and that the moon was a sign given to make people remember.

question: Which surah is named after the Day of Resurrection?
explanation: Surah 75 is called Al-Qiyama.
detail: Surah 75 opens with an oath on the day it is named for: "I swear by the Day of Resurrection" (75:1). It answers those who doubt that a scattered body can be brought back: "Does man think that We will not assemble his bones? Yes, We are able even to proportion his fingertips" (75:3-4). In its middle it tells the Prophet ﷺ not to hurry his tongue with the revelation, because its collection is upon Allah (75:16-17). A Muslim learns that Allah, who made the fingertips, can remake the whole.

question: Which prophet gives his name to surah 14?
explanation: Surah 14 is called Ibrahim.
detail: Surah 14 carries Ibrahim's name because it holds his long prayer for Makkah and his family. He asks: "My Lord, make this city secure and keep me and my sons away from worshipping idols" (14:35), and explains: "Our Lord, I have settled some of my descendants in an uncultivated valley near Your sacred House" (14:37). He thanks Allah for Isma'il and Ishaq given in old age (14:39) and asks that his descendants keep up the prayer (14:40). A Muslim learns Ibrahim's prayer as the beginning of the story of Makkah.

question: What does 'Al-Hadid', the title of surah 57, mean?
explanation: Al-Hadid means 'the iron'.
detail: Surah 57 takes its name from a verse that counts iron among Allah's gifts: "And We sent down iron, in which is great strength and benefits for the people" (57:25). The same verse says that Allah sent the messengers with clear proofs, the Scripture and the balance, so that people would stand up for justice. The surah opens: "Whatever is in the heavens and the earth exalts Allah" (57:1). A Muslim learns that even the iron in a nail is among the favours of Allah.

question: How does the Qur'an tell us to speak to our parents?
answers: With respectful words, not even saying 'uff'
explanation: 'Do not say to them uff, and speak to them a noble word' (17:23).
detail: The verse comes in Surah Al-Isra, joined to the command to worship Allah alone: "Whether one or both of them reach old age with you, say not to them a word of annoyance and do not repel them, but speak to them a noble word" (17:23). The next verse adds a prayer: "My Lord, have mercy upon them as they brought me up when I was small" (17:24). A Muslim learns that even the smallest sound of impatience is too much for a parent.

question: What is a gift given freely, out of kindness, called?
explanation: Sadaqa is voluntary charity, small or large.
detail: The Qur'an uses the word sadaqa for what a person gives from his own wish. It says: "If you disclose your charities, it is good; but if you conceal them and give them to the poor, it is better for you" (2:271), and pictures such a gift as a seed that grows seven ears (2:261). Unlike zakat, sadaqa has no set amount and no set time. A Muslim learns that a coin, a meal or a shared toy given for Allah's sake all count as sadaqa.

question: What does the Prophet ﷺ advise about speech, for whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day?
answers: Let him say something good or stay silent
Let him speak only to his family
explanation: 'Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him say what is good or keep silent.'
detail: The hadith recorded in Sahih al-Bukhari 6018 joins three duties to one condition: the Prophet ﷺ said that whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day should not harm his neighbour, should honour his guest, and should say what is good or keep silent. The Qur'an gives the same weight to words: "Not a word does he utter except that with him is an observer prepared" (50:18). A Muslim learns to test a sentence before saying it: if it is not good, silence is better.

question: How did the Prophet ﷺ tell us to treat our neighbour?
explanation: 'Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him be generous to his neighbour.'
detail: The hadith recorded in Sahih al-Bukhari 6015 belongs to the chapter of good manners in which the Prophet ﷺ tied kindness to the neighbour to belief in Allah and the Last Day, beside honouring the guest and speaking good or keeping silent. The Qur'an had already set the neighbour among those owed kindness: "to parents do good, and to relatives, orphans, the needy, the near neighbour, the neighbour farther away" (4:36). A Muslim learns that the family next door has a claim on him that his faith demands.

question: Who is Allah with, according to the Qur'an?
explanation: 'Indeed, Allah is with the patient' (2:153).
detail: The verse gives the believers two helpers together: "O you who have believed, seek help through patience and prayer. Indeed, Allah is with the patient" (2:153). Two verses later Allah says what the patience is for: "We will surely test you with something of fear and hunger, but give good tidings to the patient, who, when disaster strikes them, say, 'Indeed we belong to Allah, and indeed to Him we will return'" (2:155-156). A Muslim learns that being patient is not being alone.

question: What does the Qur'an forbid doing to the orphan?
explanation: 'So as for the orphan, do not oppress him' (93:9).
detail: Surah Ad-Duha is addressed to the Prophet ﷺ himself, and just before this command Allah reminds him of his own childhood: "Did He not find you an orphan and give you refuge?" (93:6). Then come three instructions that answer three gifts: "So as for the orphan, do not oppress him. And as for the one who asks, do not repel him. But as for the favour of your Lord, speak of it" (93:9-11). A Muslim learns that whoever received kindness when small owes it to the orphan in his turn.

question: Which kind of speech does the Qur'an tell us to avoid?
explanation: 'And avoid false speech' (22:30).
detail: The command comes among the verses of Surah Al-Hajj that describe the pilgrimage: "So avoid the uncleanliness of idols and avoid false speech" (22:30). A lie is placed in the same sentence as an idol, as something a believer keeps well away from. The Qur'an praises the servants of the Most Merciful as those "who do not witness falsehood" (25:72), and commands: "be with those who are true" (9:119). A Muslim learns that telling the truth is part of keeping his worship clean.

question: Along with the close relative, who does the Qur'an tell us to give their due?
explanation: 'Give the relative his due, and the poor, and the traveller' (17:26).
detail: The verse follows straight after the verses on parents in Surah Al-Isra: "And give the relative his right, and the poor and the traveller, and do not spend wastefully" (17:26). The next verse explains why waste is named alongside giving: "Indeed, the wasteful are brothers of the devils" (17:27). Wealth is to travel outward, to family first, then to the poor and the stranger far from home. A Muslim learns that what he gives is called a right, something owed, not a favour.

question: What does Allah promise to the one who thanks Him?
explanation: 'If you are grateful, I will surely increase you' (14:7).
detail: The promise is recalled by Musa to his people in Surah Ibrahim. He reminds them how Allah saved them from Pharaoh's people (14:6), then repeats what their Lord had declared: "If you are grateful, I will surely increase you; but if you deny, indeed, My punishment is severe" (14:7). The word for giving thanks, shukr, is the same word by which the Qur'an calls the family of Dawud to "work in gratitude" (34:13). A Muslim says al-hamdu lillah for what he has because the Qur'an ties thankfulness to receiving more.

question: How do you say 'patience' in Arabic?
explanation: As-sabr is steadfastness in hardship and in obedience.
detail: The Qur'an names sabr again and again as the believer's strength. "O you who have believed, seek help through patience and prayer" (2:153); "Indeed, the patient will be given their reward without account" (39:10); and to the Prophet ﷺ: "And be patient, and your patience is not but through Allah" (16:127). Luqman gives it to his son as advice: "be patient over what befalls you" (31:17). A Muslim learns as-sabr as a word to say to himself when something is hard.

question: What is remembering Allah, repeating His praise, called?
explanation: Dhikr is the remembrance of Allah with tongue and heart.
detail: The Qur'an asks for dhikr in many verses and promises what comes of it. "So remember Me; I will remember you" (2:152); "O you who have believed, remember Allah with much remembrance" (33:41); and: "Verily, in the remembrance of Allah do hearts find rest" (13:28). In daily practice, dhikr is the subhan Allah, al-hamdu lillah and Allahu akbar said after every prayer; it needs no place, no time and no wealth.

question: Which is the first month of the Islamic year?
explanation: The hijri year opens with the month of Muharram.
detail: The Islamic calendar counts its years from the Prophet's ﷺ migration from Makkah to Madinah, which is why it is called hijri, and each year begins with Muharram, as any hijri calendar shows. The Qur'an fixes the number of months: "Indeed, the number of months with Allah is twelve months in the register of Allah; of these, four are sacred" (9:36). Muharram is one of those four, and its name itself means sacred. A Muslim learns that his year opens with a month set apart for peace.

question: What is turning back to Allah after a sin called?
explanation: Tawba is repentance: to regret, to stop, and to return to Allah.
detail: The Qur'an calls for tawba and promises that it is accepted. "O you who have believed, repent to Allah with sincere repentance" (66:8); "Indeed, Allah loves those who are constantly repentant" (2:222); and to those who fear it is too late: "do not despair of the mercy of Allah. Indeed, Allah forgives all sins" (39:53). The first tawba in the Qur'an is Adam's: "Then Adam received from his Lord some words, and He accepted his repentance" (2:37). A Muslim learns that no sin closes the door back to Allah.

question: Who provides for every creature on earth?
explanation: 'There is no creature on earth but that its provision is due from Allah' (11:6).
detail: The verse opens a passage of Surah Hud on how completely Allah knows His creation: "And there is no creature on earth but that upon Allah is its provision, and He knows its place of dwelling and place of storage. All is in a clear register" (11:6). The word dabba covers every animal that moves on the ground, the ant as much as the camel; Allah provides for each one (29:60). A Muslim works for his living while trusting that provision comes from Allah.

question: In which city is the pilgrimage performed?
explanation: The hajj takes place in Mecca and its holy sites.
detail: The Qur'an names the city and its House: "Indeed, the first House established for mankind was that at Bakkah, blessed and a guidance for the worlds," and in the next verse: "due to Allah from the people is a pilgrimage to the House for whoever is able to find a way" (3:96-97). Ibrahim and Isma'il raised its foundations (2:127), and the Qur'an also speaks of "the valley of Makkah" (48:24). A Muslim turns towards Makkah five times a day and hopes to travel there once.

question: What is someone performing the pilgrimage called?
explanation: The pilgrim is called a hajj.
detail: The Arabic word hajj names the pilgrimage, and the one who performs it is called a hajj, or hajji, from the same root. The Qur'an tells Ibrahim: "And proclaim to the people the hajj; they will come to you on foot and on every lean camel, coming from every distant pass" (22:27), and fixes its season: "The hajj is during well-known months" (2:197). After returning home, a pilgrim is often addressed by that title. A Muslim learns the word as a name of honour earned by answering Ibrahim's call.

question: What does Allah know, according to the Qur'an, even if it is hidden?
explanation: 'Whether you conceal what is in your breasts or reveal it, Allah knows it' (3:29).
detail: The verse comes early in Surah Al 'Imran: "Say, whether you conceal what is in your breasts or reveal it, Allah knows it. And He knows that which is in the heavens and that which is on the earth" (3:29). Another surah says Allah is closer to a person than his jugular vein (50:16). A Muslim learns that a thought kept inside is already known, so the heart deserves as much care as the tongue.

question: Upon whom was fasting prescribed, according to the Qur'an?
answers: Upon the believers, as upon those before them
explanation: 'O you who believe, fasting is prescribed for you as it was for those before you' (2:183).
detail: The verse is the first of a group in Surah Al-Baqara that lays down the fast: "O you who have believed, fasting is prescribed for you as it was prescribed for those before you, that you may become righteous" (2:183). The verses that follow name the month, "the month of Ramadan in which was revealed the Qur'an" (2:185), and the hours, from the white thread of dawn until the night (2:187). A Muslim learns that when he fasts he joins a line of believers reaching back long before him.

question: What is the great Friday congregational prayer called?
explanation: Salat al-jumu'a gathers the Muslims at midday on Friday.
detail: Surah Al-Jumu'a commands the Friday prayer: "O you who have believed, when the call is made for the prayer on the day of Jumu'a, hasten to the remembrance of Allah and leave trade" (62:9). The next verse releases the people afterwards: "And when the prayer has been concluded, disperse within the land and seek from the bounty of Allah" (62:10). In every mosque a sermon comes first, then two rak'ahs in place of Dhuhr. A Muslim learns Friday as the day the neighbourhood prays together.

question: How do you say 'fasting' in Arabic?
explanation: As-sawm is fasting, the fourth pillar of Islam.
detail: The Qur'an commands the fast with this word: "O you who have believed, fasting (as-siyam) is prescribed for you" (2:183), and fixes its month: "whoever sights the month, let him fast it" (2:185). The root of the word means to hold back, and the Qur'an uses it in that sense for Maryam too: "I have vowed to the Most Merciful a fast (sawm), so I will not speak today to any person" (19:26). A Muslim learns that as-sawm means holding back from food and drink for the sake of Allah.
